Sports.title: Featured Comment: Budget cap not to blame for lack of winning teams in F1 | Brief
Sports.content:
This week’s poll asks whether Formula 1 needs to rethink its budget cap as the series’ top four team have pulled further away from their rivals this year.

But reader @Skydiverian suggests it might not be realistic to expect F1 to regularly have more than four race-winning teams:

Four competitive teams has happened before but it’s still not great and the problem is as it always is, money. And I’d like to see more teams in a season have a realistic shot of winning races. It’s unfortunate that the stats are not on my side.

Pretty much since the late 80s the problem has been that the best teams could throw more money at the problem to fix it. Now, teams that are significantly behind can’t throw more money at the problem to catch-up due to the cost cap, rather than simply not having the money in the first place as was common in the 80s. (This season is interesting. It seems that Mercedes blew most of it’s cap early to get and maintain their advantage, whereas Red Bull didn’t and that’s in part why Max has had a better car the last two races. But it’s not like Williams or Aston Martin can fix their problems by spending more money to fix the deficit).

The problem is that ultimately there’s no easy fix, but spending millions to be the so-called best of the rest basically seems pointless if there is a very unlikely chance of a team outside of the top four having a realistic shot at the podium or even a win. And that’s always been a problem going back decades.

Some number crunching by looking at the history books: the 500th race was 1990 Australia, 1,100th being Vegas 2023. In those 600 races I’ve found six that were won by drivers driving for teams who finished outside the top four in the constructors championship.

That’s six of 600 races over 33 years where we had a winner driving for a team who finished outside the top 4 in that years constructors championship, 1% of all races. Seven if you count Johnny Herbert’s win at the Nurburgring which to me was a genuine surprise at the time. To me those stats aren’t good enough.

Whether that’s the fault of teams with no money, teams with too much money or teams with a cash limit so they can’t design their way out is up for debate. But my point is that I’d like to see more teams have a reasonable chance of winning. F1 has never really had that and will continue not to unless something changes (maybe by letting teams further down have a bigger budget the following season rather than just more CFD time).

I’d rather that at least 70% of drivers have a realistic chance of winning, ideally 100% of teams. It’s the reason I preferred IndyCar before Alex Palou showed up, results were unpredictable and smaller teams have a chance of getting a win or two. That’s just so rare in F1 and the current cost cap rules will continue to make unlikely.

@Skydiverian

Sports.title: Early coronation for Antonelli? Five talking points for the United States Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli could win the world championship this weekend in only his second year as a Formula 1 driver. Here are the talking points for the United States Grand Prix.

Will Antonelli clinch the title?

The odds are stacked heavily in favour of Mercedes’ new star clinching the title at some point, but most likely not this weekend. That said it is not beyond the realm of possibility team mate George Russell could have another poor weekend and come away point-less while Antonelli takes his ninth victory of the season, putting him over the line.

The title has been won at this track twice before, and both times it was by a Mercedes druver: Lewis Hamilton won the championship there in 2015 and 2019. But regardless of whether Antonelli does clinch the title this weekend it is clearly a matter of ‘when’ not ‘if’.

Verstappen dominating again?

The driver most likely to delay Antonelli’s championship celebrations is not his team mate but Max Verstappen. Red Bull have made a breakthrough with their RB22 and as well as winning the last two grands prix plus a sprint race, Verstappen could have taken victory in Baku as well with better luck.

He arrives at this weekend’s race looking like the driver to beat, with every indication he could dominate the final rounds of the season, setting himself up for a shot at the title next year.

McLaren’s driver headache

McLaren arrive in Austin in a curiously similar situation to last year: a clash between their drivers at the previous race in Singapore has created an obvious tension. What’s more, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s collision during the sprint race in Singapore was more costly than the one they had in the grand prix 12 months ago.

Norris’s radio messages during the grand prix gave the distinction impression he was looking for ways to make amends, having eventually accepted he was the one at fault for their collision. But above all the team will be anxious to avoid a repeat of the first-corner collision which wrecked their sprint race at the circuit 12 months ago. Particularly as a resurgent Red Bull are poised to relegate the reigning constructors’ champions to fourth place in the standings.

US teams’ driver decisions

Of the two teams competing in their home event this weekend, one has settled its driver plans for 2027. Haas has announced Rafael Camara as the replacement for Esteban Ocon, whose Formula 1 future is in serious doubt as few likely alternatives remain for next year.

Could Cadillac be one of them? F1’s new American team is yet to confirm its plans for next year. However its hopes IndyCar star Colton Herta would take Formula 2 by storm and make himself an obvious candidate for promotion have been dashed: he lies 19th in the standings, 181 points behind fellow rookie and championship leader Camara.

Are Colapinto’s die-hards paying attention?

Last week Franco Colapinto spoke out in criticism of the element of his fanbase which has sent vile abuse to his rival drivers, team members and FIA officials since he made his F1 debut this year. The Alpine driver told those attacking others in his name that they are not helping his cause in F1.

Will they take his words on board? We’ll get an indication the next time he is involved in any kind of incident on-track – however slight it may be.

Are you going to the United States Grand Prix?

If you’re heading to USA for this weekend’s race, we want to hear from you:

Who do you think will be the team to beat in the United States Grand Prix? Have your say below.

Sports.title: On This Day: Ralf Schumacher wins Formula Nippon title despite spinning out | Brief
Sports.content:
30 years ago today Ralf Schumacher won the Formula Nippon title despite retiring two laps into a rain-lashed race.

Schumacher arrived at the final race at Fuji Speedway just two points ahead of team mate Naoki Hattori. But Schumacher spun out two laps into the rain-hit race (see 3’50 in the video below).

That left Hattori on course for the title, which looked increasingly secure as the laps ticked down. But conditions worsened, and seven laps from home he spun out too, handing Schumacher the 1996 title. Schumacher made his F1 debut the following year for Jordan (now Aston Martin).

Katsutomo Kaneishi won ahead of future Formula 1 driver Pedro de la Rosa. Another future F1 driver, Shinji Nakano, took fourth place behind Masahiko Kageyama. Just seven of the 26 starters were running at the finish.

Sports.title: Jaron Ennis Calls Sebastian Fundora Too Small
Sports.content:
Jaron Ennis laughed off Sebastian Fundora’s knockout claims, calling the towering champion “too small” to back up his words. Ennis is eyeing Fundora down the line, but he’s making sure business with Josh Kelly gets handled first.

That comment flips the script on Fundora. Opponents usually spend training camp obsessing over his massive reach, but Ennis seems far more eager to exploit openings than worry about incoming fire.

“He too small. He not big enough,” Ennis said to YSM Sports Media when told about Fundora’s knockout comments. “But we focused on Josh Kelly, and that’s the main focus, main target right now. We’ll talk about him later on.”

Ennis kept a close eye on Fundora’s clash with Ermal Hadribeaj, scouting for future business rather than just watching for fun.

“Definitely watching to pick him apart,” Ennis said. “Just to see what he got, and it’s what I’ve been knew.”

Fundora didn’t dial back his confidence at the post-fight presser either. When reporters brought up potential bouts with Ennis or Vergil Ortiz Jr., he insisted he’d halt both.

“If it was those guys, I’d still knock them out,” Fundora said. “These guys can’t hurt me.”

That confidence would face a different examination against Ennis. Choosing to fight inside is one thing against Hadribeaj; giving Ennis opportunities at close range would require Fundora to account for his speed and combinations.

Ennis even took a jab at the Hadribeaj stoppage, arguing the challenger beat the count right as the bell sounded. Regardless, he made it clear he wanted Fundora looking sharp so there are zero asterisks later.

“I don’t want nobody to say nothing,” Ennis said. “No excuses.”

Kelly is the obstacle between that talk and a possible Fundora fight. Ennis described him as a “sharp” and “smart” fighter. Beating him must come before Ennis can turn his confidence against Fundora into something more substantial.

Ennis is spotting the exact same tactical flaw everyone else saw against Hadribeaj: Fundora simply cannot resist fighting like a phone booth brawler. Calling a 6’6″ fighter with an 86-inch reach “too small” sounds bizarre on the surface, but Ennis is talking about physical density and ring presence, not height.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Claims Floyd Mayweather Title Fight Agreement
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia claims he and Floyd Mayweather have agreed to fight for the WBC welterweight title, putting a championship label on a matchup that looks more like a celebrity event than serious business at 147.

The selling point is obvious: Garcia gets a chance to put the first loss on Mayweather’s professional record. Whether beating a 49-year-old version of Floyd would prove much about Ryan’s ability is another question.

“Trust me at first I thought this was bull***,” Garcia posted on X. “But it’s real Floyd and I agree to a fight.”

Garcia added: “147 for the WBC welterweight championship of the world. 50-0 vs The current champ.”

That is Garcia announcing an agreement. His post does not provide a date, venue, or broadcaster, and it does not establish that the WBC has approved Mayweather as a title challenger. Those details still need to follow before this can be treated as a confirmed championship fight.

As a commercial idea, it is easy to understand. Mayweather’s undefeated record gives the promotion something to sell beyond the usual exhibition routine. Ryan would be chasing the “0,” while Floyd would be selling the possibility that he can still beat a much younger champion.

As a title defense, it is a circus.

Mayweather’s reputation was earned against elite fighters over a long career. That reputation does not tell us what he can do at 49 against a current welterweight champion. Putting his record on the line would make the result official, but it would not turn back the clock.

Garcia would also leave himself open to an obvious criticism. Beat Floyd, and he has beaten a retired great approaching 50. Struggle with him, and the questions about Ryan become considerably louder.

There will be people willing to buy it. Two famous names and the possibility of Mayweather finally losing are enough to draw attention beyond boxing’s regular audience.

That is the appeal Garcia is selling. The WBC belt adds decoration, but the attraction is celebrity, money, and a famous unbeaten record.

Sanctioning this as an official WBC welterweight title defense would make a complete joke of the belt and freeze out actual contenders at 147. If two massive names want an unsanctioned exhibition to generate huge pay-per-view numbers, boxing fans understand the drill.

Celebrity events happen all the time now. Slapping an authentic world championship onto it crosses the line from entertainment into parody. Mayweather turns 50 next February and has not fought in a sanctioned professional bout since 2017. He is not ranked by the WBC.

Handing him an immediate shot at a real crown purely because of his fame insults every active fighter grinding through eliminators for a mandatory spot. For Garcia, putting the belt up brings zero boxing credit. If he blows out a 49-year-old retired legend, nobody takes it seriously as a legitimate championship victory.

If he looks bad or gets touched up by Floyd, critics will tear him apart. Keeping it as an exhibition protects the credibility of the sanctioning body, keeps the division moving, and lets fans enjoy the spectacle for what it really is. Turning it into an official title fight cheapens the entire sport.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma Could Fight Four Times In 2027
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma could box four times in 2027, with promoter Frank Warren targeting a January return to give the heavyweight an early start on a busy year.

Warren wants at least three appearances, though fitting in a fourth will depend on the opposition. No opponent or venue has been announced for Itauma’s next fight.

“I would like him to have a minimum of three fights, maybe four if we can fit them in, depending on the opposition as well, of course,” Warren told BoxNation.

That last qualification leaves room for the schedule to change. Four fights would give Itauma regular work, but the value of that activity will come from who Warren puts in front of him. An opponent who makes him solve different problems could provide more than another quick finish.

Warren expects to reveal the next step shortly.

“I think we’ll be sometime next week, towards the end of next week, announcing something, but he’ll be fighting very early next year, probably in January,” he said.

January remains a target rather than a confirmed booking. Still, getting Itauma out that early would leave Warren enough room to spread three more appearances across the remainder of 2027, provided the fights and recovery periods allow it.

The opponent announcement will tell us more about the ambition behind that schedule. Warren offered no names and made no commitment to a world title fight during this interview. His comments were about getting Itauma into the ring regularly.

There is also a practical balance to find. As the opposition improves, fights can require longer preparation and leave less room for a quick turnaround. Warren’s preference for three, with four possible, gives him flexibility without committing Itauma to dates before the opponents are secured.

A busy calendar is a reasonable starting point. The next question is whether those appearances move Itauma closer to the heavyweights he eventually needs to beat.

Sports.title: Dmitry Bivol vs Callum Smith Gets DAZN Confirmation
Sports.content:
DAZN has officially confirmed its coverage of Dmitry Bivol’s December 12 title defense against Callum Smith in Yekaterinburg, Russia, where the Briton will challenge for the WBA, IBF and WBO light heavyweight belts.

The fight was announced on October 12, with DAZN already identified as the broadcaster. Wednesday’s promotional post provides the platform’s own confirmation, although it adds no new date, venue or opponent.

“An unmissable world title unification between Dmitry Bivol & Callum Smith lands on DAZN,” the broadcaster posted.

Bivol will defend his three belts at the UMMC Arena against Smith, who gets an opportunity to become a two-division world champion. Winning those titles requires solving a difficult boxing puzzle on the champion’s home turf.

Smith’s power gives him a threat if he can get close enough to use it. Bivol’s footwork and quick combinations can leave opponents losing rounds while trying to get into punching position. Smith cannot afford to follow him around without producing enough offense.

His prolonged absence has also taken some of the interest out of this fight. Smith’s February 2025 victory over Joshua Buatsi gave him something to build on, but fans will have waited almost 22 months to see him fight again by December 12.

That layoff was not entirely by choice. Smith was scheduled to defend his WBO interim title against David Morrell on April 18 in Liverpool before a training camp injury forced him out less than two weeks before the event. The fight never happened.

The injury explains the canceled return, but it cannot restore the attention lost during his absence. The Buatsi victory has faded into the background, leaving Smith without a recent performance to get fans talking about his chances against Bivol.

There is a sporting cost, too. Smith must find his timing against a champion who can score and move before an opponent gets his punches off. Spending several rounds settling in could leave the challenger chasing a substantial lead.

DAZN has confirmed where fans can watch. Smith’s task is to make this competitive after spending so long out of the ring.

Sports.title: Jack Catterall Ready As Teofimo Lopez Deadline Hits Tomorrow
Sports.content:
Jack Catterall has made it known he is ready to get down to business with the October 22 deadline running out for talks on his ordered WBA welterweight title fight against Teofimo Lopez.

The British southpaw went onto social media while waiting to see if he lands his mandatory crack or gets hit with another postponement.

“READY FOR A FIGHT,” Catterall posted, tagging DAZN Boxing to make sure the network heard him loud and clear.

That puts Catterall’s stance out there in four words. He wants an official date on the calendar, yet the WBA process has not produced one.

Teofimo’s side has tried to get special permission to go after a different opponent, looking into a massive unification clash against Ryan Garcia for early 2027. Catterall stands as the main roadblock for that route because the WBA already issued the order for its super champion to face him next.

Catterall picked up the WBA regular title by beating Shakhram Giyasov back in May. Grabbing that strap put him in direct position for the bout he is trying to nail down right now. Five months have gone by, and he finds himself still stuck waiting for that mandatory pathway to deliver an actual ring return.

The deadline hits at the close of business Eastern Time on Thursday, October 22. It represents the conclusion of the official discussion window set up by the WBA, not an automatic guarantee that Teofimo gets stripped on the spot.

The pending appeal keeps Catterall hanging around for a ruling that will dictate who he faces and how quickly he gets back under the lights. He recently talked about his career being stalled out, and his latest message makes it obvious that no agreement came together behind closed doors.

There is a huge cash reason for Teofimo to chase Ryan Garcia instead. That matchup pulls in massive public interest compared to a mandatory chore against Catterall. Still, Catterall followed every single sanctioning body rule to earn his spot, and a giant commercial payday for the champion does nothing to restore the lost months Catterall spent on the shelf.

Sports.title: Brandon Figueroa’s Team Believed 75% Would Beat Kameda
Sports.content:
Brandon Figueroa’s corner figured a three-quarters version of their fighter could still handle Tomoki Kameda. Instead of an easy night, pushing through a wrecked training camp produced a blown scale reading along with a scrapped title defense.

How they talked themselves into that position tells the real story. They watched Kameda struggle against Angelo Leo, convincing themselves they had spotted an opponent Figueroa could overpower on cruise control. Counting on an opponent’s flaws while dragging a hurt fighter through a brutal cut was asking for trouble from day one.

Chris Mannix outlined that logic after sitting down with Figueroa alongside trainer Manny Robles during fight week. According to Mannix, the team rolled the dice on the belief that a seventy-five percent Figueroa could handle a fully prepared Kameda. Robles pointed directly to Kameda hesitating to let his hands go against Leo as justification. Spotting flaws in Kameda did nothing to heal Figueroa’s compromised body.

“They took a calculated risk that they believed that 75% of Brandon Figueroa was going to be good enough to beat 100% of Tomoki Kameda,” said Mannix on his channel.

Sergio Mora painted a grim scene from the hotel. Figueroa looked completely drained, showing sunken cheeks alongside zero energy in his voice. Mora also picked up zero real belief from the camp members standing around him.

Those details leave the team with little defense. This went beyond routine fight-week sluggishness. Their own timeline showed an injury disrupting preparation, followed by an obvious physical collapse trying to make the limit.

Mora mentioned Tim Bradley stepping up to challenge the room, asking them directly why they were walking toward the ring while compromised. Bradley told them bluntly that no purse justifies risking long-term health. Mora suspected Bradley played a major part in talking them off the ledge, even if that remains his personal read on the room.

Purses drove the train too. Mora noted the team nodded in agreement when he brought up walking away from guaranteed money. Mannix pointed out another worry, specifically that Figueroa lacked any guarantee about landing another broadcast date anytime soon.

Uncertainty explains the pressure. It still fails to justify putting a fighter in harm’s way.

Kameda did his job, locked in his weight, then watched his title shot vanish on fight morning. Figueroa completely dumped the momentum built from stopping Nick Ball.

Pulling the plug was the only acceptable move once Figueroa broke down. The heat belongs squarely on the days leading up to it, when his corner treated Kameda’s flaws as an excuse to ignore their own fighter’s reality.

Figueroa blew the biggest payday of his career in the process. Keeping that belt would have placed him directly in the crosshairs for Naoya Inoue’s planned jump to featherweight in 2027. Holding a world title gave him the one bargaining chip the Japanese star actually needs.

That belt was Figueroa’s golden ticket. Facing Kameda was simply supposed to be the routine checkpoint to keep him in line for the jackpot.

Instead, he walked out of Las Vegas with an empty bank account, no strap, plus a ruined argument for landing Inoue. While that clash was never locked in stone, tossing the hardware away stripped Inoue’s handlers of any reason to look his way.

That reality turns the corner’s gamble into pure negligence. Figueroa’s team got tunnel vision worrying if a three-quarters version could slide past Kameda, completely blind to what blowing the scale would cost down the road.

Sports.title: Keith Thurman Expects Less Volume From Vergil Ortiz
Sports.content:
Keith Thurman is already spinning Vergil Ortiz Jr. as a more manageable problem than Sebastian Fundora, which tells you everything about how veteran fighters rationalize dangerous matchups.

Thurman is betting that a drop in incoming punches equates to breathing room. Trading Fundora’s exhausting, awkward flurries for Ortiz’s firepower is a terrible bargain.

Fundora drowned Thurman in non-stop punches, but Ortiz does not need triple-digit punch outputs to ruin someone’s night. He sits down on every single delivery, cuts off escape routes, and forces opponents into survival mode.

“Virgil might be holding back his volume, but his power is going to be more intense,” Thurman told MillCity Boxing. “So, once again, it’s dangerous.”

Thurman talking about Ortiz holding back volume sounds like wishful thinking from a fighter trying to talk himself into believing he will get space to operate. He even tries to compare the transition to his past fights against Shawn Porter and Danny Garcia. Porter brought a relentless dogfight, while Garcia offered pauses between exchanges that allowed Thurman to reset his feet.

“I think he’s going to be easier to match the volume, the two-punch combos, the three-punch combos,” Thurman said.

The fatal flaw in that logic is simple: Garcia let fighters off the hook. Ortiz hunts. Those quiet moments Thurman thinks he will exploit between short combinations will not be rest periods. They will be traps where Ortiz walks him into the ropes and forces him to backpedal under heavy artillery.

At 37, Thurman’s legs look gone compared to his prime. He used to circle the perimeter, plant his feet, fire a quick combination, and skip out of range before anyone could touch him. Against Fundora, he had no snap left to hold his ground, which is why he spent from rounds 3 to 6 of that fight purely in track-and-field mode.

If Thurman refuses to sit down on his shots, Ortiz Jr. will walk through him. A dangerous puncher only respects what is coming back at him. The moment Ortiz Jr. realizes Thurman is strictly on his bicycle and throwing nothing to deter him, he will pin his ears back, cut off the ring, and trap Thurman on the ropes. Without pop on his punches to gain Ortiz’s respect, running just delays the inevitable while draining Thurman’s dwindling gas tank.

The threat of a referee stoppage is very real here. Against Fundora, Thurman reached a point where he was offering zero offensive resistance, and ringside officials will step in every time if a guy looks like target practice and shows no intention of fighting back.

Sports.title: Frank Warren Backs Tyson Fury To Stop Anthony Joshua
Sports.content:
Frank Warren is convinced Tyson Fury stops Anthony Joshua inside the distance, pinpointing AJ’s defensive lapses during his own offensive bursts as the decisive flaw.

Fury’s timing and counterpunching remain central to Warren’s prediction. The promoter views the dynamic much like he viewed Daniel Dubois’s upset win over Joshua, even while admitting neither man is operating at their athletic peak.

“Styles make fights. I believe the same as I believed Daniel, when he fought AJ, he would knock him out and beat him. I think Tyson would do the same thing,” Warren said to Sky Sports Boxing. “I just feel that Tyson has his number, in my opinion. Maybe wrong. The one thing about AJ, as we all know, he can whack.”

Warren’s logic involves the split second Joshua commits to his combinations. While Joshua’s power creates danger whenever he fires, his delayed guard gives an elite counterpuncher clear targets before his hands return home.

“When he throws his shots, he leaves himself very vulnerable, and Tyson’s a good counterpuncher,” Warren added.

Capitalizing on those windows requires sharp reflexes, something that naturally diminishes with age. Warren admitted the bout will look different than it would have years ago, predicting a tighter, less mobile collision where neither heavyweight retreats.

“I think they’ll both be a little bit slower than they were,” Warren said. “I think it’ll be very exciting whilst it lasts.”

Warren dresses it up with complex talk about technical openings and counter angles, but the fundamental flaw is Joshua’s punch resistance. Once a heavyweight’s chin cracks, no amount of technical adjustment can compensate for it.

The warning signs were impossible to miss against Kristian Prenga. Surviving Dubois is one thing because Daniel hits with concussive force, but getting buzzed and nearly closed out by a fringe guy like Prenga signals that Joshua’s internal alarm system is permanently compromised. Every time clean contact lands, his legs betray him immediately.

Fury does not possess one-punch power, yet that makes little difference when the target crumples under ordinary pressure. With his towering frame and natural bulk, Fury merely needs to absorb the initial storm, step into the pocket, and let his hands go until something connects flush. A clean tap on a ruined chin does the exact same job as an explosive shot.

Ghana News.title: ‘Ghana must not miss the AI train’ – Zipline Ghana Director
Ghana News.content:
Ghana cannot afford to miss the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence (AI), the Country Director of Zipline Ghana, Daniel Kwaku Merk, has warned, saying the consequences of falling behind could last for decades or even centuries.

He said technological disruption should not be viewed only as a threat to jobs, businesses and established ways of working but also as an opportunity to unlock possibilities that may not be immediately apparent.

Speaking at the JoyNews Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, October 21, Mr Merk said experience with emerging technologies had shown that their full potential often became clear only after they were put to use.

“If I take a step back and I look at disruption versus opportunity, I think disruption in itself is an opportunity, and that's what we definitely have experienced,” he said.

He explained that technological advances could deliver results beyond what people initially imagined, making it important for countries and businesses to explore their potential rather than be deterred by uncertainty.

“Things are possible in terms of technology delivery; you can't anticipate the outcome until you actually do it. So there's far more possible that you can envision initially,” he said.

A window Ghana must seize

Mr Merk said the pace of technological change made it imperative for Ghana to position itself to benefit from AI, warning that the country could face long-term consequences if it failed to take advantage of the emerging opportunities.

“But I would also like to add that, for me, the way I see it, it is an opportunity that we cannot miss. I think it's like one of those technologies that, if we miss the train, will last for decades, if not centuries,” he said.

His comments come amid growing debate about how AI could reshape economies, change workplace practices and transform the delivery of services across sectors.

For Ghana, the challenge is not simply to adopt new technologies but to identify where they can solve practical problems, improve productivity and support economic development.

That will require investment in digital infrastructure, relevant skills and innovation, alongside efforts to ensure businesses, workers and public institutions are equipped to adapt as AI becomes more widely used.

Turning promise into practical gains

Mr Merk’s remarks placed emphasis on the need to experiment with new technologies to understand what they can achieve. The benefits, he suggested, may be greater than initially expected.

Zipline, which uses autonomous aircraft to deliver medical supplies, offers an example of how technology can be applied to practical service-delivery challenges. Its operations in Ghana have focused on getting essential medical products to health facilities, including those in hard-to-reach communities.

The wider AI debate raises similar questions about how emerging technologies can be used to improve public services, support businesses and expand access to opportunities.

However, turning technological promise into lasting economic gains will depend on how effectively Ghana prepares its workforce, develops local expertise and creates an environment in which innovation can flourish.

Ghana News.title: ‘Government is an impediment rather than an enabler’ – Bright Simons on digital platforms
Ghana News.content:
Vice-President and head of Research at the IMANI Centre for Policy and Education, Bright Simons, warned that government can obstruct the digital opportunities ordinary Ghanaians rely on for work and income.

He urged policymakers to remove barriers to digital platforms and avoid licensing requirements that have not been properly considered.

Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, Mr Simons pointed to ride-hailing and e-commerce services as examples of platforms delivering benefits to ordinary people.

“I'm a big believer in the fact that when it comes to those kinds of things, typically the government is an impediment rather than an enabler.”

He said users had learnt to navigate these platforms with little formal instruction. He noted that drivers and delivery workers had developed the skills to use maps and location services.

“Nobody taught them how to use mapping services. Very few people tried to teach them how to do that. Somehow we figured out how to use mapping services, how to do geolocation and deliver food and the rest of it.”

For Mr Simons, that experience should shape how government approaches digital policy. The practical value of policy includes removing obstacles that prevent people from using technology productively.

He recalled opposing proposals to license Uber, Bolt and other platforms. He said those proposals would have imposed onerous obligations on local governments.

He also cited the public reaction to proposed licensing requirements for developers in Ghana as a warning against poorly considered rules.

“So we have to think about policy as also to include the things that remove barriers and bottlenecks for ordinary people, because when it comes to the basic capabilities, map reading, WhatsApp use.”

Mr Simons extended the argument to content creation. He said people had developed the skills to use social media and build audiences without dedicated schools teaching them how.

“Who builds schools to teach people how to use WhatsApp? Who builds schools to teach influencers how to do YouTube influencing?”

He maintained that identifying regulatory obstacles was a practical contribution to improving people’s lives. He argued that such interventions should not be dismissed as theoretical discussions.

“Often they are impediments and bottlenecks in their way, and people like us who point them out should not be seen as discussing theory. It's very practical.”

Ghana News.title: Bright Simons questions Sam George on feasibility of Ghana’s AI compute centre, cites power and water costs
Ghana News.content:
Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons, has questioned Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations Minister Samuel Nartey George over the feasibility of Ghana’s planned AI compute centre, citing concerns about electricity costs, water supply and the country’s history with locally developed technology projects.

Speaking during JoyNews's Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, October 21, Mr Simons argued that the government must address the practical constraints facing the project rather than assume it will succeed.

He said electricity costs would be a major determinant of the facility’s operational efficiency, warning that Ghana could struggle to compete if its energy prices remained significantly higher than the rates the Minister cited for AI computing facilities.

“Nobody builds an AI centre unless the energy, say, the price of energy is roughly 3 cents to 5 cents. So if Ghana does it from 10 cents to 12 cents, that AI data computing centre will not be efficient,” he said.

Mr Simons argued that the facility would either have to charge users more for its services or depend on government subsidies to remain operational.

“If it doesn't charge more, the government will have to subsidise it,” he said.

He also questioned whether Ghana could guarantee a reliable electricity supply for a facility of that scale, noting that affordable power alone would not be enough without consistent availability.

“Even in terms of the power itself, even if you had the pricing right, the actual availability of power in a country where we were struggling with so-called capacity issues is important. You have to mention that as well,” he said.

The IMANI Africa Vice President also raised concerns about water supply, saying the government needed to account for the substantial volumes required to operate a large data centre. He cited Ghana’s experience with managing a desalination plant as an example of the challenges associated with major infrastructure projects.

“The amount of water you need for a big data centre of that sort is unbelievable,” he said.

Mr Simons further questioned Mr George what had changed in Ghana’s technology ecosystem to make the proposed initiative more likely to succeed than previous efforts to develop and use locally built digital services.

He referenced past attempts to establish locally developed government email services and payroll management software, pointing to the experience of Ghanaian technology entrepreneur Herman Chinery-Hesse, who he said had pushed for the adoption of local software solutions but failed to secure the desired outcome.

“So the question is, why did Herman fail and why would the Honourable Sam George succeed? I want to understand that dynamic. What has changed? What is new? What new ideas have completely transformed that ecosystem?” he asked.

Mr Simons said the government needed to demonstrate what had changed in the country’s technology ecosystem and identify the new ideas or approaches that would prevent the proposed project from encountering similar difficulties.

He called for a rigorous assessment of the initiative, urging the government to open the process to contributions from think tanks and other stakeholders before making final decisions.

“My argument is, let's learn from history. Let's do these things analytically, open up, ask think tanks to submit memos, debate it rigorously, finally choose something that is well grounded and robust,” he said.

He criticised what he described as a tendency to praise government initiatives without adequately scrutinising their feasibility, arguing that major technology investments required evidence-based debate and careful analysis.

Mr Simons maintained that his concerns were rooted in a pragmatic assessment of the project’s challenges rather than pessimism.

“It's not that I'm pessimistic. I'm empirical, I'm pragmatic, and I'm a realist,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Meta fined $25bn for ‘lies’ over user data privacy
Ghana News.content:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".

Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.

Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.

Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.

They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.

"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday.

"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."

The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.

Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.

He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.

Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.

While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.

It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.

New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.

The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".

As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.

Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people.

"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.

To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.

The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.

Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.

Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock.

Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

Ghana News.title: Ghana must build its own email services to address US data concerns – Bright Simons
Ghana News.content:
IMANI Centre for Policy and Education Vice-President and Head of Research Bright Simons says concerns about US access to Ghanaian data would require the country to build its own email services.

Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he pointed to the use of foreign email platforms as a challenge for those seeking greater control over their information.

“So if we're worried about our data being exposed to the U.S. government, then we have to literally build our own email services because already the U.S. government sees everything that you put on Gmail or any of those things.”

Simons made the claim while discussing data exposure and the policy choices surrounding digital services.

He also urged policymakers to remove obstacles that prevent ordinary people from benefiting from technology.

Drawing on ride-hailing and delivery services, he said many users had acquired practical digital skills without formal training.

“The second point is that when you look at Uber and all the ride-sharing apps and all the e-commerce apps, a lot of the people that have benefited are ordinary people. Nobody taught them how to use mapping services.”

He said people had learnt to use geolocation and mapping tools to deliver food and support other commercial activities.

For Simons, such experiences should shape how government approaches the digital economy. He argued that regulation could obstruct opportunities when obligations were introduced without sufficient consideration of their effects.

“I'm a big believer in the fact that when it comes to those kinds of things, typically the government is an impediment rather than an enabler.”

He recalled opposing attempts to impose licensing requirements and local government obligations on ride-hailing platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

He also cited the public backlash over proposed licensing requirements for developers in Ghana as evidence that policy decisions have practical consequences.

“So we have to think about policy as also to include the things that remove barriers and bottlenecks for ordinary people,” he said.

Simons pointed to the widespread use of WhatsApp and the growth of YouTube creators as further examples of people developing digital capabilities outside formal classrooms.

“Who builds schools to teach people how to use WhatsApp? Who builds schools to teach influencers how to do YouTube influencing?”

He maintained that identifying regulatory obstacles was essential to making technology useful to ordinary people.

“Often they are impediments and bottlenecks in their way, and people like us who point them out should not be seen as discussing theory. It's very practical.”

Ghana News.title: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November
Ghana News.content:
From an awards-tipped role for Andrew Scott to another Hunger Games prequel, here are the films to watch at the cinema and stream at home this month.

1. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth

Cliff Booth was the laidback stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Quentin Tarantino's Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019). Pitt won a best supporting actor Oscar for his performance, and Tarantino liked the character so much that he has written him a spin-off comedy-thriller. That's surprising enough, given that Tarantino isn't known for sequels – but a bigger surprise is that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is directed by David Fincher (Fight Club, The Social Network). That makes this the first film to be scripted by Tarantino and directed by someone else since From Dusk Till Dawn back in 1996. It's set in 1977, a time when Cliff Booth is employed to clean up Hollywood's messes. His latest clients include a talent agent (Elizabeth Debicki) and a TV actor (Scott Caan) who are mixed up with gangsters. "What was once a fairytale is now a crime story," says the film's official synopsis, "a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in LA."

Released on 25 November in the UK, the US and Canada

2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

It's been more than a decade since Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen triumphed in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2, but audiences are still hungry for more. The first Hunger Games prequel, subtitled The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, was a hit in 2023. And now there's a sequel to that prequel, which is set 40 years after Songbirds and Snakes and 24 years before Katniss's adventures. Confused? Us too, but it'll all make sense to anyone who is already a fan of Suzanne Collins's bestselling dystopian novels. Sunrise on the Reaping stars Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson's character from the original films, and Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, who was played by Donald Sutherland. Other younger incarnations include Jesse Plemons as Philip Seymour Hoffman's character, Kieran Culkin as Stanley Tucci's, and Elle Fanning as Elizabeth Banks's.

Released on 19 and 20 November internationally

3. Elsinore

In 1989, Daniel Day-Lewis was playing Hamlet at London's National Theatre when the pressure got too much for him, and he walked off the stage. It was his last ever theatre performance. His replacement was Ian Charleson, who had starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire a few years earlier. Charleson had Aids, a condition that was fatal at the time, but he was determined to take on the greatest and most demanding stage role of all before he died. In Elsinore, Charleson is played by Andrew Scott, with Olivia Colman as his doctor and Billie Piper as his best friend. Directed by Simon Stone (The Dig) and written by Stephen Beresford (Pride), the film is heart-rending yet joyous – and Scott is sure to be Oscar-nominated. "I wept like a baby," says Nick Howells in The Standard. "This is a performance of a lifetime, and one the Academy voters would need a collective bout of insanity to ignore."

Released on 20 November in the US, 25 November in France and 29 January in the UK and Ireland

4. Club Kid

Jordan Firstman, the comedian and actor best known as Charlie in HBO's I Love LA, has made one of the most acclaimed films of the year, a festival favourite with a 100% score on the Rotten Tomatoes reviews aggregator site. As well as writing and directing Club Kid, Firstman stars as Peter, a gay club promoter who organises New York's wildest parties with his business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingne). But after a decade of this drug-fuelled lifestyle, Peter is feeling old and jaded. It's then that he meets Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the 10-year-old British son he never knew he had. Wendy Ide in Screen Daily says that Firstman's "joyous, raw comedy drama" is "a crowd-pleasing triumph – an acidic, spikily funny portrait of New York's hedonistic gay scene which celebrates empathy, community and the unconditional love between a father and his son".

Released on 4 November in France, 6 November in the US and 13 November in Canada

5. Hexed

Disney's most recent animated films have been sequels and prequels – Moana 2, Mufasa: The Lion King, Zootopia 2 (aka Zootropolis 2) – but the studio is having another crack at new material with Hexed. Its typically plucky heroine is Billie (voiced by Hailee Steinfeld), a suburban teenager who discovers that she was born with magical powers. She then learns the art of sorcery after she is zapped through a portal to Hogwarts – sorry, Hexe – a mysterious realm of witches and enchanted creatures voiced by Jodie Foster, Tracey Ullman, Stephen Fry and Dan Stevens. Hexed isn't the only cartoon to explore magical worlds this month, either: an animated adaptation of Dr Seuss's The Cat in the Hat is in cinemas on 5 November.

Released on 25, 26 and 27 November internationally

6. Focker-in-Law

The Devil Wears Prada 2 was a box-office hit earlier this year. Will another legacy sequel to a 2000s comedy classic have the same appeal? Sixteen years after the third instalment of the Meet the Parents franchise, and 26 years after the first, Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro are back as the neurotic Greg Focker and his disapproving father-in-law, Jack. Three more of the usual suspects are back, too: Owen Wilson, Blythe Danner and Teri Polo as Greg's wife Pam. (Alas, there's no sign of Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman, who played Greg's parents in the last two films.) New cast-members include Beanie Feldstein as Greg and Pam's daughter, Skyler Gisondo as their son, and, most importantly, Ariana Grande as their son's fiancée. The twist this time is that Jack welcomes the newcomer into his "circle of trust", while Greg is the one who has his doubts.

Released on 25, 26 and 27 November internationally

7. I Play Rocky

When Sylvester Stallone was an aspiring actor in the 1970s, he decided to write himself his dream role, so he bashed out the screenplay for Rocky in three-and-a-half days. Studio executives loved it, but they saw it as a vehicle for Clint Eastwood or Charles Bronson, rather than some unknown wannabe with a mumbly voice. But Stallone wouldn't sell out – which explains the title of this behind-the-scenes drama: I Play Rocky. Anthony Ippolito stars as the young Sly, alongside Matt Dillon as his father, AnnaSophia Robb as his first wife, and Stephan James as Carl Weathers (Apollo Creed in Rocky). Directed by Peter Farrelly (Green Book / Dumb and Dumber), the true-life underdog story is "stirring, inspiring, surprisingly hilarious and easy to love", says Johnny Oleksinski in the New York Post. "And refreshingly, it's not reverential or museumish, but created in the off-beat, tenacious, can-do spirit of Rocky."

Released on 6 November in the UK, the US and Canada

8. Wild Horse Nine

Martin McDonagh's The Banshees of Inisherin was nominated for eight Oscars (including four different acting awards). His new film is tipped to do similarly well, with its star, John Malkovich, being an almost-certain best actor nominee. He and Sam Rockwell play a pair of buffoonish CIA agents having a short holiday on Easter Island. Like the bickering best friends in The Banshees of Inisherin and In Bruges, they share some wonderfully eccentric dialogue and some scenes of explosive violence, but Wild Horse Nine is distinguished by its hard-edged political commentary and by Malkovich's character's regrets. McDonagh's "latest could be the best yet", says Phil de Semlyen in Time Out, "a bittersweet hangout film about lonely, crumpled men facing up to mortality, dealing with the consequences of violence and chewing the fat to outlandishly funny effect."

Released on 4, 5 and 6 November internationally

9. Being Heumann

Siân Heder is the writer-director of Coda, which won the Oscar for best picture in 2022. Her follow-up, Being Heumann, is another inspiring drama featuring disabled actors. It's drawn from the autobiography of Judith Heumann, a US disability rights activist. In 1977, she and a group of protesters occupied the San Francisco Federal Building because equal rights regulations were being ignored. Mark Ruffalo plays the government official who wants to kick her out, and Ruth Madeley, a wheelchair user herself, stars as Heumann. "The remarkable thing about the British actress's performance is that she makes us embrace a character so fiery and flawed and exasperatingly unrelenting," says Steve Pond in The Wrap. "There's no question that [Heder has] pulled off another crowd-pleasing film, but the key to Being Heumann is that its importance goes beyond those audience smiles."

Released on 6 November in cinemas in the UK, the US and Canada, and on 13 November on Apple TV+

10. Josephine

Kate Erbland in IndieWire calls Josephine a "stunning film… [that I will] heartily recommend and never, ever watch again". That's fair enough: Beth de Araújo's drama is gripping, intelligent, groundbreaking and important, but it's not exactly a pleasure to watch. It's the story of an eight-year-old girl (Mason Reeves) who is in a San Francisco park one Sunday morning with her father (a career-best Channing Tatum). They lose sight of each other for a few minutes – and during that time the girl witnesses a brutal sexual assault. The questions now are: How will this horrific experience affect her? How can her father and mother (Gemma Chan) help her? And does she have a responsibility to testify in court? Erbland says that "De Araújo's masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability".

Released on 20 November in the UK, the US and Ireland, and on 27 November in Canada

11. All of a Sudden

Ryusuke Hamaguchi's Drive My Car was one of the sensations of the 2022 Academy Awards: it didn't just win the best international feature prize, but was nominated for best picture, best director and best adapted screenplay, too. His quirky follow-up, Evil Does Not Exist, made less of an impression, but his deeply humane new film, All of a Sudden, is another awards contender. Virginie Efira plays the manager of a care home for the elderly in Paris. Tao Okamoto plays a Japanese theatre director who is visiting the city. The women's friendship deepens over the course of a three-hour drama which is "a gentle and infinitely tender exercise on life and death, full of immersive, philosophical musings that wash over our souls", says Tomris Laffly in Elle. "Patient and tranquil, All of a Sudden feels like a meditation that transforms a viewer into a better version of themselves."

Released on 25 November in the US

12. Paper Tiger

Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver and Miles Teller are on top form in Paper Tiger, another gritty, New York-based crime drama from James Gray (Little Odessa, The Yards, We Own the Night). Echoing events from the writer-director's own childhood, it's set in the borough of Queens in 1986. Johansson and Teller play Hester and Irwin, a happily married, successful-enough couple with two sons. Driver plays Irwin's brother Gary, a flashy ex-cop with political connections and charisma to burn. He brings his brother in on a scheme to clean up a polluted canal for a group of Russian immigrants. What with Irwin's engineering know-how and his own street-smart confidence, Gary reasons, the deal can't go wrong. But, of course, it can go very wrong indeed, what with the Russians being ruthless gangsters. "As with his finest work, Gray strikes a beautiful balance between fraught interpersonal drama and nail-biting thrills," says Nick Schager in The Daily Beast. "Paper Tiger pulsates with heart, rancour, and terror."

Released on 13 November in the US and Canada

Ghana News.title: Think about how we sign these agreements – Sam George warns over health data
Ghana News.content:
Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations Minister Sam Nartey George has urged closer scrutiny of agreements involving Ghana’s health records.

The Ningo-Prampram MP is warning that assurances from foreign technology companies may not guarantee control over sensitive data.

Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he questioned whether contractual promises could protect Ghana’s information from access under foreign laws.

His warning comes as Ghana disagrees with the United States over data-sharing provisions in a proposed health compact.

“The last point I just want to make is about the use of foreign resources and even the perception of a tailored arrangement that gives you sovereignty over your data,” he said.

“That is a mirage that is sold to many African companies, not just Ghanaian companies.”

Mr George said his concerns had prompted exchanges with Google and Amazon Web Services over the protections offered in their agreements.

“So I've had this back and forth with Google and Amazon Web Services, where they give you all kinds of agreements that say you are protected and data sovereign.”

He argued that the US CLOUD Act could override assurances made by private technology companies. He linked that concern directly to how Ghana’s health information is handled.

He urged decision-makers to examine both the agreements they sign and the platforms they use.

“Especially when you look at what they try to do with our health records, extremely important that we begin to think about how we sign this agreement and how we utilise those platforms.”

Ghana rejected the proposed US health compact after raising concerns about health data, financing obligations and regulatory authority. President John Mahama said the terms included access to Ghana’s pathogen profile and medical records.

The US Embassy disputed the suggestion that Washington sought identifiable patient records. It said the proposed arrangement required aggregate health data without personally identifiable information, mainly to assess health programmes.

The proposed compact involved $109 million in US assistance over five years. Mahama later said Washington had requested further discussions on the contested clauses, with a view to amending or removing them.

Ghana News.title: ‘Real-world skill sets’ – Sam George makes case for One Million Coders programme
Ghana News.content:
Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations Minister Sam Nartey George says the One Million Coders programme is designed to equip people with practical skills they can use in everyday life and business.

Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he urged the public to enrol in the programme's courses.

His comments followed a question about scaling up training that helps ordinary people become more productive in their daily activities and businesses.

George said that practical focus was central to the programme’s purpose. He described it as giving people “real-world skill sets that are applied in real-world situations.”

He said about 37 programmes were currently running on the portal to help people acquire those skills.

“It's extremely important,” he said.

His appeal emphasised how people apply their training. He explained that the programme aims to give participants skills useful in the situations they encounter.

The minister also raised concerns about data sovereignty when businesses use foreign technology platforms.

He questioned whether contractual assurances sufficiently protect data held by those providers.

“That is a mirage that is sold to many African companies, not just Ghanaian companies.”

George cited the U.S. Cloud Act as the basis for his concerns. He argued that it superseded private agreements promising data protection and sovereignty.

He said he had discussed those concerns with Google and Amazon Web Services.

The minister urged greater scrutiny of agreements with foreign providers, particularly where health records were involved.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
