World.title: Enes Freedom directed to private suite for WNBA Finals amid safety concerns, won't be allowed to sit courtside
World.content:
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom has been directed to watch Wednesday night’s WNBA Finals game from a private luxury suite with additional security after contacting authorities and basketball officials about concerns for his safety. Freedom was seen saying "I guess they'll have to drag me," in a video of a phone conversation with arena security, defying the directive.

The arrangement for Game 3 between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries at State Farm Arena follows Freedom’s public claims that he received death threats over his planned attendance. He previously told OutKick he was in contact with the FBI and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp's office about the threats.

State Farm Arena provided a statement to OutKick outlining the security arrangements. Freedom contacted federal, state and local authorities, along with the WNBA, the Dream and arena officials.

WNBA MOVES FINALS GAMES 3 AND 4 TO STATE FARM ARENA, GIVING ATLANTA DREAM THOUSANDS MORE SEATS

"Enes Kanter Freedom has contacted federal, state and local authorities, the WNBA, the Atlanta Dream and State Farm Arena officials to express concerns about his personal safety during his planned attendance at Game 3 of the WNBA Finals tonight. The safety and security of our guests and team members is our highest priority," the statement read."

"Following consultations with the WNBA, Dream ownership, State Farm Arena leadership and security officials, we have directed Mr. Freedom to watch tonight’s game from a private luxury suite. This arrangement is intended to address his security concerns and help provide a safe and positive experience for him and other guests. The suite will have additional security and will be his designated viewing location for the game. State police have also assigned an officer to Mr. Freedom at his request."

Freedom posted a video on X of his conversation with a security representative about the arrangements.

"I don't want a suite, I would like to to sit on the seat that I bought and purchased. I do not want a suite, I'm going to come and sit on the seats that I just bought, that's it," Freedom said when the representative informed him that he would have to sit in a suite.

The representative responded, telling Freedom, "The only thing available to you tonight is the suite."

Freedom subsequently responded, declaring, "Do you know everyone, every media that is going to hear about this right?" later adding, "I guess they'll have to drag me."

ENES KANTER FREEDOM OPENS UP ON CONFRONTATION WITH NATASHA CLOUD THAT LED TO EJECTION, WNBA PURSUIT

Freedom previously told OutKick he had received "thousands of death threats" after announcing his plans to attend, including messages warning that he would be "the next Charlie Kirk." The number of threats he described has not been independently verified.

"My DMs are full of pictures and videos of the moment that Charlie Kirk got shot," Freedom said, adding that the messages warned he would suffer the same fate. He also posted a compilation Tuesday showing messages he presented as threats against him.

Freedom said he had contacted the FBI and arranged his own security. A spokesperson for Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp separately told OutKick that the governor’s office had connected Freedom’s team with the appropriate law enforcement resources.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Despite the threats, Freedom said he intended to attend to support women’s basketball. Asked how he would respond if a player confronted him, he said he would avoid escalating the encounter and would remain off the court.

Freedom’s planned appearance comes after his removal from an August game between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever following a heated interaction with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. He was subsequently banned from the Chicago arena.

The former NBA center has challenged the WNBA over eligibility for transgender athletes and announced an attempt to enter its draft.

WNBA TELLS CONGRESS THAT ENES KANTER FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ARE ‘BOTH MEN’ IN ELIGIBILITY DISPUTE

World.title: Travelers to hot spot sternly warned by State Department as officials deny wider Gulf shutdown
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans traveling in and through the Middle East have a new wrinkle to sort out.

The U.S. State Department has pushed back against circulating reports that it directed nonessential government personnel and their dependents to leave the entire Gulf region, clarifying that the departure order applies only to Saudi Arabia.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott dismissed the broader regional claims, calling them "inaccurate" after the department released a formal statement confirming the targeted drawdown within the kingdom.

"The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," the department said.

AMERICANS WARNED AGAINST TRAVEL PLANS AS TERRORISM THREATENS POPULAR DESTINATION

The clarification arrived amid an uptick in militant strikes aimed at key regional transit hubs.

In the statement shared with Fox News Digital, the spokesperson noted that "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions."

Officials warned the security environment remains highly volatile, adding the conflict "has the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area."

The department emphasized that the safety and security of its staff and its households remain its highest priority.

US STATE DEPARTMENT WARNS AMERICANS OF GROWING SECURITY RISKS IN HISTORIC REGION

The United States "will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them as they return to the U.S.," the spokesperson said.

The current security environment remains highly volatile.

In late September, the State Department renewed its warning to Americans traveling in and through the Middle East amid escalating regional tensions.

The warning came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched a ballistic missile toward Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted.

Residents reported hearing an explosion and later seeing a plume of smoke near King Khalid International Airport, according to The Associated Press.

No casualties or damage from the attack were reported at the time.

CLICK HERE TO 

In an X post in September, the State Department's Bureau of Consular Affairs warned that the security environment in the Middle East "remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation."

The agency added, "Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions."

Officials specifically cited hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in their warning.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports," the post said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly. Americans outside the Middle East should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region."

The agency also advised those traveling to or from the region to monitor airport and airline operations, warning that U.S. diplomatic facilities have been targeted, including outside the Middle East.

In June, U.S. officials similarly urged Americans across the Middle East to remain vigilant as tensions mounted across the region.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

At the time, officials warned that airspace closures, demonstrations and threats to locations associated with the United States could disrupt travel with little notice.

The State Department also maintained its "Level 3: Reconsider Travel" advisory for Oman in an Aug. 30 update, warning of risks from armed conflict and terrorism, including the threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran.

But tensions can run high even when things are going well. Just ask head coach Kyle Shanahan and quarterback Brock Purdy after the latter screamed toward his leader on the sideline in a now-viral exchange in Week 6.

Purdy was heard shouting, "Hey, Kyle!" with clear frustration, and the clip quickly found its way around social media. It appeared that Purdy wasn’t happy that Shanahan didn’t have the play-call in his ear in time.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Ahead of the 49ers’ matchup with the Atlanta Falcons this week, Shanahan told a different story on the exchange.

"Yeah, it’s actually not to call a play faster," Shanahan replied when asked about it by a reporter. "It’s, ‘I need it again,’ and it gets cutoff at 15 [seconds]."

'WHAT THE F--K, CALL IT!': AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY CURSE AT EACH OTHER DURING HOT MIC MOMENT

Communications within a quarterback’s helmet can sometimes cause issues with getting play calls in on the sideline in time. That seemed to be the case here.

But I did hear him a couple times in this game, and I look up and try to do it again as long as it’s not past 15 seconds."

So, there’s no disconnect on that front, as Shanahan has seen Purdy be one of the top signal callers in the game thus far through this undefeated start.

World.title: California mayor insists cash handout program will solve affordability challenges, but critics question cost
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A California mayor insisted that handing out monthly cash payments is an effective tool to combat the state's soaring cost of living, even as local leaders face steep hurdles in securing permanent taxpayer funding to keep guaranteed income programs alive.

"I believe that guaranteed income programs like our Rise Up Alameda (RUA) pilot program are a valuable and effective tool to address the affordability crisis, based on the documented experiences of program participants," Alameda Mayor Marilyn Ezzy Ashcraft told Fox News Digital.

"The average age of the 150 program participants was 49 years, with 26% being 62 years or older, and most participants were either employed or retired."

Ashcraft’s comments follow the completion of Rise Up Alameda, the city's first-ever guaranteed income pilot project. City staff presented the program's final 24-month evaluation report to the Alameda City Council on Oct. 6.

ALBUQUERQUE USES WEED TAX TO FUND 'NO-STRINGS-ATTACHED' GUARANTEED INCOME, SPARKING POLICY DEBATE

According to city documents, the pilot aimed to "reduce economic instability for program participants, help to change local narratives and perceptions surrounding poverty and the provision of public benefits and help to support and inform the national discussion regarding public benefits and anti-poverty policies."

The Alameda City Council previously allocated $4.6 million in federal pandemic relief funds from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) to finance the initiative, which provided 150 low-income households with $1,000 per month in no-strings-attached cash over two years. However, city notices confirm that because ARPA was a one-time federal allocation, the pilot has officially concluded, and the city has no plans or budget allocated for a permanent continuation.

"As mayor, I believe our responsibility is to advance practical, compassionate and evidence-informed policies that help residents meet their basic needs, preserve their dignity and build a more stable future for themselves and their families," Ashcraft told Fox News Digital when asked whether she planned to implement a permanent program.

BALTIMORE MAYOR BACKS BALLOT MEASURE CREATING TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'BABY FUND' FOR NEWBORN FAMILIES

The faces behind the program

Ashcraft highlighted several personal accounts of local residents who received monthly payments through the pilot.

Among them was Andrea, a certified nursing assistant who used the funds to stay afloat following the death of her mother. The financial boost helped cover medical bills, rent, gas and Bay Area bridge tolls while allowing her to care for her father and ailing brother.

Another participant, Dolores, a retiree in her 70s living in affordable senior housing after a 41-year career at AT&T, used the extra $1,000 a month to pay off credit card debt and build an emergency savings account.

Other recipients included Haroon, a rideshare and transit driver; Julia, a woman with a disability who was able to buy new mattresses, groceries and a set of car tires after an eviction forced her to move in with her sister; and Tyronne, a Navy veteran and former truck driver at the decommissioned Alameda Naval Air Station who relied on the extra money to cover medical bills and stabilize his housing.

While Ashcraft praised these personal outcomes, she acknowledged that direct cash payments are not a full remedy for California's economic pressures.

"These stories demonstrate the value of direct, unrestricted cash in helping residents navigate financial hardship, maintain stability and improve their overall well-being," Ashcraft said.

"While guaranteed income is not a stand-alone solution to the affordability crisis, programs like Rise Up Alameda can provide meaningful support as we pursue longer-term solutions to the high cost of housing, health care, transportation and other basic needs."

GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE

How will municipalities fund these programs?

Alameda's program underscores a funding challenge local governments face across the nation regarding how to sustain guaranteed income pilot programs now that temporary federal pandemic relief funding is ending.

Many local guaranteed income pilots were underwritten by temporary pandemic-era ARPA allocations. With federal deadlines requiring municipalities to spend remaining relief funds, mayors and advocacy groups are searching for ways to convert short-term experiments into permanent, taxpayer-funded government programs.

A major organization advocating for guaranteed income is the Economic Security Project (ESP). Founded in 2016 by a network of entrepreneurs, activists and researchers, ESP has helped support more than 100 guaranteed income pilots nationwide. California leads the country with more than 60 pilot launches.

ESP has urged governments to consider taxpayer-funded measures to establish permanent minimum-income guarantees.

When asked by Fox News Digital whether local pilots are transitioning into permanent public policies, ESP indicated that multiple municipalities are actively working on legislative proposals.

"We can say, however, that there’s an active and growing movement for cash in hundreds of communities across the country," Shafeka Hashash, director of cash initiatives at the Economic Security Project, told Fox News Digital.

"We regularly take calls from some of the 1,500 members of the Guaranteed Income Community of Practice — researchers, nonprofits, local government officials and community leaders all interested in bringing cash to their neighborhoods," Hashash added.

"We just can’t announce any pilots or policies before the localities do."

MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS

One pilot program has become permanent in Cook County, Illinois. To sustain the initiative without federal aid, the Cook County Board of Commissioners approved $7.5 million for guaranteed income in the county budget, signaling a shift toward long-term local funding.

Republican state officials and conservative policy groups have sought to block guaranteed income programs. Critics argue unconditional handouts discourage work, increase dependence on government assistance and misuse taxpayer funds.

"The affordability crisis is hitting Americans across backgrounds, geographies and party lines, and it's imperative that state and federal leaders adopt a solutions-focused approach," Mayors for Guaranteed Income founder Michael Tubbs told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Banning policies that have proven effective at the local level is not only undemocratic, it is incredibly counterproductive to solving the key problem facing American families," he added.

"We should be unlocking innovation at the local level to boost economic security, stabilize households and restore faith in the American dream."

World.title: JD Vance visits Cincinnati Bengals practice and quarterback Joe Burrow is convinced it was mostly about him
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance is a longtime Cincinnati Bengals fan to the extreme that he watched his team lose an AFC wild card game to the Pittsburgh Steelers – while he was serving in Iraq in January of 2006.

Well, on Wednesday, the Veep got a closer look of his favorite team when he visited at their training facility and watched parts of practice.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Vance toured the team's locker room, shook hands with several players, coach Zac Taylor and others, and came away with a football. It is unclear if Vance brought the ball to be autographed or the club gave it to him as a memento.

ZAC TAYLOR FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK SEASON AS BENGALS REBUILD DEFENSE AROUND JOE BURROW'S SUPER BOWL WINDOW

The Trump administration is making a lot of campaign stops before the November 3 midterm elections and it seems athletes from all sports have been engaged and more than happy to tag along with the President and others.

Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart introduced the President at a New York event in May.

Pro Football Hall of Famer Joe Thomas participated in Wisconsin event in June.

Roger Clemens introduced Trump at a San Antonio rally earlier this month.

Todd Gurley flew on Air Force One and appeared on stage at a Georgia rally this month.

Danica Patrick took her turn on Air Force One this week as did Richard Petty.

Baltimore Ravens players joined the President at one rally in Pennsylvania and even rode in his motorcade with him.

And Super Bowl winning coach Jon Gruden attended a Trump rally in Ohio.

JON GRUDEN FIRES UP TRUMP RALLY CROWD IN OHIO AS IF DELIVERING A LOCKER ROOM SPEECH THEN DELIVERS ENDORSEMENT

Wednesday, meanwhile, wasn't the Bengals following Vance around. It was a Bengals fan following the team he's loved since he was a boy.

The strange thing about this visit, though, was that Vance didn't interact with quarterback Joe Burrow, who is undoubtedly the biggest star on the team.

The two didn't talk at all.

"We did not," Burrow told reporters. "We did not. He came with everybody and left with swiftness and efficiency before the end of practice, so I didn't get to."

Burrow turned a question about what happened while Vance was at practice into a statement about himself.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Yeah, a lot of people, a lot of people around, you know, that's what I love about what I do is, it brings a lot of people together, and people want to take time out of their day to come and watch what we do, watch what I do, and watch all the work that I've put in to come and watch greatness, and that's everybody in the locker room," Burrow said.

"That's why we do what we do, and whether it's on the TV, whether it's in person, whether it's on the practice field, and that's what we do."

Yes, we now understand who Burrow believes the stars are when the vice president of the country visits.

Vance arrived in a motorcade befitting a world leader – six black SUVs, some police vehicles, and some motorcycle cops.

His SUV (mini-tank?) rolled past a back gate at the Kettering Health practice fields adjacent to Paycor Stadium.

Vance is a Middletown, Ohio native. He has a home in Cincinnati’s East Walnut Hills neighborhood so he was obviously feeling quite at home when he arrived in town to deliver a speech at the FBI's Cincinnati Field Office and then hold a campaign rally at the Sharonville Convention Center.

World.title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, the retired American teacher freed by Russia?
World.content:
Stephen James Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was released by Russia on Wednesday after nearly five years in detention in the midst of an apparent warming of ties between Washington and Moscow.

The 74-year-old from Michigan had been living in eastern Ukraine for years when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. He was detained two months into the war as Russia captured swaths of Ukrainian territory. Two years later, he was convicted by a Russian court of serving as a mercenary.

The news of his release came out of a meeting between President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, where they were due to discuss an end to the Ukraine war.

01:06 Son of Stephen Hubbard says 'no evidence' his father was a mercenary 00:00 00:00

Witkoff thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard during their on-camera talks. He later met Hubbard in person in St. Petersburg before boarding a flight back to the United States.

In a video from Russian state news agency RIA, Hubbard can be seen smiling as he met Witkoff. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” he tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding, “From today, it’s a new life.”

During the meeting, Witkoff said on X, Trump “called Stephen to check on him and reaffirm his unwavering commitment to bringing all Americans wrongfully detained home.”

Witkoff shared an image of Hubbard on a plane next to the American flag and several other people, writing that he was “headed back home to his family.”

Martin De Luca, Hubbard’s lawyer, told NBC News in a phone interview Wednesday that he had spoken with Hubbard as he was “getting ready to take off” on a plane bound for the U.S. and that his client was overjoyed to be released.

“He was overwhelmed with joy,” De Luca said. “The No. 1 thing he was excited about was seeing his children and family, who will be waiting for him when he arrives in the U.S. tonight. He was in a fragile state, so it wasn’t a long conversation, but he’s OK, which is what’s important.”

Stephen Hubbard. Trisha Hubbard via Facebook

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin released Hubbard “on humanitarian grounds,” though Russia did not provide more details.

Hubbard’s family acknowledged both Trump’s and Putin’s roles in securing his release.

“We have been gravely concerned for his safety and health since his 2022 detention,” Hubbard’s son, Joseph Coleman, said in a statement on behalf of the family. “Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” the statement said.

Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest who lives in Cyprus, wrote Putin “a long and very emotional letter” last month, De Luca said.

In the letter, Coleman told the Russian leader that Hubbard’s family “feared he would die without ever seeing his kids or grandchildren,” De Luca said. Coleman had also outlined his father’s background and family history and emphasized his faith.

NBC News’ Garrett Haake spoke Wednesday with Coleman, who again thanked both Putin and Trump for his father’s release.

Coleman said that it was his “understanding” that Putin had read his letter.

Asked about the Russian accusation that his father was a mercenary fighting for Ukraine, Coleman replied, “And I say the moon is made out of cheese.”

“There’s no evidence to that effect,” he added.

Coleman said his father is not political and may have been targeted because of his American nationality.

“I think my father was in the wrong place at the wrong time,” he said. “I think it served the interests of low level military men to say, hey, we got this American. It’s a trophy.”

Coleman said that his father had lived with him in Cyprus for a period of time before deciding to move to Ukraine to live with his girlfriend for economic reasons.

Coleman only had a brief conversation with his father while he was on the tarmac in Russia.

“He was just looking forward to seeing family,” Coleman said.

Trump cheered Hubbard’s return, framing it as a demonstration of the Kremlin’s “respect” for its American counterparts.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump said Wednesday on Truth Social, shortly after Witkoff announced Hubbard’s release. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia.”

There was no “swap” necessary for this release, Trump added, though in a later post he said “those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt” had the U.S. gone ahead with sanctions that he waived last week.

Stephen Hubbard in Moscow City Court in 2024. Moscow City Court / via AP

Hubbard was sentenced in a closed-door trial in 2024, with very little information about his case reported by Russian state media.

At the time, Russian prosecutors alleged that as the Kremlin launched its “special military operation” in Ukraine in February 2022, Hubbard voluntarily joined a territorial defense battalion in the eastern city of Izyum, where he had been living since 2014. The prosecutors said Hubbard took part in the Ukraine war and regularly received financial compensation before his detention in April 2022 as advancing Russian forces captured the city.

“He was aware of the unlawful nature of his actions, yet — with the deliberate intent of personal enrichment — he carried out the orders of his superiors, which entailed direct participation in combat operations on the side of the Armed Forces of Ukraine against service members of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” according to Russia’s prosecutor general’s office.

Russian state media reported that he pleaded guilty to the charges. Following Hubbard’s release Wednesday, De Luca stood by his previous statements that Hubbard had told him the charges were false and that he was not part of any combat or military unit.

The New York Times reported last year that Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, disputes that he fought for Ukraine, as do three former Ukrainian prisoners of war held with Hubbard.

The paper also cited Fox as saying that her brother had a master’s degree in English, and had lived in Japan and Cyprus before moving to eastern Ukraine, where he had a Ukrainian partner. Fox also said that Hubbard taught English online when he needed money, and did not speak either Ukrainian or Russian.

Izyum, where Fox said her brother settled, was occupied by Russia for six months in 2022, but was later recaptured by Ukraine in a major counteroffensive. It is currently held by Ukraine and is not part of the four Ukrainian oblasts Russia has illegally annexed.

Hubbard’s release from Russian custody comes just months after former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who spent more than four years in a Russian prison, was set free in August.

Washington has accused Moscow of arbitrarily detaining American citizens in Russia for years, with their cases often used to negotiate prisoner swaps, including for state-backed intelligence operatives, detained around the world.

In some of the more high-profile cases, U.S. journalist Evan Gershkovich was released in a swap in 2024, alongside Marine veteran Paul Whelan — both had been jailed on espionage charges. WNBA star Brittney Griner, detained on drug charges in 2022, was freed after the Biden administration negotiated her release in exchange for a Russian arms dealer.

John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine and the senior director of the Atlantic Council think tank’s Eurasia Center, said that despite the depiction of Hubbard’s release, “it was not a freebie. It was not a gift to the United States.”

He told the “Here’s the Scoop” podcast that it came after the release of a prominent Russian war blogger, Mikhail Zvinchuk, who was detained in Montenegro in October and freed after the U.S. opted not to extradite him.

“Russia’s got back a bad guy who we should have taken into custody, and we got back an American who was innocent. That’s the pattern,” he said.

Meanwhile, on the day Hubbard was released, Russia said it had detained a German national accused of serving in the Ukrainian army.

Russia’s Federal Security Service didn’t release the man’s name or any other identifying details, and did not say where or when the man was taken into custody.

World.title: Teacher who survived Bend shooting tried to close door, ‘but the shooter was already there’
World.content:
A teacher who was shot by a teenage gunman in a Bend, Oregon, elementary school last week said she saw the attacker and tried to shut the classroom door, “but the shooter was already there.”

Becky Drury said she was shot at close range in the rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday.

“Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured,” Drury said in a statement Wednesday.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” she said. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”

Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher were killed in the attack, which began around 1 p.m., officials said.

The gunman was fatally shot by a bystander who saw him fire at a truck and enter the school, police have said. The bystander followed the 16-year-old gunman and shot him as another teacher was wrestling with him over the weapon, according to police.

The motive remained under investigation Wednesday.

Investigators are looking into whether the shooter viewed any extremist material online, including material associated with “nihilistic violent extremism,” also known as NVE, two senior law enforcement officials briefed on the investigation told NBC News.

The gun was purchased legally, Bend police said in a statement Wednesday.

Police have said that it was a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun and that the shooter used birdshot, buckshot and slugs.

Police have not said who purchased the gun. Two senior law enforcement officials previously told NBC News that the shooter’s mother bought it in August, around the time of his birthday.

“Bend Police detectives continue this complex investigation. They have served search warrants at the shooting suspect’s home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms,” police said in a statement Wednesday.

“That work continues, and it takes time,” the police department said.

Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed in the Oct. 13 attack. Mathieu Lewis-Rolland / Getty

Students in the greater Bend-La Pine Schools district returned to class Wednesday, although not at Silver Rail Elementary, where the shooting occurred.

“Through heartfelt artwork and messages of love, they are making sure every student who walks through the doors knows they are cared for, supported and loved,” the district said Tuesday as it prepared to welcome most students back.

Authorities have publicly identified two of the victims who were killed, 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and teacher Megan Lambert.

Drury, the wounded teacher, said in her statement that she heard a noise last week and went to investigate.

“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on,” she said.

“I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” she said.

Drury said that there was nothing more she could have done and that “I was shot before I had any chance to act.”

“What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy,” she said.

“My thoughts are with those who were hurt, those we lost, their families, our school, and the Bend community,” she said. “I am truly grateful for the kindness and support we have received as we face the difficult days ahead together.”

World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

World.title: Trump hopes to flatter Putin into negotiating on Ukraine, experts say
World.content:
WASHINGTON — In recent weeks, President Donald Trump has taken measures that strengthen Russia’s position and may rehabilitate Russian President Vladimir Putin’s soiled reputation in the international community.

Trump returned to office vowing to swiftly end the Russia-Ukraine war, proclaiming last year that he was on “nobody’s side” except “humanity’s side.” But the neutral posture he said he has adopted is peeling away.

A specific strategic goal underlies Trump’s overtures to Putin, foreign policy experts said. The idea is to entice him to come to the negotiating table and end a war that is now in its fifth year. Whether it will work is another question.

Trump’s lead negotiator in the Russia-Ukraine war, Steve Witkoff, called Putin “a humanitarian” in St. Petersburg on Wednesday upon the release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had detained since 2022. Even Republican lawmakers balked at the remark.

00:43 Witkoff thanks Putin for release of retired American teacher 00:00 00:00

“I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He’s certainly not a humanitarian,” Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is in a tough fight for re-election, said Wednesday.

“He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine,” she added at a campaign stop at a factory in Norway, Maine.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who isn’t running for re-election following public disagreements with Trump, was blunter. “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” he posted on social media.

Freedom House, a nonprofit that works to expand freedom and democracy, describes Russia as an authoritarian country where power is “concentrated in the hands of President Vladimir Putin.” The Kremlin “manipulates elections and suppresses genuine dissent,” the group says.

Trump tends to see diplomacy through the prism of personal relations, and he has made no secret of his regard for Putin. When he hosted Putin for a summit meeting in Alaska last year in a futile attempt to end the war, the U.S. rolled out a red carpet. A picture of Trump and Putin standing side by side hangs in the White House’s Palm Room.

By contrast, Trump has stepped up his on-again, off-again criticism of Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As he left the White House on Monday for a campaign trip, he said Zelenskyy “is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

Blandishments are a tool Trump is using to get Putin to strike a deal, said Robert O’Brien, who was White House national security adviser in Trump’s first term. Not much else has worked.

“We thought we could get the war settled two years ago, but Putin has been intractable in not coming to the table. President Trump is using cordiality to get Putin to negotiate,” O’Brien said in an interview.

“There’d be no hope of getting Putin to engage in talks, with the U.S. as the mediator, if he viewed Trump as 100% aligned with Ukraine in this situation,” he added.

Michael Kimmage, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution think tank, said the Trump administration’s “theory of the case is that by distancing themselves from Ukraine and by flattering the Russians, they can accomplish something at the bargaining table.”

He doesn’t expect the gambit to succeed, though.

“In the absence of a clear agenda coming from the White House and in the absence of very serious forms of leverage over Russia — which the Trump administration has shied away from — progress at the negotiating table is very difficult to imagine,” he said.

Asked about Trump’s warmer attitude toward Putin in recent weeks, the White House pointed to his comments at a roundtable on cybercrime when he was asked about Witkoff labeling the Russian leader “a humanitarian.”

Trump responded: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose — for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out.”

He went on to add that the U.S. is negotiating with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and was complimentary towards Russia for having “not gotten involved with Iran.” Trump said that some “stupid people” were critical of his position and “the last thing I want to do is upset an apple cart where we’re getting close to settling a war.”

Ending the war between Russia and Ukraine was one of Trump’s signature promises in the 2024 campaign. He had confidently predicted he’d get it done on his first day back in office, but he has since conceded that the problem is more stubborn than he’d envisioned.

As Trump works to broker a peace deal, one of his recent gestures to Putin is to treat him as a statesman, rather than a global outcast.

Trump thanked Putin on Oct. 9 after they reached a deal in which Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel into global markets. Trump said the move would ease energy costs, but relief at the pump hasn’t happened yet. Since then, the average price of a gallon of diesel has risen 4 cents a gallon, from $6.26 to $6.30.

Trump invited Putin to attend the G20 international summit meeting at his Doral golf resort in Miami, and he said this week that he’s open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss nuclear weapons.

A summit meeting alongside the leaders of the world’s two largest economies would be a boon to Putin, whom the West has ostracized since Russia invaded Crimea in 2014. World leaders expelled Putin from an elite international organization called the G8 after that attack.

“There’s no question that Trump has been trying to reintegrate Putin into polite society,” said Brett Bruen, who was director of global engagement in the Obama White House.

At the G20 summit at Trump’s golf club in December, Putin would be “the shiny object that Trump would dangle in front of the world press corps as purported progress toward peace,” Bruen said.

A question Europeans are asking is what sort of peace deal does Trump visualize. Would it be fair to Ukraine or carve up the country at Putin’s behest, they ask? If Ukraine ceded territory to Putin as the price of ending the war, that would only embolden him to threaten more states, a European official said.

Marko Mihkelson, chairman of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee in Estonia, which borders Russia, said in an interview: “If you reward aggressors” and signal that they can “achieve their goals through aggression, then that doesn’t stop them from continuing.”

Faced with a war in Iran that he started and a war in Europe that he can’t stop, Trump is advised by a thinning inner circle. A senior aide, press secretary Karoline Leavitt, left the White House over the summer. Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., one of Trump’s confidants and a Russia hawk, died unexpectedly in July.

Two months later, Trump signed a bill named after Graham that sanctioned Russian officials and parts of the country’s economy.

Trump waived those sanctions last week — which Graham might have warned against in their many phone calls and golf games.

“Lindsey Graham is rolling over in his grave,” Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., told reporters Wednesday.

World.title: Trump’s growing list of campaign pledges: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we dive into the increasing number of promises President Donald Trump is making to persuade voters to back Republicans in the November elections. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines the fallout from Russia’s releasing an American from prison.

— Adam Wollner

Trump keeps promising ‘goodies’ if Republicans win the midterms

By Megan Shannon, Sarah Dean and Sahil Kapur

President Donald Trump is pledging to deliver “goodies” as he campaigns across the country — but only if voters keep Republicans in charge of Congress in the midterm elections.

Rallying Monday in Kansas, Trump promised a favorable policy move by his administration if Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is re-elected.

“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Trump said, referring to the sale of fuel blended with 15% ethanol, which is often restricted in the summer for environmental reasons. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.”

Yesterday in North Carolina, Trump vowed to instruct his Justice Department to settle claims by veterans regarding contaminated water at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune in North Carolina.

“If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible and get it off the books and get it finished,” Trump said. “If we don’t win, there’s no money. If we do win, you’re getting it, and it’s going to be finally over with that nightmare that’s been going on for so many years.”

And Saturday in Kentucky, Trump declared that the Defense Department will invest $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Anthea’s manufacturing facility based in the state.

“But you have to win, Andy. Otherwise, forget it,” he said, referring to GOP Senate candidate Andy Barr.

In some cases, delivering on his campaign trail promises would require Trump to have allies in Congress to pass them. But in other cases, Trump wields executive authority to make good regardless of the outcomes.

At nearly every one of his rallies, Trump touts his promise to send every American adult a $5,000 payment if Republicans hold the House and the Senate. But GOP leaders have made no such promise, and some key players on Capitol Hill doubt it would happen, saying they haven’t even seen a plan from Trump for where the funds would come from.

A recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll found that just 14% of U.S. adults expect to receive such payments in that scenario, while 71% don’t expect it. Even self-identified Republicans said by 47% to 28% that they don’t expect to see $5,000 payments.

Read more →

Witkoff’s praise for Putin draws bipartisan backlash

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

The diplomatic gifts Russian President Vladimir Putin has received from the Trump administration over the last 10 days have been considerable, undermining Ukraine and rattling U.S. allies throughout Europe — perhaps none more than special envoy Steve Witkoff’s declaration today that Putin is a “humanitarian.”

In St. Petersburg with Putin, Witkoff was expressing gratitude for Russia’s release of an American prisoner, Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia captured in Ukraine a few months after the start of the war. He was convicted by a court in Russia — which has long been accused of holding show trials — of serving as a mercenary, charges he denied.

Described by several former U.S. officials to NBC News as a “low level” prisoner who had not been working for the U.S. government, Hubbard, 74, a retired teacher, was not viewed by Moscow as able to garner a significant trade. Putin produced Hubbard at the perfect moment to build on his considerable advantage with President Donald Trump and generate favorable publicity. He could hardly have wished for anything better than to be described as a humanitarian by Witkoff, the top American negotiator.

Asked about Witkoff’s praise for Putin, Trump said: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out. But, you know, I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other.” He later credited Hubbard’s release to his waiving Russian sanctions he had just signed into law, as well as his personal request to Putin in their last telephone call.

Vice President JD Vance said the country should “celebrate” that an American hostage was coming home, not be “complaining about what Steve Witkoff said in order to get it done.” But outside the White House, Witkoff’s labeling of Putin drew bipartisan backlash.

Among Democrats, Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Mark Warner, D-Va., called it “insulting,” adding that the prime mover of the sanctions bill, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., was “rolling over in his grave.” House Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Jim Himes, D-Conn., said, “Donald Trump is on Putin’s side, and that’s why Witkoff says the kinds of things that he says.”

Meanwhile, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is a tough re-election campaign in Maine, said: “I would describe Putin as a warmonger. He’s certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine.” Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., was more graphic, writing on X: “WTF Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian.’ What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”

Witkoff and his fellow negotiator, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, also reported that Putin has agreed to restart trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine that have not been held since February. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said they should be held no later than November. There’s no word on whether Putin will accept the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced unilaterally a week and a half ago, which Zelenskyy adhered to for several days while Russia’s missiles pounded Kyiv and Kharkiv.

All this comes after Trump’s diesel deal with Russia gave Putin desperately needed revenue without lowering diesel prices in the U.S., according to energy experts. Plus, there has been a week of conflicting explanations for a sudden interruption in U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine and a slowdown in Ukraine’s vital connection to the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink.

After days of devastating Russian attacks on civilians in Kyiv and Kharkiv, Kristen Welker asked Zelenskyy on “Meet the Press” last weekend whether Ukraine can win the war without the U.S. He answered: “If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable. It’s tragedy. It’s historic mistake and big tragedy.” If that happened, Zelenskyy added, “of course we will not prevail.”

World.title: Mom whose son was found alive in morgue speaks out: ‘It’s an unexplainable feeling’
World.content:
The mother of a toddler found alive in an Arizona hospital morgue in February more than five hours after he was pronounced dead said Wednesday she thought she heard him breathing when she hugged him goodbye.

But instead of listening to her gut, Alexus Fiordilino said, she believed the doctor who told her those were 18-month-old Vincent’s last gasps and that any further attempts to save him would just prolong his agony.

“As a mom you don’t want to hear that,” Fiordilino, 30, said in an interview. “I didn’t want him to suffer. It seemed to be they’d done everything they could. And then he called it.”

Fiordilino was referring to Dr. Aryan Toosi, who pronounced Vincent dead at 6:20 p.m. on Super Bowl Sunday at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Arizona.

A little over five hours later, Fiordilino said, police were questioning her and her husband, Angelo, when a detective burst into the room and told them that a medical examiner’s employee who had come to collect Vincent’s body had discovered he was still alive.

“My husband and I just screamed in relief,” she said. “We were praising the Lord. We were crying. To go from hearing he was gone and then finding out he isn’t gone, it’s an unexplainable feeling.”

Fiordilino spoke out more than eight months after her son’s remarkable story of survival after he nearly drowned in the family swimming pool made national headlines and sparked multiple investigations into what happened on Feb. 8.

The Gilbert Police Department had recommended filing child abuse charges against both parents for losing track of Vincent while a Super Bowl party was going on at their residence.

“Both admitted to smoking marijuana the morning of the drowning,” the police report said.

But Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell announced in July that the Fiordilinos would not be charged.

Fiordilino’s lawyer, John Brewer, said he plans to file a formal complaint this week against Toosi and the hospital. He said a review of Vincent’s medical records shows that critical test results that Toosi cited to justify ending efforts to save the child were not completed until after the toddler was declared dead.

“The parents were faced with having to decide whether to keep trying to revive their son, and the doctor provided them with false information,” Brewer said. “That’s beyond a conscious disregard for human life.”

Brewer’s office turned its records over to the Gilbert Police Department, which said it forwarded everything to the state attorney general’s office for review. The AG’s office said Wednesday that it has not made a decision to review this case.

Toosi’s lawyer, Scott Holden, released a statement in response.

“Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” it said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.”

Meanwhile, the hospital called the situation “heartbreaking” in a statement.

“Out of respect for the patient’s privacy, we cannot share any information and we are unable to comment on those involved in patient care,” it said. “Patient safety and exceptional care are our highest priorities.”

Asked how Vincent is doing now, Fiordilino said, “He’s getting better.”

Brewer said that while the boy is home with his family, he has many health challenges.

“Vincent is severely brain-injured,” he said. “He can’t swallow. He seizes up. He can’t sit up on his own or crawl.”

The tragic turn of events began around 5:38 p.m. Feb. 8 with a 911 call for help after Vincent was found floating face down in the family pool and a relative tried to revive him by performing CPR, according to a police report obtained by NBC affiliate KPNX of Phoenix.

Vincent was rushed to the emergency room at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where an ER team that included Toosi took over the effort to save him.

At 6:13 p.m., according to the report, Toosi went out to deliver bad news to the boy’s parents.

Vincent Fiordilino. via GoFundMe

“As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call time of death,” Toosi said, according to the report.

Then, “at approximately 18:20 hours, Dr. Toosi called the time of death and requested a moment of silence.”

Just as Fiordilino told NBC News, police officers who had been in the ER said in the report that the child still appeared to be gasping for breath after he was declared dead.

A detective reported then hearing “another audible gasp” at around 7:18 p.m. as the ER workers were preparing to move Vincent from the trauma room to the “cold room” that serves as the hospital’s morgue and where the temperature is set at 36 to 39 degrees.

The same detective said that when he returned to photograph the body an hour later, he “again observed what appeared to be a gasp or air release.”

“The nurse again stated it was agonal breathing and explained it was due to compressions, oxygen, and possible pressure applied by family members while saying goodbye,” the report says.

And at 7:23 p.m., “the cold room door was closed,” the report says.

More than four hours later, when the medical examiner’s team arrived at 11:52 p.m. to retrieve the boy, “he was found breathing,” the report says.

“The family was notified immediately,” and the boy was airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.

Fiordilino said that when she saw her son again in the pediatric intensive care unit, “he was hooked up to all kinds of monitors and things.”

“He looked like a different baby,” she said. “It’s something I hope no other parent has to live through.”

World.title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
World.content:
Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.

"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."

To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.

"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."

The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.

Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."

The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.

"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.

A ban on Hinge

One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."

That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.

"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."

"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.

Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.

"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

World.title: Son of Stephen Hubbard, American freed from Russian jail, speaks out
World.content:
Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison.

"He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.

Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.

President Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release.

In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange.

"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.

Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.

Martin De Luca, Hubbard's U.S.-based attorney, told CBS News that when his legal team took on the case in February 2025, neither the family nor the U.S. Embassy knew precisely where Hubbard was being held.

Lawyers in Russia eventually located him and arranged for legal visits, money for food and basic necessities, and the brief phone call with his son.

De Luca said the isolation had taken an enormous toll.

"It's just being isolated from everybody you've ever known and just from the outside world," he said.

After Putin granted Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised the Russian president as a "humanitarian," prompting swift backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes involving the deportation of Ukrainian children, and Russian forces have been accused of widespread abuses during the war.

Asked about Witkoff's description of Putin, Coleman called his father's release "a small step toward peace in this greater conflict" and thanked Putin for signing off on the deal.

He described the decision as an act of "compassion and even mercy."

Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony following a closed-door trial.

His family has consistently disputed the charges.

Photo shared by President Trump and special envoy Steve Witkoff shows Stephen Hubbard on a plane with U.S. officials after being released from Russian detention, Oct. 21, 2026. @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social

De Luca said his legal team conducted its own investigation, interviewing people who knew Hubbard and examining his circumstances before the invasion. He said they found no evidence that Hubbard had served in the Ukrainian military or was physically capable of doing so at roughly 70 years old.

"We have not seen any evidence to support those allegations," De Luca said. He added that the Russian case file was largely sealed and that his team had repeatedly sought evidence substantiating the charges.

De Luca and Coleman both credited the Trump administration's diplomatic engagement with Moscow for securing Hubbard's freedom.

Asked whether recent U.S. decisions benefiting Russia — including sanctions relief and purchases of Russian diesel — were connected to Hubbard's release, De Luca said he did not believe there was a direct link, though he acknowledged that bilateral relationships involve multiple overlapping interests.

Mr. Trump, however, has explicitly said that allowing new sanctions to take effect would have prevented Hubbard's release.

And despite Hubbard's release, as many as 20 Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including some whose families dispute the charges against them. The State Department continues to warn Americans against traveling to Russia because of the risk of wrongful detention.

De Luca said he was not concerned that the administration's engagement with Moscow would encourage further detentions, arguing that diplomatic dialogue had helped secure several Americans' freedom.

But Russia has not been designated a state sponsor of wrongful detention under a new Trump administration policy, despite its history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges. Iran and Afghanistan have both received the designation.

Coleman stopped short of blaming his father for his circumstances but acknowledged he might have made a mistake by remaining in Ukraine as Russian forces advanced.

"The Russian forces told foreign nationals to leave and he did not," Coleman said. "I do not like what happened to my father. I am ecstatic that he is free. But he was living in an area that was a war zone."

"I'm not saying his detainment was justifiable. I'm not saying that," he said. "But these things happen in war."

World.title: Stephen Hubbard's son after his release from Russian prison: "I want to embrace him"
