World.title: Milei says Argentina will pursue the Falklands diplomatically: “We do not believe in military solutions”
World.content:
Milei says Argentina will pursue the Falklands diplomatically: “We do not believe in military solutions”

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 00:07 UTC Full article

At the same event, Milei defended his alliance with the United States and Israel

Argentine President Javier Milei said in Madrid on Wednesday that he is confident of recovering the Falklands through diplomacy and repeated three times that his government “does not believe in military solutions”, amid an escalating dispute with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

“The Malvinas are Argentine. In fact, Spain had bought them and when we took over the territory they became ours. The original population was Argentine and was expelled by the English,” he said at a breakfast organised by the Nueva Economía Forum. “We will keep negotiating until they return the islands, because we are the legitimate owners,” he added. Milei also said that “the geopolitical and demographic problems” the United Kingdom is facing represent “a risk for the region”, without specifying what he meant.

The United Kingdom maintains that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have the right to decide their own future. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The remarks come less than three weeks before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on November 10 and 11 on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. London has said it will take part in the proceedings and has approved measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions, while the sovereignty bill promoted by Milei, which toughens those sanctions, remains stalled in the Chamber of Deputies.

At the same event, Milei defended his alliance with the United States and Israel while championing trade with China: “The United States trades with China. So why can’t we trade too?”

World.title: Paraguay’s president travels to Washington and will meet the CIA director
World.content:
Paraguay’s president travels to Washington and will meet the CIA director

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 19:14 UTC Full article

Peña has declared himself an ally of the White House on foreign policy

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña travelled to Washington on Wednesday for a brief visit that includes a meeting with US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe and a keynote address at the annual gala of the Inter-American Dialogue think tank.

Peña will be away until Friday, accompanied by Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez and the head of the presidential Civil Cabinet, Javier Giménez, according to the Senate. The president confirmed he will be “meeting the CIA director”, without giving further details. He will also take up an invitation from George Washington University, and the Inter-American Dialogue gala will be held at the headquarters of the Organization of American States.

Before leaving, Peña accompanied US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in the Alto Paraná department on the final day of his official visit to Paraguay. The two toured a new military unit created to fight terrorism and organised crime in the Triple Frontier area with Brazil and Argentina, and the binational Itaipú dam. Landau is now continuing his tour in Buenos Aires.

Peña has declared himself an ally of the White House on foreign policy. In January he signed in Davos, together with Argentine President Javier Milei, the founding charter of the Board of Peace promoted by Donald Trump to oversee the Gaza peace plan, and Paraguay is a member of the Shield of the Americas, the regional security alliance promoted by Washington.

World.title: An unusual die-off of southern right whales in Argentine Patagonia alarms scientists
World.content:
An unusual die-off of southern right whales in Argentine Patagonia alarms scientists

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:44 UTC Full article

Neither researchers nor the provincial government will give an official figure until the season ends; unofficially, more than 300 dead whales are being mentioned

Scientists monitoring the southern right whale population at Península Valdés, in Argentina’s Chubut province, have recorded since July an unusual number of deaths among calves and adults which, they expect, could make this the worst year on record. They are investigating the role of a bacterium and of a toxic algal bloom known as “red tide”.

Neither researchers nor the provincial government will give an official figure until the season ends; unofficially, more than 300 dead whales are being mentioned. Until now, the highest figures recorded by the health monitoring programme run by the Whale Conservation Institute since 2003 were 113 dead calves in 2012 and 28 adults in 2022.

In calves, the deaths have been linked to the bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which causes erysipelas and can enter through wounds, such as gull bites, or through feeding, explained Mariano Coscarella of the Centre for the Study of Marine Systems at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet). In adults, the cause is still under study, although red tide, which caused the 2022 peak, is suspected. According to Coscarella, no evidence has been found that direct human activity caused the deaths, although climate change or El Niño may have influenced ocean conditions.

The health monitoring programme, led by veterinarian Marcela Uhart of the University of California, Davis, is carrying out necropsies and analyses and will add sampling of water and shellfish in the Nuevo and San José gulfs.

Península Valdés is South America’s largest sanctuary for southern right whales. The population visiting it grew from about 500 whales in the late 1990s to a peak of 2,110 in 2025; this year 1,375 were recorded, including 409 calves. The Whale Conservation Institute warned that, as this is a long-lived species, the consequences of a die-off “are not immediate and cannot be measured from isolated figures”.

World.title: Milei calls Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” in Madrid in the middle of Spain’s election campaign
World.content:
Milei calls Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” in Madrid in the middle of Spain’s election campaign

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:31 UTC Full article

Milei explained why he has not met Sánchez on any of his seven visits to Spain as head of state: “I’m not going to see a criminal thief like Pedro Sánchez”

Argentine President Javier Milei on Wednesday called Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator”, “corrupt” and “authoritarian”, and urged Spaniards to “kick the socialists out” of power, at his first public event in Madrid, just over a month before the snap general election on November 29.

At a breakfast organised by the Nueva Economía Forum, Milei explained why he has not met Sánchez on any of his seven visits to Spain as head of state: “I’m not going to see a criminal thief like Pedro Sánchez because I’m not willing to have to sew my pockets shut so I don’t get robbed.” He added: “Wherever there is an enemy of freedom, I will go and confront him.” Of Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, whom he will meet in the afternoon, and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, he said they “have healthy and positive ideas to lift Spain out of decline”.

The Socialist Party greeted him with a banner on the façade of its headquarters: “Hello Milei, we lefties welcome you to Spain, the fastest-growing country in Europe.” Sánchez released a video in which he says “I am a leftie”, in a reference to the term Milei uses to insult his left-wing opponents. In May 2024, Spain withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires after remarks by Milei about Sánchez’s wife.

The Argentine president linked his trip to his campaign for re-election in 2027. “If we are re-elected, the following four years will be unforgettable,” he said, inviting Spaniards to invest and settle in Argentina, which he said would become “the promised land where good business flows”. He also called the Argentine newspaper Clarín “corrupt” and its journalists “serial liars”.

Milei attributed not being received by King Felipe VI to scheduling problems. According to Royal Household sources quoted by El País, a meeting with the monarch must necessarily be accompanied by one with the prime minister. The Argentine president did not say whether he will attend the Ibero-American Summit, to be held in Madrid on November 4 and 5.

World.title: Lula ramps up public handouts in the final stretch of Brazil’s presidential campaign
World.content:
Lula ramps up public handouts in the final stretch of Brazil’s presidential campaign

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:21 UTC Full article

The largest items are the Bolsa Família increase and subsidies for taxi drivers, ride-hailing drivers, truckers and transport operators to renew their vehicles

Some 20 million Brazilian families begin receiving this week a 15% increase in the Bolsa Família social programme, the centrepiece of a broad package of aid, subsidies and tax cuts announced by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the final stretch of the campaign for Sunday’s runoff, in which he faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a statistical tie.

According to calculations by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, the measures announced by Lula over the past year, accelerating during the campaign, add up to almost 300 billion reais, about US$57 billion, over the rest of 2026 and 2027. The largest items are the Bolsa Família increase and subsidies for taxi drivers, ride-hailing drivers, truckers and transport operators to renew their vehicles. After the first round, the president also promised a payment of 5,000 reais to micro-entrepreneurs and partial forgiveness of their debts, scrapped taxes on fuel and pledged free public transport at weekends. Earlier he had launched a new personal debt renegotiation programme and banned online betting.

“This is my last campaign for president and I want this term to be historic,” Lula said on Tuesday at a rally in São Luís. The president, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, also challenged his rival to lift secrecy over his family’s assets and phone records, as he has pledged to the electoral court to do for his own.

Bolsonaro promises sharp cuts in public spending, which he put at 250 billion reais in Sunday’s debate, and says he will maintain Bolsa Família and other social programmes, though he has not explained how he will reconcile both goals. Brazil’s public debt stands at around 82% of GDP.

The measures have barely moved the polls, which still show a statistical tie with a slight edge for Bolsonaro, who won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%. The two candidates will face each other on Friday in their second and final debate, on TV Globo.

World.title: Amazon fires rise 62% in October as deforestation falls to a record low
World.content:
Amazon fires rise 62% in October as deforestation falls to a record low

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 13:29 UTC Full article

Satellites detected 9,045 fire hotspots in the Brazilian Amazon in the first half of October, 62% more than in the same period last year, amid a drought aggravated by El Niño. The increase contrasts with the fall in deforestation, which over the past year reached its lowest level since 1988.

The situation is particularly serious around Manaus, the capital of Amazonas state, home to more than two million people, which has been covered in smoke for weeks with air quality among the worst in the world. On Saturday, civil defence sent a “severe alert” to residents’ mobile phones urging them to stay at home, and classes were suspended at some schools. The federal government deployed more than 300 firefighters and 11 aircraft to support the fire services.

According to Ane Alencar, director of science at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute, most of the fires are set deliberately, generally to clear land for cattle, and the drought has turned the forest into a tinderbox. Alencar noted that September was the second month with the fewest fires on record and that the situation changed after the first round of the presidential election on October 4, and suggested as a hypothesis that the expectation of a change of government may have played a role: “I think the prevailing thought is ‘we won’t be punished’.” The head of the federal environment agency Ibama, Jair Schmitt, told the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo that the police and the intelligence agency are investigating whether there is “something orchestrated and structured”.

Between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,355 square kilometres of the Amazon were deforested, 42% less than in the previous period and the lowest figure since 1988, against 11,600 square kilometres in 2022. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government has set a target of zero deforestation by 2030.

The campaign of opposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces Lula in Sunday’s runoff, has used the smoke to criticise the government’s record. His programme proposes eliminating illegal deforestation by 2029 using artificial intelligence and satellite imagery. He has not responded to the researcher’s hypothesis.

World.title: The area of Antarctic ozone hole during September reached 15 million km2, says Copernicus
World.content:
The area of Antarctic ozone hole during September reached 15 million km2, says Copernicus

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 13:01 UTC Full article

“CAMS provides high-quality data, forecasts and analyses needed to understand the state of the ozone layer and track its long-term recovery,” Laurence Rouil said

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (*) has found that the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole reached a significant size threshold slightly earlier than average, aligned with 2025. It has also stayed ahead of average, unlike the previous year.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole has been developing at a typical rate since the second half of August, consistent with the previous 46 years. The area of this ozone hole reached 15 million km2 – more than the area of Antarctica, 14.2 million km2– by the end of August 2026, which was slightly earlier than average and similar to development of last year’s ozone hole, which reached the same area on 30 August 2025.

In the first half of September, the area of this year’s ozone hole increased sharply, to an estimated 25 million km2 on 12 September – around 5 million km2 above the average for this period – with forecasts showing a possible further increase in area in mid-September. Ozone depletion in the Southern Hemisphere stratosphere occurs as cold temperatures allow the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, which play a role in activating the chemical removal of ozone via halogens in the presence of sunlight during the austral Spring (August to November). The rapid development of the 2026 ozone hole coincided with a sudden decrease in the minimum temperature at approximately 20km above the South Pole (50 hectopascal / hPa).

However, other ozone hole diagnostics monitored by CAMS, including the ozone column minimum value within the defined area of the ozone hole and the ozone mass deficit, remained close to the average values.

“The Antarctic ozone hole’s development can vary considerably from year to year, depending on a range of atmospheric and chemical factors. While we have seen its area increase rapidly in early September this year, other indicators remain close to historical averages. These findings highlight the importance of monitoring the complicated interaction between human-made disturbances and natural factors. CAMS provides the high-quality data, forecasts and analyses needed to understand the state of the ozone layer and track its long-term recovery,” according to Laurence Rouil, Director of CAMS.

The ozone layer protects life on Earth against harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, a major cause of skin cancers, by absorbing much of it. Over almost half a century, human-caused emissions5 have resulted in the thinning of this protective layer, putting people at risk. Additionally, global warming tends to cool the stratosphere, which favors the formation of polar stratospheric clouds which, in turn, play a key role in ozone depletion. The thinning of the ozone layer is most pronounced over the Antarctic – where the area of low pressure and cold air (polar vortex) and stratospheric winds are more stable – with the ozone hole there opening each year during the austral Spring.

The Antarctic ozone hole, which has been monitored by ground-based and satellite observations since the late 1970s, spanned a record 29.6 million km2 on 9 September 2006. It also covered its largest average area over a consecutive multi-week period in that month. However, recent years have seen smaller and shorter-lived ozone holes, indicating recovery.

(*) Copernicus is the Earth observation component of the European Union’s Space program, looking at our planet and its environment to benefit all European citizens. The program is coordinated and managed by the European Commission and implemented in partnership with the Member States and European organizations.

The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) is both a research institute and a 24/7 operational service, producing global numerical weather predictions and other data for our Member and Co-operating States and the broader community. It operates a world-class supercomputer facility for weather forecasting and holds one of the largest meteorological data archives.

World.title: Falklands: UK Statement at the UN Fourth Committee on Decolonization
World.content:
Falklands: UK Statement at the UN Fourth Committee on Decolonization

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 10:15 UTC Full article

“Hydrocarbon activities on the Falkland Islands continental shelf are regulated under Falkland Islands law and conducted in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS”

Statement by Ambassador Kate Foster, UK Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, at the UN’s Special Political and Decolonization Fourth Committee. “The United Kingdom has no doubt about its sovereignty over both the Falkland Islands, and South Georgia, and the South Sandwich Islands, and their surrounding maritime areas”.

“Nor do we have any doubt about the Falkland Islanders’ right of self-determination.”

“This is enshrined in the UN Charter and in Article One of both UN covenants on human rights, by virtue of which they are free to determine their political status and pursue their economic, social, and cultural development.

“In the 2013 referendum, which was conducted in line with international standards and was observed by independent, international observers, 99.8 per cent of those who voted wanted to remain their current status as a British Overseas Territory.

“Argentina’s decision to initiate arbitration against the United Kingdom under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is the latest attempt to undermine the rights and livelihoods of the people of the Falkland Islands.

“The people of the Falkland Islands have freely and democratically chosen their future, and they have every right to develop and manage their natural resources without intimidation, coercion, or interference from others.

“Hydrocarbon activities on the Falkland Islands continental shelf are regulated under Falkland Islands law and conducted in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS.

“The United Kingdom will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Falkland Islands Government and the Falkland Islanders.

“We will robustly defend their wishes, their economy, and their right to determine their own future”.

World.title: Mexican Senate passes bill to limit, and sometimes prohibit, cash payments
World.content:
The Mexican Senate on Tuesday approved a bill to enact the Digital Economy Law for Digital and Electronic Payments, paving the way for a ban on cash payments at gas stations and highway tollbooths.

Seventy-three senators voted in favor of the bill while 34 senators voted against it. The bill was supported by the ruling Morena party, which controls both houses of Congress.

The Digital Economy Law will take effect after its promulgation by the federal government via publication in the Official Gazette of the Federation. President Claudia Sheinbaum submitted the bill to Congress and is expected to promptly sign it into law.

The law, approved by the Chamber of Deputies earlier this month, gives the federal Finance Ministry (SHCP) the authority to determine “the strategic sectors and relevant activities in which the acceptance of digital and electronic payment methods will be the only form of payment.”

Sheinbaum said in March that cash payments at gas stations and highway toll booths would be eliminated starting this year. She said on Wednesday that she expected government tax revenue would increase as a result of eliminating cash payments at gas stations and tollbooths.

While the law could enter into force as soon as this Thursday, it is not yet clear when cash payments at gas stations, toll booths and possibly some other locations will be eliminated. Morena lawmakers said that the transition will take place in an “orderly” fashion.

Unlike some other countries, cash is still widely used in Mexico.

Law aims to promote digital and economic payments across the economy

The federal Senate said in a statement that the aim of the Digital Economy Law for Digital and Electronic Payments is to “promote the adoption and implementation of these modes of payments in government procedures and in the purchase of goods and services.”

The law seeks to make digital and electronic payments more accessible to consumers, thus reducing the need for cash. It also seeks to encourage more businesses to accept digital and electronic payments, promote financial inclusion, combat tax evasion and increase traceability of transactions. Municipal, state and federal authorities will all be required to accept digital and electronic payments after the implementation of the law.

Morena Senator Emmanuel Reyes, president of the Senate’s Economy Committee, said Tuesday that the Digital Economy Law “establishes a framework of coordination” that allows authorities, financial institutions and other “participants in economic activity” to contribute to the broadening of access to digital and electronic payment methods.

The Senate said that the law seeks to make “new forms of payment” available to consumers, including payment through the use of “QR codes, near-field communication devices, debit and credit cards, direct deposits and transfers of funds, among other methods.”

The Senate also said that the law “incorporates the Digital CURP [identity code] and the Expediente Digital Ciudadano [a personal digital document file for government procedures] as trusted mechanisms for signing up for financial services.”

The law doesn’t ban cash payments at any businesses, but, as noted above, gives the Finance Ministry the power to ban them in “strategic sectors.” The SHCP will publish an initial list of the sectors that won’t be allowed to accept cash payments within 15 days of the law’s publication in the Official Gazette of the Federation.

The Senate noted that the law specifies that “the use of cash or checks” to pay for goods and services will be permitted in affected sectors if digital payment systems are temporarily unavailable for any reason.

Reyes: New law will benefit small and medium-sized businesses

Senator Reyes said that small and medium-sized business will have “the possibility of increasing their payment methods” as a result of the implementation of the new law.

He said that the adoption of digital and electronic payment methods will facilitate distance sales, reduce transaction times and aid the creation of “verifiable records” of businesses’ income.

Those records could allow financial institutions to have a better understanding of businesses’ “economic activity” and provide them with more information to evaluate the possibility of giving them a loan.

Last year, Sheinbaum signed an agreement with the Mexican Banking Association to boost credit access for small businesses, saying at the time that access to loans was a critical factor in stimulating economic growth. According to Reyes, the Digital Economy Law could further facilitate that access for both small and medium-sized businesses.

Opposition senator says new law promotes exclusion, not inclusion

Senator Francisco Daniel Barreda of the Citizens Movement party said that promoting the digitalization of payments is not a problem in itself.

“The problem,” he said, “is forcing” people to stop using cash by making digital and electronic payments “the only form of payment” accepted in some sectors.

“From a government office, the activities for which a person can no longer pay cash can be decided,” Barreda said.

“… One thing is giving people more options and another very different thing is taking people’s options away. That’s not [financial] inclusion, it’s digital exclusion,” he said.

National Action Party (PAN) Senator José Máximo García suggested that the government and ruling party are out of touch with the reality in Mexico, where cash is the most commonly used payment method.

“Morena is seeking to eliminate cash? What country do they live in? Which Mexico are they legislating for?” he asked.

García also said that “forcing” small and medium businesses to offer digital payment methods obliges them to connect to the internet, “rent a [payment] terminal” and pay bank commissions ranging from 1.5% to 4.5% of the value of each sale.

“… As a small business can’t absorb that cost, it will increase the price of eggs, milk and tortillas,” he said.

“Congratulations to the government! They invented digital inflation by decree,” García said.

The PAN senator also accused the government of “voracity” for tax income.

The law might have “a pretty wrapping of modernization” and “financial inclusion,” but it is in fact “tax collection voracity and [wolf-like] tax inspection in sheep’s clothing,” García said.

“… They’re coming to take the last centavos from people’s pockets,” he said.

Institutional Revolutionary Party Senator Claudia Anaya questioned the viability of the law given that 55% of workers in Mexico are employed in the informal economy — and thus are normally paid in cash — while millions of people don’t use the internet and a large number of adults don’t have bank accounts.

Morena Senator Gerardo Fernández Noroña sought to counter the criticism of the law by claiming that opposition lawmakers were defending “corrupt people who receive money in cash.”

With reports from Expansión, El Economista, El Financiero, Imagen Radio and Excélsior

World.title: The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 2: Education
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND MEXICO WELL-BEING SERIES

A data-driven look at well-being in Mexico

MND Intelligence · Part 2: Education

Last month, we launched the MND Mexico Well-being series, a collection of articles designed to complement — and more importantly, supplement — the MND Sheinbaum Index™ and the MND Economy Index™, both of which we publish on a monthly basis.

Part 1 of the series focused on eight key health and healthcare indicators.

In the inaugural article, we noted that the MND Mexico Well-being series would present a range of data that is directly relevant to Mexicans’ well-being, including indicators in the areas of education, healthcare, poverty, happiness and gender equality.

In this series, we draw on the most recent internationally comparable data, as well as data from the past decade, to compare Mexico to other countries and assess what has changed in Mexico during the eight years that the ruling Morena party has been in office.

As we previously noted, improving the well-being of Mexico’s most disadvantaged people is a stated priority of both Morena and President Sheinbaum.

Today, we continue the MND Mexico Well-being series with Part 2, which focuses on education. As with health and healthcare, there are numerous education indicators we could examine. For this article, we selected eight that we believe are among the most important.

Before we delve into the data, it’s worth remembering that the majority of Mexican primary and secondary school students (around 84% in the 2024-25 school year) are enrolled in Mexico’s public education system rather than the private education system.

Just as patients’ experiences can vary considerably within and between Mexico’s public and private healthcare systems, students’ experiences can differ widely within and between its public and private education systems, depending on the resources, facilities and teaching staff available.

One issue that causes periodic disruptions in education in Mexican public schools — particularly in some states — is teachers’ protests and strikes. For example, almost 20,000 schools across Mexico — including 95% of those in Oaxaca — closed for a period last year while CNTE union-affiliated teachers were on strike. Teacher absenteeism is another story, which MND has covered extensively over the years.

Below you will find a snapshot of education in Mexico. In parentheses after the subheading for each of the eight indicators we present is Mexico’s comparative position among the countries for which comparable OECD data was available, expressed as a decile where the size of the comparison group allows for one.

Before we look at each of the eight education indicators, a reminder that we are always interested in hearing about your views on the issues we cover. What do you think about education in Mexico? Please share your views or experiences in the comments section below.

* The data in this article comes from the OECD “Education at a Glance 2026” report, unless otherwise specified.

EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATION ENROLLMENT RATES (bottom decile)

According to UNICEF, “Decades of evidence show that the first few years of a child’s life are critical in supporting their physical, mental, and emotional development long-term.”

“Because of how quickly children’s brains and bodies are growing – particularly in the first three years of life – the experiences they have can have lifelong effects. One of the experiences that can help is high-quality early childhood education and care (ECEC),” UNICEF says.

Consequently, we chose to include Mexico’s ECEC enrollment rates in this report.

Among two-year-old children in Mexico in 2024, just 4% were enrolled in early childhood educational development programs that meet the criteria of the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) by combining education and care. The OECD average was significantly higher at 50%. Mexico ranked last on this measure among 30 OECD and OECD partner/accession countries for which comparable data were available.

Among children between the age of 3 and the starting age of primary education, 75% were enrolled in ECEC in Mexico in 2024. The OECD average was 90%. Mexico ranked 42nd on this measure among 46 OECD and OECD partner/accession countries for which comparable data were available. It was thus in the lowest decile among the countries assessed. The only countries with lower enrollment rates than Mexico in 2024 were Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Indonesia and Costa Rica.

According to a 2021 Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) report, public child care services in Mexico “are fragmented across various institutional agencies serving different population groups — largely children of formal workers, with different care modalities and different regulatory frameworks.”

In a country where more than half of workers are employed in the informal sector, “these many factors make coordination in the child care sector very challenging and exacerbate inequalities in access,” according to the IADB.

Has Mexico improved on these indicators over the past decade?

No.

The early childhood education enrollment rate was 5% among two-year-olds in Mexico in 2015, one percentage point higher than in 2024. The OECD average was 40% in 2015. The gap between the enrollment rate in Mexico and the OECD average widened from 35 points in 2015 to 46 in 2024.

The ECEC enrollment rate in Mexico among children between the ages of 3 and the starting age of primary education was 79% in 2015, four points higher than in 2024. The OECD average was 86% in 2024. The gap between the enrollment rate in Mexico and the OECD average widened from 7 points in 2015 to 15 in 2024.

EXPENDITURE ON EDUCATION AS A PERCENTAGE OF GDP (bottom decile)

In 2023, Mexico’s government spent the equivalent of 2.9% of GDP on education, well below the OECD average of 4.2%.

Among 42 countries included in the “Education at a Glance 2026” report, Mexico ranked 39th on this measure, placing it in the bottom decile. The only countries that spent lower proportions of their GDP on education in 2023 were Ireland, Romania and Japan.

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

No.

In 2015, Mexico spent the equivalent of 4.4% of GDP on education. Thus, Mexico’s expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP declined 1.5 percentage points between 2015 and 2023.

In 2015, Mexico’s expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP was on par with the OECD average, whereas in 2023, its spending was 1.3 points below the average.

The OECD noted that Mexico was one of various countries (including Brazil, Ireland and Bulgaria) that recorded a “notable” decrease in expenditure on education between 2015 and 2023.

EDUCATIONAL ATTAINMENT RATES (second lowest decile and below)

In 2025, according to the OECD, 40% of Mexicans aged 25-34 didn’t have an upper secondary education (prepa) qualification. That percentage is well above the OECD average of 12%.

Among 47 countries included in the “Education at a Glance 2026” report, Mexico ranked 44th on this measure, placing it in the bottom decile. The only countries with a higher proportion of 25-34-year-olds without an upper secondary education qualification were India (56%), Indonesia (42%) and South Africa (42%).

In 2025, 28% of Mexican men aged 25-34 had a tertiary education qualification, while the figure for Mexican women of the same age was 30%. The figure for men was 12 points below the OECD average. The figure for women was 24 points below the OECD average.

Among 45 countries included in the OECD report, Mexico ranked 39th for its tertiary attainment rate both among men and among women aged 25-34, placing it in the second lowest decile.

Has Mexico improved on these indicators over the past decade?

Yes.

In 2015, the share of 25-34-year-olds in Mexico without upper secondary attainment was 55% — 15 points higher than in 2025.

The gap between the share of Mexicans without upper secondary attainment and the OECD average was 38 points in 2015. The gap in 2025 was 28 points.

The OECD said that Mexico has made “significant progress” in reducing the percentage of the population without an upper secondary education qualification.

The percentage of Mexicans aged 25-34 with tertiary qualifications increased from around 21% in 2015 to 29% in 2025.

TEACHER QUALIFICATIONS (fourth-lowest decile and below)

Preschool, primary school and lower secondary school teachers in Mexico are supposed to have a bachelor’s degree or equivalent, but not all of them do.

In 2024, around two in ten pre-primary teachers in Mexico, and about one in ten primary and lower secondary teachers, didn’t meet the minimum national educational attainment requirements. The exact numbers were as follows:

In 2024, 82% of pre-primary teachers in Mexico met the education attainment requirement, five percentage points below the OECD average of 87%.

In 2024, 92% of primary teachers in Mexico met the education attainment requirement, four points above the OECD average of 88%.

In 2024, 87% of lower secondary teachers in Mexico met the education requirement, two points below the OECD average of 89%.

For its share of teachers meeting national minimum educational attainment requirements, Mexico ranked equal 17th out of 23 countries at preschool level, 17th out of 27 countries at primary level and 27th out of 37 countries at lower secondary level.

These positions placed Mexico in the third-lowest decile for preschool and lower secondary school teachers, and the fourth-lowest decile for primary school teachers.

Has Mexico improved on these indicators over the past decade?

No.

The percentage of teachers meeting the bachelor’s-level educational attainment requirement fell from 87% to 82% in preschool, from 97% to 92% in primary school and from 93% to 87% in lower secondary school between 2017 and 2024 — declines of 5, 5 and 6 percentage points, respectively.

AVERAGE CLASS SIZES IN PRIMARY AND LOWER SECONDARY EDUCATION (second/third lowest decile)

According to the OECD, “Smaller classes are often perceived as allowing teachers to focus more on the needs of individual students and reducing the amount of class time needed to deal with disruptions.”

“They contribute to a better learning environment for the students, and to improved working conditions for teachers and staff,” the OECD says.

In Mexico, average class sizes in primary schools and lower secondary schools in 2024 were above the OECD average, but not by much.

Across all primary schools (both public and private), the average class size in Mexico was 23 students in 2024. The OECD average was 21 students.

Across all lower secondary schools (secundaria), the average class size in Mexico was 25 students in 2024. The OECD average was 23.

The average primary school class size in Mexico in 2024 was larger than those in 30 of 38 countries for which comparable data were published in the OECD report. Three other countries also had average primary school class sizes of 23 students: Australia, the Netherlands and Türkiye. Among the countries with larger average primary school class sizes in 2024 were Japan (26), the United Kingdom (26) and Chile (30). The United States was just below the OECD average, with an average of 20 students per class.

Mexico ranked in the second-lowest decile on this measure, on the basis that smaller class sizes are considered better.

The average lower secondary class size in Mexico in 2024 was larger than those in 27 of 38 countries. Spain and Brazil also had average secondary class sizes of 25 students. Among the countries with larger average lower secondary class sizes in 2024 were Colombia (27), Costa Rica (28), Chile (31), Japan (32) and Thailand (36). Once again, the United States was just below the OECD average, with an average of 21 students per class

Mexico ranked in the third lowest decile on this measure.

Has Mexico improved on these indicators over the past decade?

Yes and no.

The average primary school class size in Mexico in 2015 was 22 students, one fewer than in 2024. The gap between the average primary school class size in Mexico and the OECD average increased to two in 2024 from one in 2015. Therefore, Mexico did not improve on the primary school class size indicator.

The average lower secondary class size in Mexico in 2015 was 28 students, three more than in 2024. The gap between the average lower secondary school class size in Mexico and the OECD average declined to two in 2024 from five in 2015. Therefore, Mexico improved on the lower secondary school class size indicator.

PISA SCORES (sixth decile and below)

Mexican 15-year-old students performed below the OECD averages in reading, science, mathematics and computational problem solving, according to the results of the 2025 PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) tests.

As Mexico News Daily reported when the results were published in September, Mexican students recorded the following scores:

408 points in reading, 53 points below the OECD average (461).

414 points in science, 68 points below the OECD average (482).

388 points in mathematics, 75 points below the OECD average (463).

453 in computational problem solving, 47 points below the OECD average (500).

In reading, Mexico ranked equal 52nd out of 90 countries and jurisdictions, placing it in the sixth (or fifth-lowest) decile. Albania and Brazil tied with Mexico, with all three countries scoring 408 points in reading.

In science, Mexico ranked equal 63rd out of 91 countries and jurisdictions, placing it in the seventh (or fourth lowest) decile. Colombia tied with Mexico, with both countries scoring 414 points in science.

In mathematics, Mexico ranked equal 64th out of 90 countries and jurisdictions, placing it in the eighth (or third-lowest) decile. Jordan tied with Mexico, with both countries scoring 388 points in math.

In the science/math/reading triad, 41.8% of Mexican students scored below the basic level. That percentage is more than double the OECD average of 19.7%.

Have Mexico’s PISA results improved over the past decade?

No.

Mexico’s scores in reading, science and mathematics were all lower in 2025 than in 2015.

The largest decline was in mathematics (-20 points), followed by reading (-15 points) and science (-2 points).

Mexico was by no means alone in recording lower PISA scores in 2025 than in 2015.

The OECD said that “over the most recent decade (2015-2025), the trend in performance has been negative in all three core subjects, on average across 35 OECD countries with available data.”

The declines in the OECD average PISA scores in reading, science and mathematics exceeded the decreases in Mexico. Thus, the gap between Mexico’s scores and the OECD averages narrowed between 2015 and 2025.

STUDENTS’ EXPOSURE TO BULLYING (fifth decile)

According to the OECD, “Bullying undermines students’ sense of safety and belonging at school and can have lasting detrimental consequences for learning and well-being.”

According to the 2025 PISA results, 19.5% of Mexican students aged 15 and 16 reported being bullied at least a few times a month at school. That percentage is just below the OECD average of 19.6%.

Mexico’s bullying breakdown was as follows:

10.7% of students said other students made fun of them.

3.5% of students said they were threatened by other students.

4.7% of students said they got hit or pushed around by other students.

12.1% of students said other students spread nasty rumors about them.

2.8% of students said that information about them that was upsetting was published online without their consent.

Out of 88 countries and jurisdictions for which bullying data is included in the latest PISA results report, Mexico has the 38th lowest bullying rate. Mexico is therefore in the fifth decile, with the first decile representing the lowest bullying rates and the tenth the highest.

The bullying rates in Vietnam and Hungary (19.9% in both countries) and in Canada (19.3%) in 2025 were similar to Mexico’s rate.

Has Mexico’s bullying rate declined over the past decade?

Yes.

In 2015, 20.2% of Mexican students reported being bullied at least a few times a month, according to the 2015 PISA results report. That is 0.6 percentage points higher than in 2025.

Mexico’s bullying rate was 1.5 percentage points above the OECD average in 2015 (18.7%).

As indicated above, Mexico’s bullying rate was 0.1 percentage points below the OECD average in 2025.

NEET RATE (third lowest decile)

According to the OECD, “Youth and young adults who are neither employed nor in education or training (NEET) are a key policy concern, as prolonged periods of inactivity at a young age can have lasting negative effects on socio-economic outcomes later in life.”

In Mexico, 19% of all 18-24-year-olds were NEET in 2025. That percentage was five points above the OECD average of 14%.

Young women were much more likely than young men to be NEET in 2025. The rate was 29% for women, compared to 10% for men.

People who aren’t studying or working are colloquially (or pejoratively) known as ninis (ni estudia ni trabaja) in Mexico.

In the “Education at a Glance 2026” report, the OECD says that “national averages often mask significant subnational variations, as regional disparities in labour-market conditions and access to education can create very different outcomes for youth within the same country.”

“… The most pronounced regional disparities in NEET rates are seen in Canada, Italy, Mexico, Romania and Türkiye, where the gaps between the regions with the highest and lowest NEET rates reach or exceed 20 percentage points,” the OECD says.

Among 41 countries for which the OECD published comparable data, Mexico had the joint ninth-highest NEET rate in 2025, tied with Chile and Greece. In other words, thirty of the 41 countries had lower NEET rates than Mexico, including Czechia (7%), Australia (10%), Canada (13%) and the United States (14%).

Among the countries with higher NEET rates than Mexico were Israel (20%), Brazil (22%), Colombia (26%) and South Africa (48%).

Has Mexico improved on this indicator over the past decade?

Yes.

In 2015, 23% of all 18-24-year-olds in Mexico were NEET, four percentage points higher than in 2025.

The gap between the NEET rate in Mexico and the OECD average declined to five percentage points in 2025 from seven percentage points in 2015.

The overall picture

Mexico’s education performance compares poorly with that of the other countries assessed across most of the eight indicators examined in this article. Early childhood education enrollment and government education spending as a share of GDP are well below OECD averages, while the proportion of young adults without an upper secondary qualification remains high, despite a significant decline over the past decade. Mexican students also score below OECD averages in reading, science, mathematics and computational problem solving.

The data in this report reveal challenges at several stages of education, from limited participation in early childhood programs to weak learning outcomes among teenagers and relatively low tertiary attainment among young adults. Low public spending and declining shares of teachers meeting minimum educational attainment requirements add to the concerns. However, Mexico is close to OECD averages on some indicators: average class sizes are only modestly above OECD averages, while reported exposure to bullying is slightly lower than the OECD average.

The longer-term picture is mixed. Over the past 10 years or so, Mexico has made significant progress in reducing the share of young adults without an upper secondary qualification, while tertiary attainment has increased. The proportion of young people neither employed nor in education or training has also fallen, although young women remain much more likely than young men to be in that situation. Lower secondary class sizes have decreased, and reported bullying has declined slightly.

However, other trends are less encouraging. Early childhood enrollment rates and education spending as a share of GDP have fallen, as have the shares of teachers meeting minimum educational attainment requirements. Mexico’s PISA scores have also declined. Although the gaps with OECD average scores have narrowed, that reflects larger declines in OECD PISA score averages rather than improvements in Mexican students’ performance.

As with health and healthcare, the data in this report should not be read as a verdict on a single administration. The periods examined span several federal governments, and educational attainment among today’s adults reflects schooling received over many years.

A 34-year-old who was counted among Mexicans with a tertiary qualification by the OECD in 2025 was a pre-school student in the mid-1990s, when Mexico was still a virtual one-party state under the rule of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. That timeline underscores how educational success, or failure, reflects a combination of factors — including access to educational opportunities, family circumstances, teaching quality and policy choices — spanning decades and successive governments.

What is the federal government doing to improve education outcomes and education and training in Mexico?

Listed below are some of the education initiatives that have been implemented in Mexico in recent years or are currently in the process of being implemented. Click the links in the bullet points to read more about the different initiatives.

As the case with recent healthcare programs and policies, the success and wisdom of the various education initiatives outlined above are debated in some cases. As expected, the government defends them while opposition parties have been critical of some of the initiatives.

World.title: 4 white rhinos from France and Germany find a home in Guadalajara
World.content:
Four white rhinoceroses arrived in Guadalajara from Europe on Wednesday in an effort to preserve genetic diversity as successful breeding leaves European zoos running short of space.

The three females and one male traveled aboard an Air France cargo flight from Paris after more than a year of preparation.

Their destination, the Guadalajara Zoo — possibly one of the “happiest” zoos in Latin America — already features rhinos in its safari attraction, and other Mexican facilities also keep rhinos: Africam Safari in Puebla houses black rhinos, while the León Zoo in Guanajuato state has a white rhino named Yuri.

The new arrivals are Salma, 5, and Moana, 9, from Serengeti Park Hodenhagen in Germany; Lewa, 4, from Safari de Peaugres in France; and Wami, a 15-year-old male from the Paris Zoo.

Their relocation is part of conservation and captive breeding programs coordinated by the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria.

Wami’s genetic lineage is particularly valuable in the Americas because it’s not represented there, said Alexis Lécu, the Paris Zoo’s scientific director.

Meanwhile, Europe’s captive breeding program has “less and less space” as rhino reproduction programs succeed, Lécu told the newspaper La Jornada.

European association members hold 326 white rhinos across 83 parks, with five to 10 births annually across the continent, La Jornada reported.

An estimated 15,752 white rhinos were in the wild at the end of 2024, down 25% from more than 21,000 in 2023, according to the International Rhino Foundation’s 2026 report. Poaching remains the major threat — which is why captive-breeding programs are viewed as vital.

Wami — who was born at the Beauval Zoo in Saint-Aignan, France, on Oct. 16, 2011 (belated happy birthday!) — has already had his sperm used for assisted reproduction in European parks. The same is expected to occur in North America.

Getting the rhinos aboard was no small undertaking.

The transfer required more than a year of preparation, including months spent familiarizing the rhinos with their transport crates so they could enter calmly, Guadalajara Zoo officials said.

It reportedly took more than an hour to get Wami, who weighs 2.4 tonnes (about 5,300 pounds), into his container for the 12-hour flight that arrived early Wednesday morning.

Visitors will have to wait to meet the hefty newcomers.

The rhinos, which can live for 35 to 40 years in captivity, will undergo quarantine, examinations and an adjustment period. The newspaper El Heraldo de México reported they would spend 40 days in dedicated accommodations while adapting.

The zoo will announce their public debut after assessing their progress.

The Guadalajara Zoo occupies about 124 acres of developed grounds, according to its website. It houses more than 7,000 animals representing 300 species, the zoo’s general director, Luis Soto Rendón, said on Imagen Radio last week.

He called the quartet’s arrival “the culmination of an extraordinary effort.”

With reports from El Heraldo de México, La Jornada, El Informador and Guadalajara Secreta

World.title: 24 hours later, protesters are still blocking the Mexico-Toluca highway
World.content:
The blockade of the Mexico City-Toluca highway passed the 24-hour mark Wednesday morning, causing severe delays and kilometer-long lines as hundreds of motorists were prevented from reaching the capital.

The protest is taking place at kilometer 48+500 in Lerma in the Mexico City-bound lanes, near the Constituyentes interchange. It is the work of relatives of missing persons, who are demanding a formal dialogue with Mexico state Attorney General José Luis Cervantes Martínez to discuss unresolved cases

The closure started in both directions on Tuesday around 11:00 a.m. and continued through the night even as temperatures dropped and rain fell on protesters. The Toluca-bound side of the highway reopened on Tuesday afternoon.

The protesters have let vehicles pass for brief periods, allowing some to continue their journeys, although the road remains heavily congested. Some truck drivers, stranded overnight, were forced to sleep in their vehicles.

The blockade is said to be led by the Flores en el Corazón (Flowers in the Heart) collective, as well as members of the Madres Mariposas Buscadoras (Searching Butterfly Mothers) and Buscando Justicia (Searching for Justice) groups.

Families are seeking detailed information about more than 40 disappearance cases, some of which have remained unsolved for over a decade.

The remaining duration of the blockade is uncertain and will largely depend on negotiations between the collectives and the authorities of México state. Meetings were held with authorities from the Attorney General’s Office of México state early on Wednesday morning, but no agreement was reached to end the blockade.

There have been numerous reports on social media of violent clashes between motorists and protesters over the ongoing closure.

There have been additional reports of a blockade on the alternative Libramiento Bicentenario (Bicentennial Bypass) route near Xonacatlán.

Alternatie routes to avoid the blockade

Motorists heading from Toluca to Mexico City are advised to use alternative routes and check traffic reports before leaving, with heavy congestion expected due to detours.

Alternative routes include:

The Toluca-Naucalpan Highway

World.title: El Jalapeño: Ministry of Agriculture reassures nation no Mexican agave will escape fermentation
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Following exhaustive botanical reviews, federal agriculture officials confirmed Tuesday that every last specimen of native Mexican agave will eventually be accounted for, fermented, distilled or otherwise converted into an intoxicating spirit, reassuring a watchful public that no succulent will be left behind to pursue a pointless career as mere flora.

According to a sweeping directive released by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (SADER), Mexican researchers have successfully mapped more than a dozen distinct traditional beverages — including tequila, mezcal, pulque, bacanora, raicilla, tutsi and tepe — but warned that allowing any of the country’s 159 endemic species to complete their natural life cycle without encountering a copper alembic would constitute a historic administrative failure.

“We have documented agaves that resemble artichokes, agaves that resemble octopuses and specimens that grow 33-foot flower stalks at a rate of four inches a day,” said lead research coordinator Dr. Mateo Escalante, standing beside an experimental fermentation vat containing a rare Agave parviflora. “Yet, despite these incredible evolutionary adaptations, our mandate is absolute: no agave shall evade the barrel.”

The report noted that while pre-Hispanic societies historically utilized the agave plant for structural fibers, construction materials and sewing needles, modern bureaucratic planning has successfully streamlined the plant’s destiny toward liquid form. Officials acknowledged that while smaller varieties may yield little more than a thimble of artisanal spirit per harvest, diligent planning ensures that even roadside succulents will find their way into a clay copita.

Addressing historical anomalies, such as Sonora’s 1915 prohibition on bacanora designed to prevent moral perversion, SADER officials emphasized that government policy has fully pivoted. Rather than restricting regional output, the current administration actively monitors the nation’s flora to guarantee that every municipality exercises its legal right to produce a smoky, high-proof distillate from whatever happens to be growing in the dirt.

“Our ancestors spent thousands of years discovering that Agave tequilana flowers in seven years while Agave deserti takes 55,” Escalante added. “Our duty to future generations is to ensure that no matter how long a plant takes to mature, a distillation schedule is waiting for it the moment it ripens.”

World.title: Over 2,500 arrested for fuel theft since October 2024: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⛽ Mexico targets fuel theft with thousands of arrests: Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling. 🔥🇺🇸 Sheinbaum: No commitment to buy more U.S. natural gas: Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants.

Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants. ✈️ Sheinbaum praises Ambassador Johnson despite disagreements: The president said U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson “has helped us on many issues,” including by providing assistance to Mexico to get U.S. restrictions on new flights from Mexico City airports AICM and AIFA lifted. She acknowledged her government has disagreed with some of his public remarks, including his comments on corruption in Mexico, but stressed that Mexico wants “the best possible relationship with the United States.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

At President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference, Energy Ministry officials provided an update on the government’s fight against fuel theft (known colloquially as huachicol or huachicoleo) and a fuel smuggle/tax evasion scheme known as huachicol fiscal. Both crimes have cost the federal government and state oil company Pemex huge amounts of money in lost revenue.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as the president told reporters that Mexico has not made any commitment to purchase more natural gas from the United States, as U.S. President Donald Trump has reportedly urged it to do.

Mexico is already heavily reliant on the United States for its natural gas supplies.

On Wednesday morning, Sheinbaum also offered praise for U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson, highlighting that he assisted Mexico in its efforts to have U.S. restrictions lifted on new flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport.

More than 2,500 huachicol-related arrests since Sheinbaum took office

Juan José Vidal Amaro, deputy energy minister for hydrocarbons, reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol offenses since the government took office in October 2024.

He said that authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles used to transport fuel as well as 173.7 million liters of fuel.

Vidal said that the data provides evidence of the progress that has been made in combating “illegal activities in the fuel market.”

Earlier in the press conference, he reported that 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without holding the applicable permits. Vidal also said that 2,032 gas stations have been fined for not having adequate “volumetric controls” on their gas pumps.

In addition, the deputy minister said that 180 companies have been removed from the government’s registry of approved fuel importers due to their alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Sheinbaum says Mexico hasn’t agreed to purchase more natural gas from the US

A reporter raised the possibility of Mexico purchasing more natural gas from the United States in order to reduce the U.S. deficit in the bilateral trade relationship. “Wouldn’t this be a backward step for Mexico in the quest for energy sovereignty?” she asked the president.

Sheinbaum responded that Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to purchase more gas from the United States.

Her remarks came almost two weeks after the Financial Times reported that she and U.S. President Donald Trump had “discussed the prospect of Mexico increasing purchases of U.S. natural gas, on which it already depends for about three-quarters of its demand.”

Sheinbaum acknowledged that the possibility of Mexico buying more U.S. gas is “something that the United States has put on the table” as the Trump administration seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico.

“It’s not that they’re particularly interested in selling more gas,” she said, explaining that what Trump is interested in is reducing the United States’ trade deficit with Mexico, which increased more than 20% year over year in the first eight months of 2026 to reach almost US $156 billion.

Sheinbaum said that her government has told its U.S. counterpart that its objective is to produce more gas in Mexico, in part to ensure sufficient supplies for new combined-cycle power plants.

“If for any reason we can’t produce the gas [needed for new power plants] in Mexico, we’ll have to get the natural gas from somewhere. But the objective is to produce it in the country,” she said.

The government is open to using fracking to boost natural gas production in Mexico, but no clear timeline has emerged for when new projects could begin.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena told Congress earlier this month that, “the conditions for proceeding with hydraulic fracturing operations currently do not exist, nor is there any authorization from the president.”

Sheinbaum: Ambassador Johnson ‘has helped us on many issues’

A reporter asked the president about her recent description of U.S. Ambassador Johnson as “a good ally of Mexico” shortly after she called on him to respect Mexico’s laws in light of the United States cooperation with the state of Querétaro on an “international police training academy” project that hadn’t been authorized by the federal government.

Sheinbaum responded that Johnson, ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, “has helped us on many issues.”

She said that Johnson helped her government “a lot” on the issue of “air transport” after the United States last year revoked approval for existing and planned flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA).

The U.S. Department of Transportation last week lifted restrictions on new flights to the U.S. from AICM and AIFA, allowing Mexican airlines to launch new routes to U.S. airports. The lifting of the restrictions — which were imposed due to aviation disputes between Mexico and the U.S. — will allow U.S.-bound passenger flights to depart from AIFA for the first time.

Sheinbaum said that Johnson worked with Mexican and U.S. officials on the “whole process” related to Mexico’s efforts to have the U.S. restrictions lifted.

“We have to say it, and finally the [U.S.] sanction was lifted,” she said.

“[Johnson] helped on this issue,” Sheinbaum said.

“There are other issues on which the ambassador helped us,” she added.

Sheinbaum acknowledged that her government has disagreed with some of Johnson’s public remarks, including those he made about corruption in Mexico during an address in Sinaloa in April. She said that she and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have expressed their disagreement to the ambassador.

“But there are issues on which he has helped us,” Sheinbaum reiterated.

“… We don’t have any problem in saying it. What do we want? The best possible relationship with the United States, always with respect for our sovereignty and respect for our compatriots in the United States,” she said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Hurricanes keep coming, golf course disruption, free drinking water fountains
World.content:
It is feeling a little bit like “Groundhog Day” in Puerto Vallarta as we closely watch the trajectory of Hurricane Trudy, the fourth hurricane to come our way in recent weeks. If we are lucky, the storm will follow the path that Polo, Rachel and Simón took and skirt the coast without making landfall. While the storms’ impacts have been relatively moderate in Vallarta, they have caused flooding on the Baja California peninsula and El Niño-linked erosion damage in Southern California, and our hearts go out to communities affected.

Major headlines this month include the ordered demolition of a controversial condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit; infrastructure issues and the tragic loss of five lives due to recent storms; the rollout of a new program to bring free drinking water fountains to schools, sports, civic and tourist areas throughout the city; and devastating tree culling at the Marina Golf Course.

Recent storms cause beach erosion, flooding and five deaths

Puerto Vallarta is recovering from four back-to-back hurricanes that skirted the city’s southern coast and Banderas Bay. The first hurricane, Polo, rolled in on Sept. 23, followed by Rachel, then Simón and Trudy. The storms brought major tidal surges and pounding waves to Vallarta’s beaches, filling the Malecón with rocks and sand, eroding beaches and leaving just rocks behind.

Impressive photos and videos show waves hitting the Malecón seawall and bouncing many feet into the air. Communities of Yelapa and Boca de Tomatlán were evacuated as a preventative measure as Hurricane Simón approached. Heavy rainfall also caused sewer system backups in the Versailles neighborhood and street flooding in many parts of town. Authorities also closed local beaches, but tragically, one young woman was swept away and is presumed drowned at Playa de Oro during Hurricane Polo. Four people, including two children, were killed when rushing water swept away their home in La Cuesta in the municipality of Talpa de Allende.

Profepa orders demolition of San Pancho beachfront condo

On Oct. 7, the Federal Attorney’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) ordered the demolition of two towers of the Punta Paraíso condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit. The towers sit directly on the beach in this coastal community and have been the subject of protests by residents for over a decade due to the buildings’ environmental impacts and encroachment into the protected Federal Maritime Terrestrial Zone.

Hurricanes Rachel and Simón pounded the beachfront towers, severely damaging their foundations, causing the towers to lean and necessitating the evacuation of residents.

The developer, Pacific Lifestyle Properties, was also ordered to pay a 96,220-peso (US $5,216) fine for building in the federal zone. Score one for Mother Nature and zero for illegal development.

Seapal rolls out free drinking fountains in public schools, sports fields and tourist spots

Remember to bring your refillable water bottles on your next trip to Puerto Vallarta because visitors and residents alike will soon have access to free, purified drinking water in various locations throughout the city.

This summer, Puerto Vallarta’s municipal water utility, Seapal, launched a program to bring purified drinking water fountains to public schools, civic, sports and tourist spots around Vallarta. The program aims to improve public health, increase access to safe, free drinking water, and reduce plastic pollution.

New fountains have already been installed in several schools and the Emiliano Zapata Municipal Market, and several more are planned for the Unidad Deportiva Agustín Flores Contreras sports complex, Centro Cultural y Módulo Deportivo La Lija, Seapal Vallarta’s central offices, Unidad Municipal Administrativa (UMA), and on the Malecón.

Marina Golf Course culls trees in major remodel, angering residents

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Marina Vallarta Club De Golf (@marinavallartaclubdegolf)

The Marina Golf Course has been systematically cutting down dozens of large, mature trees over the past several weeks, angering residents and displacing wildlife. Golf course administrators claim the culling of trees is part of a comprehensive remodeling project and that they plan to plant more trees than are being removed.

In the meantime, however, residents must wait decades for new trees to grow to the size of the old ones and face the constant sound of chainsaws and the sadness of watching trees being felled for many more days.

The trees being removed are mostly a nonnative species of ficus, but they provide habitat for native birds such as white ibises, great kiskadees, golden-cheeked woodpeckers, chachalacas and more.

The course has been closed most of the summer and fall during the remodeling project. Rest assured, visitors to Vallarta coming to the course this year will see a drastically different landscape.

They say the only constant is change. Let us just hope the next changes coming to Vallarta are less destructive and more positive, like the free drinking water program. But hurricane season is not over yet, so we will just have to wait and see.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Beloved Ballet Folklórico announces US tour in celebration of 75th anniversary
World.content:
Amalia Hernández’s Ballet Folklórico de México will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a tour to 24 cities in the United States, beginning Jan. 30 in Northridge, California, and concluding March 23 in Austin, Texas.

The Ballet Folklórico de México was established in 1952 by dancer and choreographer Amalia Hernández. The group revolutionized Mexican dance and laid the foundation for traditional choreographies and costumes to gain prestige in Mexico and abroad.

The company will travel with more than 50 members and present a repertoire of dances from various regions of Mexico, featuring live music, colorful garments and routines that blend folk traditions with theatrical staging.

“Our 75th anniversary is a celebration not only of Ballet Folklórico de México, but of the people, communities, traditions and artists who have kept Mexico’s cultural heritage alive,” Ballet Folklórico de México General Manager Salvador Lopez, who is also Hernández’s grandson, said in a statement.

“It is an honor to bring Amalia Hernández’s artistic legacy to audiences across the United States and to introduce new generations to the beauty and diversity of Mexico,” he added.

Where will the ballet perform?

In California, the company will perform in Northridge, Modesto, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, Chico, Davis, Berkeley, San Luis Obispo and Costa Mesa; in Arizona, in Tucson and Mesa; and in Texas, in El Paso, Lubbock, Richardson, San Antonio and Austin.

The tour will also reach Las Vegas, Nevada; Carmel, Indiana; East Lansing, Michigan; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Chicago, Illinois; Santa Fe, New Mexico; and Denver, Colorado.

Tickets are available through the official channels of the participating venues and, depending on the city, through platforms such as Ticketmaster.

In addition to its international tours, the Ballet Folklórico de México maintains a residency at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City, where it has held regular performances since 1959.

With reports from El Universal

World.title: Atlético Mineiro Reach South American Final
World.content:
BRAZIL · ARGENTINA · FOOTBALL

Published Wednesday 21 October, 9:06 p.m. ET (10:06 p.m. Montevideo) · Source: ESPN match data, beIN SPORTS

Atlético Mineiro, the Brazilian club from Belo Horizonte, will play Argentina’s Boca Juniors in the Copa Sudamericana final, even though it lost 2-0 at Montevideo City Torque on Wednesday 21 October. The return leg at the Estadio Centenario kicked off at 6:00 p.m. ET (7:00 p.m. Montevideo), and Atlético went through 3-2 on aggregate.

Boca, the Buenos Aires club, reached the final a day earlier. The one-match decider is on Saturday 21 November in Barranquilla, Colombia: see our Copa Sudamericana final 2026 guide for the date, tickets and TV.

Key Facts — Result Montevideo City Torque 2, Atlético Mineiro 0. Atlético won the tie 3-2 on aggregate.

— Final Atlético Mineiro v Boca Juniors, Saturday 21 November, Barranquilla, Colombia.

— Kick-off Not announced yet. From 1 November, Barranquilla keeps the same clock time as New York.

— Watch in the US beIN SPORTS holds the US rights. The channel for the final is not announced.

— At stake Champion US$10 million, runner-up US$2.5 million, and a 2027 Libertadores place.

— Prediction markets Polymarket, 9:03 p.m. ET, 21 October: Atlético 51.0%, Boca 39.5% (US$12,582 traded).

This story is part of our coverage of the Copa Sudamericana final 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide.

In plain English The Copa Sudamericana is the second-tier club tournament of South America, below the Copa Libertadores. Semi-finals are played over two matches, and the team with the higher total score goes through, which is why Atlético advanced after losing the second one.

How Atlético Survived a Late Scare

Atlético arrived in Montevideo with a 3-0 lead from the first leg, played in Belo Horizonte on Wednesday 14 October. City Torque, the Uruguayan club that was the surprise of the tournament, needed to win by four goals to go through.

Ecuadorian Alan Franco was sent off for a second yellow card with about 15 minutes left, and Atlético finished with ten men. The match was played in heavy rain, beIN SPORTS reported.

Kevin Silva then scored for City Torque from inside the box late in the game. Gary Kagelmacher then headed in a second goal in stoppage time.

One more goal would have levelled the tie at 3-3 and forced a decider. The final whistle came before City Torque could find it.

Who Boca Meet in the Final

Boca beat Vasco da Gama 3-1 at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro on Tuesday 20 October, after losing the first leg 1-0 at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires. They won the tie 3-2 on aggregate.

Boca won this trophy in 2004 and 2005 and have six Copa Libertadores titles. Atlético won the Libertadores in 2013. Franco’s red card means he misses the final, Infobae and La Tercera reported.

The Final in Barranquilla

The final is a single match at the Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Meléndez in Barranquilla on Saturday 21 November. The winner collects US$10 million and the runner-up US$2.5 million, according to prize figures reported by beIN SPORTS.

The champion also qualifies for the 2027 Copa Libertadores. CONMEBOL, South America’s football confederation, has not yet published the kick-off time.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket’s “Copa Sudamericana 2026 Winner” market, Atlético Mineiro traded at 51.0% and Boca Juniors at 39.5% at 9:03 p.m. ET on Wednesday 21 October. About US$12,582 had been traded, and the market still listed eliminated Vasco da Gama at 1.5%, so prices were still settling.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

The final is one match, so US fans have a single date to plan around: Saturday 21 November. Anyone travelling to Barranquilla should book refundable flights and hotels until the kick-off time is published.

What Is Not Known

CONMEBOL has not published the kick-off time, the ticket sale dates or the US channel for the final. CONMEBOL had not published a formal ruling on Franco’s suspension in the reports we reviewed.

Sources differ by a minute on the time of Silva’s goal, 88th or 89th, so we say only that it came late. More Brazilian club news is on our Brazil page.

Atlético Mineiro of Brazil will play Boca Juniors of Argentina. Atlético beat Montevideo City Torque 3-2 on aggregate, and Boca beat Vasco da Gama 3-2 on aggregate.

The final is on Saturday 21 November 2026 at the Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Meléndez in Barranquilla, Colombia. The kick-off time has not been announced.

Montevideo City Torque won the second leg 2-0 on Wednesday 21 October, with goals from Kevin Silva and Gary Kagelmacher. Atlético won the tie 3-2 on aggregate after a 3-0 first leg.

How can I watch the Copa Sudamericana final in the US?

beIN SPORTS holds the US rights to the competition. The channel for the final has not been announced, so check beIN SPORTS listings closer to the date.

The champion receives US$10 million and the runner-up US$2.5 million, according to prize figures reported by beIN SPORTS. The winner also qualifies for the 2027 Copa Libertadores.

World.title: New Rival Enters UN Leadership Race as Costa Rica’s Grynspan Faces Deadlock
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan faces a new challenge in her campaign to become the next United Nations secretary-general after a senior diplomat from the United Arab Emirates entered the race today, adding another contender to an already divided contest. Lana Nusseibeh, a 48-year-old UAE minister of state and former ambassador to the United Nations, announced her candidacy as the Security Council struggles to agree on a successor to António Guterres, whose term ends December 31.

Her entry comes at a difficult moment for Grynspan. The former Costa Rican vice president continues to lead the informal voting, but two of the five countries with the power to block the appointment have signaled opposition to her candidacy. In the October 16 vote, Grynspan received nine votes in favor, five against and one expressing no opinion. Two of the opposing votes came from permanent Security Council members, although the countries involved have not been officially identified.
