The result left Grynspan ahead of her closest competitors, Argentina’s Rafael Grossi and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, who each received eight supporting votes. However, neither Grynspan nor her rivals secured the agreement needed to move forward. The Security Council’s five permanent members, the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom, can each block a candidate. A successful candidate needs at least nine votes from the 15-member council without opposition from any of those five countries.

The October 16 vote was informal, meaning the opposing ballots were not actual vetoes. They nevertheless revealed that Grynspan faces resistance from two powerful governments before a final decision can be reached. Nusseibeh’s arrival gives Security Council members another candidate to consider as diplomatic negotiations continue.

The Emirati diplomat served as her country’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2013 until 2024 and has extensive experience working with the Security Council. She helped negotiate a resolution in December 2023 intended to increase humanitarian aid entering Gaza. In announcing her candidacy Wednesday, Nusseibeh called for a United Nations that takes a more active role in resolving international conflicts rather than simply responding to them.

She said several countries had encouraged her to consider running during the recent UN General Assembly meetings. She has also taken leave from her government position to pursue the job. Her candidacy adds a new regional dimension to the contest. Latin American countries have argued that their region should provide the next secretary-general, while there has also been a growing push for a woman to lead the organization for the first time in its history.

Nusseibeh would satisfy the call for a female secretary-general but would represent the Middle East rather than Latin America. Her entry does not mean she has secured the backing of any Security Council member. No voting results for her candidacy have been reported. For Costa Rica, the development comes as President Laura Fernández increases her involvement in Grynspan’s campaign.

Fernández met with Grynspan at Casa Presidencial on Monday, reaffirming the government’s support and announcing plans to contact other Latin American leaders to seek additional backing. Grynspan has maintained that her campaign remains active despite the opposition revealed in last week’s vote. She has emphasized that the Security Council has not held a formal vote and that countries can still change their positions.

The Costa Rican economist, who previously served as the head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, has proposed changes to make the organization more efficient, reduce overlapping responsibilities and strengthen its ability to respond to international crises. She served as Costa Rica’s vice president from 1994 to 1998 and has spent much of her subsequent career in international diplomacy.

If selected, Grynspan would become the first Costa Rican and the first woman to lead the United Nations. The Security Council is discussing whether to hold another informal vote on Friday or postpone it while negotiations continue. No date for the next round has been confirmed.

Once the Security Council agrees on a candidate, the UN General Assembly must formally appoint the new secretary-general. For now, Grynspan retains the most support recorded in the latest informal vote, but Nusseibeh’s entry adds another possibility for governments still searching for an acceptable candidate.

With fewer than three months remaining before Guterres leaves office, the Security Council has yet to agree on who should lead the United Nations beginning January 1, 2027.

World.title: Study Finds Costa Rica’s Pesticide Use More Than 10 Times Global Average
World.content:
Costa Rica uses pesticides on its farmland at a rate more than ten times the global average, according to a scientific study that raises new concerns about the potential effects of agricultural chemicals on human health and the environment. The research, published in the September 2026 issue of the scientific journal Environment International, found that pesticide use on Costa Rican cropland averaged 21.91 kilograms of active ingredients per hectare annually.

That compares with a global average of 2.18 kilograms and a Central American average of 7.16 kilograms. The findings highlight our heavy dependence on pesticides, particularly in large-scale banana and pineapple production, two of Costa Rica’s most important agricultural exports.

The study, titled Grounding Pesticide Use Intensity and Hazards with Real-World Data: Toward Correcting Global Models in Tropical Agriculture, was conducted by researchers Soledad Castro-Vargas of the University of Zurich, Santiago Alvarez-Fernandez, an independent researcher in Spain, and Ryan E. Galt of the University of California, Davis.

To determine how much pesticide is used, the researchers examined government import and export records, agricultural production statistics, and information about chemicals approved for use in Costa Rica. They then estimated how those pesticides were distributed across different crops and regions.

Banana plantations recorded the highest estimated use, averaging 78.88 kilograms of pesticide ingredients per hectare annually. Pineapple production followed at 34.07 kilograms, rice at 33.88 kilograms, tomatoes at 32.04 kilograms, and potatoes at 30.42 kilograms. The differences were also apparent across Costa Rica.

Limón, home to extensive banana and pineapple plantations along the Caribbean coast, recorded the highest provincial average at 35.77 kilograms per hectare when farmland and managed pastures were included. Heredia and Cartago followed, while Guanacaste had the lowest estimated levels.

One important distinction involves how pesticide use is calculated. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock has reported a national average of approximately 11 kilograms per hectare, but that figure includes pastures, where pesticide use is much lower. When the researchers included both cropland and managed pastures, their estimate was also approximately 11 kilograms per hectare. The higher figure of 21.91 kilograms applies specifically to cultivated crops.

The research also identified the chemicals most commonly used in Costa Rican agriculture. Mancozeb, a fungicide frequently applied to banana plantations to control fungal diseases, accounted for approximately 36% of the estimated pesticide ingredients used nationally. Other widely used chemicals included glyphosate, diazinon, and ethoprophos.

Beyond the amount of pesticide used, the researchers examined the potential dangers associated with the chemicals. Their findings showed that several health-related concerns, including cancer-causing potential and interference with the body’s hormone systems, did not show statistically significant improvements during the years examined.

The results were particularly troubling for aquatic life. Several measures of potential harm to organisms living in rivers, streams, and other waterways worsened over time, even as some other environmental indicators showed modest improvements. However, the researchers stressed an important limitation. Their study examined the hazardous properties of pesticides, not the actual exposure of individual people or the number of illnesses caused by agricultural chemicals.

The figures were also estimates based on official records and agricultural models, rather than measurements of every pesticide application on individual farms. Nevertheless, the findings challenge the idea that newer agricultural products have consistently made pesticide use less hazardous.

For Costa Rica, the research adds another dimension to a longstanding debate over the environmental costs of intensive agriculture. Costa Rica is internationally recognized for its biodiversity and conservation efforts, but its major agricultural industries continue to rely heavily on chemical treatments to protect crops from pests and disease.

The researchers argue that better reporting of pesticide applications, more detailed information about their use in individual regions, and continued environmental monitoring would help authorities better understand the possible consequences. They also call attention to gaps in scientific knowledge about how agricultural chemicals affect tropical ecosystems, where wildlife and environmental conditions can differ substantially from those in countries where much of the existing research has been conducted.

The study provides a clearer picture of where pesticides are being used most heavily and which chemicals deserve closer examination. It also raises questions about whether current agricultural practices are reducing the potential dangers to people and the environment.

World.title: US Surveillance Plane Helps Costa Rica Seize 1.5 Tons of Cocaine Off Osa
World.content:
A US surveillance aircraft helped Costa Rican authorities track a speedboat carrying about 1.5 metric tons (roughly 3,300 pounds) of cocaine off the Osa Peninsula, according to the Ministry of Public Security. Two Costa Rican men were detained. The National Coast Guard Service spotted the suspicious vessel during a routine patrol on Monday afternoon, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers, or 23 miles) off Cabo Matapalo, the peninsula’s southern tip.

The ministry said the people on board tried to flee when they noticed the patrol, setting off a chase at sea during which they allegedly threw the cargo overboard. The operation ran into the early hours of Tuesday, when officers finished recovering and counting the drugs. The Coast Guard worked alongside the Drug Control Police (PCD) and the Directorate of Intelligence and National Security (DIS).

The US Drug Enforcement Administration supported the operation, and an aircraft deployed through Joint Interagency Task Force South, a US command based in Key West, Florida, that coordinates counter-drug surveillance across the region, took part. Authorities said the air support helped keep the suspects under watch during the pursuit.

Public Security Minister Gerald Campos said police then located a house in the southern zone where more drugs were believed to be stored. Authorities said the two men were detained at the property, where officers also seized weapons and additional drugs. The two suspects have not been publicly identified, and the ministry said further details would be released as the investigation continues.

The seizure is the second this month in which a US aircraft supported a Costa Rican interdiction in the same waters. On October 15, Campos reported that authorities had seized more than four tons of cocaine in four days, including 1,175 packages from a boat 141 nautical miles (261 kilometers, or 162 miles) off Cabo Matapalo. Three Colombian nationals were detained in that case, which a US maritime patrol aircraft also assisted.

That same run of operations included 3,077 packages intercepted by the Border Police in the Térraba-Sierpe wetland, a protected mangrove system on the southern Pacific coast, and 52 kilograms (115 pounds) found at the Moín container terminal in Limón.

The latest case comes as cocaine seizures in Costa Rica have climbed nearly 50% this year and as the government deepens security cooperation with the United States, including a recent run of extraditions to US courts. The stretch of coast between the Osa Peninsula and the Panama border is a frequent focus of interdiction operations because of its proximity to northbound maritime trafficking routes from South America.

World.title: PSU responds to PM on Ministerial allowances: Accuses government of politicizing poverty, says ministers’ allowances are being used to justify vote-buying
World.content:
PSU responds to PM on Ministerial allowances: Accuses government of politicizing poverty, says ministers’ allowances are being used to justify vote-buying

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Public Service Union (PSU) President Dean Flowers has accused the Briceño administration of perpetuating a culture of political patronage in which vulnerable Belizeans are forced to depend on elected representatives for basic necessities, arguing that the government’s justification for ministerial allowances exposes deeper failures in the country’s social assistance system.

Speaking with Breaking Belize News, Flowers expanded on concerns raised in a recent PSU statement, which warned that using politicians’ personal assistance to address public needs creates a system of indebtedness, unequal access to assistance and political dependency.

The controversy follows comments by Prime Minister John Briceño, who defended ministerial allowances on the grounds that elected officials regularly receive requests for assistance with medical expenses, funerals, education and other emergencies.

Briceño said ministers frequently give away their allowances and contribute additional money from their own pockets, suggesting that eliminating those benefits would reduce their ability to assist struggling constituents.

However, the PSU’s recent statement questioned whether such assistance should depend on the personal discretion of politicians rather than established government programmes.

The union warned that when assistance is distributed through politicians, recipients can feel personally indebted to those who provide it. It argued that the arrangement encourages political patronage and creates unequal conditions for candidates who do not have access to similar financial resources.

The PSU also raised concerns about the absence of published eligibility criteria, transparent records of assistance provided and independent mechanisms through which citizens can challenge decisions to deny them help.

Instead, the union proposed transparent, institutionalized emergency healthcare and burial assistance programmes that would provide support according to citizens’ needs rather than their political connections.

Its position was summarized in the statement: “Compassion should be policy, not patronage.”

Flowers reinforced those concerns during his interview, but stressed that the PSU’s position should not be misrepresented as a personal confrontation with the Prime Minister or a demand that ministers immediately surrender their allowances.

“The PSU, in essence, said, fix the system. If the roof is leaking, don’t pat yourself on the back because you have people collecting the water in buckets,” Flowers said.

He argued that the Prime Minister’s explanation inadvertently highlighted a much larger problem: the inability of existing government institutions to adequately support vulnerable Belizeans.

According to Flowers, people should not have to visit politicians’ homes, sometimes late at night, seeking assistance to bury relatives, purchase medication or obtain medical treatment.

He maintained that such arrangements undermine citizens’ dignity and create conditions in which politicians can exploit economic hardship for political advantage.

“It is politicizing people’s poverty. It is taking advantage of people’s needs instead of creating a system that is fair, that is open, that is transparent, that people could tap into when they are vulnerable and in need. This is effectively buying votes,” Flowers charged.

He questioned why the government continues to highlight improvements in employment and economic performance while acknowledging that ministers face persistent requests from constituents unable to meet basic expenses.

Flowers argued that the reliance on politicians for assistance is evidence of shortcomings in healthcare, social protection and economic policy that cannot be sustainably addressed through political handouts.

He also challenged Briceño to provide a comprehensive accounting of the $7.2 million that Flowers said is allocated annually to elected representatives through constituency development funding.

“Report to us how you are spending that $7.2 million annually, you and your 30 colleagues in the House,” Flowers demanded.

The PSU president recalled an earlier commitment he attributed to Briceño that the Auditor General would provide annual reports on the use of those funds.

He questioned why ministers would need to justify retaining their personal allowances for charitable purposes if separate taxpayer-funded resources were already available to address constituency needs.

Briceño has rejected allegations that constituency development funds are intended to buy political loyalty, maintaining that they allow area representatives from both major political parties to respond quickly to community needs.

Flowers nevertheless maintained that assistance administered through individual politicians creates an inherently unequal system, particularly when some representatives have access to public resources while others must depend on private financing.

He argued that such arrangements also reinforce the need for campaign finance reform.

When asked whether the PSU was recommending that ministerial allowances be eliminated and redirected to the Ministry of Human Development, Flowers rejected that interpretation.

“I’m not here to say that they should cut their allowances,” he explained.

Instead, he suggested that the compensation packages of ministers should be independently assessed to determine whether their salaries and allowances are justified.

If those benefits form part of a reasonable compensation package, Flowers argued, ministers are entitled to use the money for themselves and their families. The government’s responsibility, however, is to ensure that assistance for vulnerable citizens is provided through properly administered public programmes.

He called for a more accessible and transparent social assistance system, improved healthcare, living wages and economic policies that reduce poverty rather than perpetuating political dependency.

Flowers also urged Belizeans to reconsider the expectation that elected representatives should personally provide for their constituents.

“Nobody is elected to take care of nobody,” he said, arguing that politicians should instead create conditions in which citizens can become economically independent.

The PSU president emphasized that the union’s criticisms were not motivated by partisan politics or personal hostility toward Briceño, but by concerns about a system that has become deeply institutionalized in Belize.

He maintained that meaningful reform requires political will, effective oversight and a fundamental change in the relationship between citizens and elected representatives.

“We have to empower people. Let’s give people an opportunity to thrive, an opportunity to feel good about themselves,” Flowers said.

The union’s position is that vulnerable Belizeans should have access to assistance as a matter of public policy, rather than having to depend on the goodwill or political interests of individual ministers.

World.title: 56-year-old man jailed for three months over just 0.4 grams of crack must serve four more months for unpaid fines
World.content:
56-year-old man jailed for three months over just 0.4 grams of crack must serve four more months for unpaid fines

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 56-year-old Belize City man who spent more than three months behind bars after being unable to post bail for possession of just 0.4 grams of crack cocaine has been sent back to prison for another four months because of outstanding court fines.

Wellington Williams appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, October 20, where he changed his plea from not guilty to guilty for possession of a controlled drug.

Williams had been on remand since July 17, 2026, after police allegedly found a small quantity of crack cocaine wrapped in white paper inside his pants pocket during a search on Douglas Jones Street.

The magistrate sentenced him to three months in prison but credited him for the time already spent on remand, effectively allowing him to walk free.

However, his anticipated release was short-lived after court records revealed two outstanding fines: $504 dating back to 2022 and another $555 from 2026, totalling $1,059.

Because the fines remained unpaid, Williams was committed to the Belize Central Prison to serve an additional four months.

According to information presented in court, warrants relating to the outstanding fines had not been forwarded for enforcement during the three months Williams was already incarcerated. As a result, he had not served the prison terms associated with those unpaid fines while on remand.

Williams, who reportedly suffers from a medical condition, had initially been granted bail in the drug possession case but remained imprisoned because no one was able to secure his release.

His case had been scheduled to proceed to trial, with disclosure already provided, before he decided to change his plea.

The outcome means Williams, who had already spent more time behind bars than the sentence imposed for possessing 0.4 grams of crack cocaine, must now serve another four months because of his outstanding financial obligations to the court.

World.title: Police officer accused of murdering former mother-in-law and her twin brother committed to stand trial in High Court
World.content:
Police officer accused of murdering former mother-in-law and her twin brother committed to stand trial in High Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An interdicted police officer accused of murdering his former mother-in-law and her twin brother in Hattieville Village in September 2025 has been committed to stand trial in the High Court.

Orvin Justin Williams, 26, appeared before a magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, October 21, where his preliminary inquiry was completed through a paper committal procedure.

Williams faces two counts of murder in connection with the September 15, 2025 shooting deaths of 57-year-old Paula Belisle and her twin brother, Paul Esquillano, at a residence on Ysaguirre Boulevard in Hattieville.

During the proceedings, the police prosecutor submitted 16 witness statements and documentary exhibits forming part of the prosecution’s case. Following the hearing, the magistrate committed Williams to stand trial during the January 2027 session of the High Court, scheduled to begin January 18.

According to earlier police investigations, a gunman arrived at the residence in a vehicle shortly after 2 p.m., entered the property and opened fire on the siblings before fleeing.

Belisle, a domestic worker, died while being transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while her brother was found dead inside the residence. Investigators recovered five expended 9mm shells and obtained surveillance footage showing a vehicle of interest leaving the area.

Police subsequently located the rental vehicle in Belize City. Williams was initially detained on October 1, 2025, but released two days later. He was rearrested on October 10 after investigators obtained additional evidence, including witness statements allegedly identifying him as the gunman.

The case has experienced several delays, with Williams previously receiving 201 pages of disclosure and 10 DVDs containing prosecution evidence.

Williams, who remains on interdiction from the Belize Police Department, was represented by attorney Gilroy Usher Jr. during Wednesday’s proceedings.

He remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison awaiting trial.

World.title: Stanley Flowers indicted on five counts of attempted murder after allegedly shooting at five police officers in 2025 incident
World.content:
Stanley Flowers indicted on five counts of attempted murder after allegedly shooting at five police officers in 2025 incident

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 37-year-old fisherman accused of shooting and injuring a police corporal before allegedly opening fire on other officers during a pursuit has been indicted on five counts of attempted murder in the High Court.

Stanley Moris Flowers, of Sandhill, appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, October 20, where he pleaded not guilty to all five counts involving Corporal Manuel Chub and Police Constables Sebastian Sho, Valentine Young, Joel Chi and Alfredo Serria.

The charges stem from a March 31, 2025 incident near Fire Nightclub on the Philip Goldson Highway, where police reportedly approached Flowers after receiving information about an armed man.

According to earlier police reports, Flowers allegedly pulled out a firearm and opened fire, injuring Corporal Chub. He then reportedly fled on a motorcycle toward the Burrell Boom junction, where responding officers came under gunfire during a pursuit.

The incident also resulted in damage estimated at $24,436.91 to two police vehicles.

Flowers was initially charged with several offences, including attempted murder, dangerous harm, use of deadly means of harm, aggravated assault with a firearm and firearm-related offences.

After spending nearly a year on remand, Flowers was granted bail of $15,000 by Justice Antoinette Moore in March 2026, following delays in completing his preliminary inquiry.

Flowers, who remains out on bail, is represented by attorney Leeroy Banner.

Justice Pilgrim has scheduled a case management conference for November 30, 2026, followed by a further court appearance on December 4, when a trial date is expected to be considered.

The matter will be heard by a judge without a jury.

World.title: Fisherman charged after police allegedly find nearly half a pound of crack in knapsack
World.content:
Fisherman charged after police allegedly find nearly half a pound of crack in knapsack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 37-year-old Belize City fisherman has been charged with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply after police allegedly discovered 222.9 grams of suspected crack cocaine, equivalent to nearly half a pound, inside his knapsack.

Eugene Herman Neal, of Handyside Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 21, where he pleaded not guilty to the charge.

According to police, officers conducting a mobile patrol on Handyside Street around 4:50 p.m. on Tuesday noticed Neal walking with a black schoolbag on his back. Officers reportedly became suspicious of his behaviour and stopped him for a search.

Although nothing illegal was found on his person, a search of the knapsack allegedly uncovered a bag containing a rocky substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

Neal was escorted to the Queen Street Police Station, where the substance was weighed in his presence and recorded at 222.9 grams, just under a quarter of a kilogram.

During his arraignment, the prosecution raised no objection to bail, and the magistrate granted Neal bail of $3,000 with one surety of the same amount or two sureties of $1,500 each.

However, Neal’s release was delayed after court records revealed that he still owed $405 in connection with a previous drug possession matter dating back to 2023. He was informed that the outstanding amount would have to be paid before his bail could be processed.

As a condition of bail, Neal must report to the Queen Street Police Station every Wednesday between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.

He is scheduled to return to court on December 21, 2026.

World.title: Belize City man remanded for allegedly burglarizing former employer and damaging $250 surveillance camera, Says his granny already spoke to his former boss
World.content:
Belize City man remanded for allegedly burglarizing former employer and damaging $250 surveillance camera, Says his granny already spoke to his former boss

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An 18-year-old Belize City man accused of burglarizing his former workplace and damaging a $250 surveillance camera has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after failing to meet bail.

Tyrese Tamron Williams, also known as “Nickels,” appeared unrepresented before a magistrate in Belize City on Tuesday, October 20, where he was charged with burglary in connection with an incident at Mendoza’s Automotive on Vernon Street.

According to police, the business owner reported that a surveillance camera had gone missing from his business. Upon reviewing security footage, he allegedly observed Williams, whom he had known for approximately five years, removing a white Zosi surveillance camera on September 21, 2026.

During his arraignment, Williams told the court that he previously worked for Mendoza and was willing to compensate the company for the damaged camera. He explained that his grandmother, with whom he resides, had already spoken to the businessman about the matter.

The magistrate instructed the prosecution to establish whether Mendoza would be willing to accept compensation before the next hearing.

With no objection from the prosecution, Williams was granted bail of $3,000 plus one surety of the same amount. However, he was unable to meet the bail requirements and was remanded to prison.

As conditions of bail, Williams must not contact or interfere with the complainant and must attend all scheduled court appearances.

His next court date is December 8, 2026.

World.title: Two men plead not guilty to double murder of Adelina Gillett, Felix Martinez near Crooked Tree junction
World.content:
Two men plead not guilty to double murder of Adelina Gillett, Felix Martinez near Crooked Tree junction

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men accused of the sensational double murder of a Burrell Boom couple in January 2025 were formally indicted in the High Court on Tuesday, October 20, with both pleading not guilty to the killings.

Jovannie Rashad Jones, 31, and Jerwin Ornand Segura, 25, appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim, where they were indicted on two counts of murder in connection with the shooting deaths of 40-year-old Adelita Gillett, a pharmaceutical manager at Brodies, and her husband, 37-year-old Felix Martinez, an employee of Belize Bank.

The couple was found shot to death inside their Chevrolet Equinox SUV near Mile 31 of the Philip Goldson Highway, between Biscayne Village and the Crooked Tree junction, on January 20, 2025.

Investigators believe the killings stemmed from a failed vehicle transaction. The couple had reportedly paid more than $30,000 for a vehicle they never received and had arranged to meet someone to recover their money. Police believe they were ambushed during that meeting.

The murders shocked the Burrell Boom community, particularly as the couple left behind a 10-year-old son. Gillett had worked at Brodies for approximately 20 years, while Martinez was also well known in Belize’s basketball community.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Jones, who is the son of a pastor, was represented by attorney Leeroy Banner. Segura, however, remained unrepresented and informed the court that he wanted an attorney but could not afford one.

Given the seriousness of the charges, Justice Pilgrim indicated that an attorney would be appointed to represent Segura before further proceedings could take place.

The matter was adjourned to November 27, 2026, for mention, at which time the court is expected to address Segura’s legal representation before proceeding with case management and setting a trial date.

Both accused men, who have been incarcerated since their initial arraignment in January 2025, were further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: Bukele warns Haitian gangs who kidnapped 4 Salvadorans: ‘We have already wiped out gangs in El Salvador; we can wipe you out too’
World.content:
Bukele warns Haitian gangs who kidnapped 4 Salvadorans: ‘We have already wiped out gangs in El Salvador; we can wipe you out too’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: “We have already wiped out the gangs in El Salvador, and we can wipe you out too.”

That was the stern warning issued by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele on Wednesday to Haitian gangs holding four Salvadoran military personnel hostage, as he announced the launch of combat operations to rescue them.

In a public statement on Facebook, Bukele warned the kidnappers that the military action launched on Wednesday was nothing compared to what would follow if the four Salvadorans were not released alive.

“Don’t confuse our words with an empty threat,” Bukele declared, giving the gangs an ultimatum to release the men unharmed or face further military action.

The four Salvadorans, identified as aviation technicians participating in a United Nations-backed international security mission in Haiti, disappeared on Sunday, October 18, after armed gangs ambushed their armoured vehicle near Croix-des-Bouquets, outside the capital, Port-au-Prince.

According to Reuters, the attackers opened fire and used explosives, setting the vehicle ablaze. The Salvadorans reportedly escaped the burning vehicle but have not been located. Helicopters dispatched to assist in the rescue also came under fire.

Bukele stressed that the missing men were not combatants but aviation specialists whose mission involved conducting medical evacuations and saving lives. He said they were returning from purchasing food at a local supermarket when they were abducted.

The Salvadoran president, whose sweeping crackdown on gangs has dramatically reduced violent crime in his country, warned that he was prepared to take similar action against Haiti’s powerful criminal organisations.

Haiti has been battling heavily armed gangs that control large portions of its capital, with an international Gang Suppression Force deployed to support Haitian authorities in restoring security.

Bukele ended his warning by telling the kidnappers that they still had an opportunity to avoid further bloodshed.

“Hand over our four compatriots, safe and sound, and everything will return to how it was before their kidnapping. The decision is in your hands.”

As of Wednesday, the four Salvadorans had not been confirmed rescued, and no gang had publicly claimed responsibility for their abduction.

The headline uses a natural English translation of Bukele’s Spanish statement, “Ya acabamos con las pandillas en El Salvador y podemos acabar con ustedes también.” His published English version uses “finished with” rather than “wiped out,” but the meaning is consistent.

World.title: Progress made on lots earmarked for Cooper’s Pen residents
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) in dialogue with Cooper’s Pen resident Debbie Lewis (second right) during a tour of the community. Looking on are (from left) minister of state in the Office of the Prime Minister Senator Abka Fitz-Henley; Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett; and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern Tova Hamilton. (Photo: Horace Hines)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The procurement of amenities, including water for the lots set aside for displaced residents of Cooper’s Pen, has begun, Prime Minister Andrew Holness said Wednesday.

“We have completed the survey of the land, so the land is now divided up into lots and we have started the procurement of the services to put in place the roads, the water and other basic amenities and so the residents will have access to that,” Holness said.

The prime minister shared the update while speaking at the opening ceremony of the Kingston 2 development in downtown Kingston on Wednesday.

Around 20 homes found to be illegally occupied by residents in Cooper’s Pen Trelawny, based on a court ruling, were demolished in an early morning exercise on August 11, leaving dozens of families without shelter.

READ: ‘Devastating’ demolition

The controversial demolition prompted social assistance from the government, including the provision of tents and the procurement of lots for qualifying families to purchase.

Acknowledging that relocation under any circumstances is, at best, disruptive, Holness said,

“In the best circumstances, persons are going to feel traumatised by relocation. No one wants to have their house uprooted, their furniture taken and destroyed. Nobody wants to have to move from where they have made their life. And I wish to use this platform to say to the people of Cooper’s Pen that we understand this.”

However, the prime minister emphasised that any land utilised in the relocation of residents of Cooper’s Pen will be paid for outright.

“I repeat as I did when I visited the people of Cooper’s Pen in August, it will not be free. So nobody should have that in their minds that the land will be just given freely.”

Instead, Holness said, the government will provide various modalities for residents to get fair and reasonable access, either through outright purchase, lease or other forms of contractual arrangement.

Holness also reiterated that previously announced $9.9 million relocation grants for the affected residents are not compensatory, emphasising that the government would not use taxpayers’ dollars to compensate anyone for an act that was unlawful.

READ: Displaced Cooper’s Pen residents receive humanitarian grants

“What we will do, however, which I think all Jamaicans would agree with, is that we should assist with the relocation exercise.”

Noting that the government is moving forward with an emphasis on dialogue, Holness urged the Cooper’s Pen residents not to be swayed by misinformation but to be led by the respective government agencies.

World.title: NWC seeks 51% hike
World.content:
Acting president of National Water Commission Kevin Kerr (left) speaks during Tuesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change Wayne Robertson listens. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) will decide within 10 days whether to accept a National Water Commission (NWC) application for a tariff review which could pave the way for higher water and sewerage rates.

The OUR confirmed Tuesday in a release that it received the application on Friday, October 16, covering the five-year period from 2026/27 to 2030/31.

The regulator said it would first assess whether the application meets its requirements and may request additional information from the NWC before deciding whether to formally accept it for review.

The development comes as the NWC seeks a 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates amid worsening revenue collection and rising expenses.

The utility wants to raise its annual revenue from about $40 billion to $60 billion to cover operating costs and critical investments over the next five years, while noting it owes the Government approximately $21 billion in General Consumption Tax (GCT).

The disclosures were made by NWC officials on Tuesday during a sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), where the utility’s unpaid bills and financial difficulties came under scrutiny.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the committee that the proposed increase was included in a tariff application submitted to the OUR last Friday and noted that the commission is awaiting approval from the regulator.

“So what our submission includes is a 51 per cent increase, and there are some scenarios involved if that is not provided; we will have to revise our investment plan, adjust with the determination made at the end of the process and, as usual, the public will be required to participate in a more consultative process by the OUR over the review period,” Kerr said.

Chief financial officer at the NWC Fabian Christie told the committee that the request reflected the utility’s financial challenges.

“The fact is that our revenues have worsened in terms of paying from our customers, and also the fact that we would require a tariff increase, because our expenses have been increasing dramatically,” Christie told the committee.

He also pointed to the impact of natural disasters and worsening droughts on the commission’s finances. Christie said these events could reduce the utility’s revenue by between 10 and 15 per cent in a given year, depending on their severity.

The proposed increase comes against the background of a sharp rise in the NWC’s unpaid bills.

PAC Chairman Julian Robinson, referring to the Auditor General’s findings, said the commission’s payables rose from $10.6 billion in the 2016/17 financial year to $33.2 billion in 2025/26.

The report also found that the NWC’s net receivables — money owed to the utility — stood at $4.6 billion as at March 2026.

Christie told the committee that the $21-billion owed in GCT accounted for the largest share of the NWC’s $33.2 billion in payables. He explained that the commission withholds GCT when it is billed by suppliers and is expected to pass that tax on to the Government.

Christie also confirmed that the money was being used to support the utility’s day-to-day cash needs.

He revealed that the remaining approximately $12 billion in payables includes approximately $6 billion owed to Central Wastewater Treatment Company, which treats much of the sewage from Kingston and parts of St Catherine at the Soapberry facility. The other roughly $6 billion is owed to contractors and suppliers.

Christie acknowledged that the outstanding payments were affecting the commission’s ability to carry out work.

He gave an approximate breakdown of some payments owed to contractors and suppliers, saying about $1.3 billion was between zero and 30 days overdue, $400 million between 30 and 60 days, $500 million between 60 and 90 days, and $1.6 billion outstanding for more than 90 days.

The proposed tariff increase is not the only measure being pursued to improve the NWC’s finances. Kerr said reducing non-revenue water was a priority.

He said the commission had previously undertaken reduction projects in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore, and was in the final stage of procurement for an islandwide programme, adding that the NWC hopes to select a bidder or bidders by the end of the current financial period.

The planned programme would be rolled out in stages, beginning in areas including Spanish Town, Old Harbour, May Pen, Mandeville, Montego Bay, Negril, Lucea, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio, before further work in Kingston and Portmore.

Kerr said the long-term target was to reduce non-revenue water to 30 per cent islandwide within 11 years as the current level averages between 70 and 73 per cent.

The NWC’s financial position was also a concern for Robinson, who questioned how the utility would improve its cash flow beyond seeking higher tariffs. He pointed to the growth in payables and the amount owed to suppliers, while raising the need to reduce losses and improve the collection of money owed to the commission.

Christie said the NWC was working on a plan to improve its working capital management, which he expects to submit to the board at the start of next year. He said the effort would need to improve the amount of cash available to meet the utility’s obligations.

Furthermore, Kerr said, the tariff application was tied to an investment plan designed to ensure that financing could be secured for priority projects. He noted that the NWC received an interim tariff in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 eroded its cash flow.

World.title: $2b reasons for flexi-work
World.content:
A screen shot of a section of the Ministry of National Security and Peace submission to Parliament’s Economy amd Production Committee last Wednesday.

JAMAICA’S approximately 114,000 public servants could save nearly $2 billion annually in transportation costs if more of them are allowed to work remotely under flexi-work arrangements.

This point was emphasised by representatives of the Ministry of National Security and Peace during their appearance last Wednesday before Parliament’s Economy and Production Committee to discuss the progress of flex-work arrangements in Jamaica.

A PowerPoint presentation from the ministry’s team, which was shared with the media afterwards, painted what it called the “big picture” involving public sector workers and the costs associated with their daily commute.

It shows that it costs between $12,000 and $24,000 weekly for each public servant to get to and from work.

With vacation and other days off, it is estimated that each public servant spends between $456,000 and $912,000 annually to get to work.

For all public servants combined, the annual figure is between $1.3 billion and $2.7 billion.

The document argued that if public sector employees were allowed to work from home two days each week, they would each save between $4,800 and $9,600.

Across the entire public service, workers would collectively keep between $547 million and $1.9 billion in their pockets annually.

In terms of the impact at the ministry level, the document showed that 196 or 52 per cent of its 374 employees reside in St Catherine; 160 or 43 per cent live in Kingston and rural St Andrew; and 18 or five per cent live in rural parishes.

It emphasised that each of these workers is spending between $12,000 and $24,000 every week to get to and from work.

The ministry said its embrace of flexi-work arrangements is in response to fuel-price pressures and is aimed at modernising work and strengthening public sector resilience.

The security ministry’s team underscored that more people working from home meant an overall smaller fuel bill.

The document referenced a study which shows that 10 minutes of creeping or idling in traffic burns between 300 and 500 millilitres or more than one to two cups of petrol.

Hourly idling while stuck in gridlock sees an average car wasting 0.5 litres to 1.3 litres of fuel per hour, while larger vehicles burn between 1.5 litres and 2.5 litres.

The ministry team cited the negative effects of gridlock on the economy, climate change, productivity, and mental wellness.

It referenced a 1965 World Bank appraisal which described the Kingston–Spanish Town corridor as “the most heavily travelled highway in Jamaica”.

The ministry noted that in 2008 then Minister of Transport Mike Henry indicated that motorists were taking eight times longer on typical journeys as he pointed to the economic cost of congestion

In 2023, Jamaicans were reportedly spending 90 minutes or 40 per cent of working hours daily in traffic.

This is according to a United Nations Jamaica/UWI Department of Economics panel discussion titled ‘The Economics of Congestion’.

It described the time lost as a massive cost for a small island developing state with enormous economic implications that could affect people’s psychological and physiological well-being.

The ministry said it was making the case for action now on flexi-work arrangement having considered the mental wellness of employees, national cost pressures, workforce realities, and public sector modernisation which together strengthen the case for a Government of Jamaica-wide approach.

In terms of the mental health toll, the document cited an international study of January 2025 published in the Makara Journal of Health Research which stated that a significant proportion of workers experienced stress from their commuting routines.

The study found that approximately 74.5 per cent of workers reported that commuting had a detrimental effect on their mental health, while 82.1 per cent experienced mental fatigue which directly impacted their ability to concentrate and perform effectively at work.

The security ministry said the overall approach is for a structured, phased and monitored Government-led flexible work arrangement framework, informed by its experience.

It said eligibility should be transparent, role-based and subject to operational requirements, not a universal entitlement, and argued that the roll-out should be phased in.

The security ministry pointed to positives such as reduced commuting stress and greater autonomy which, it said, can support productive time and work-life balance.

Additionally, it said flexible work can support talent retention, inclusion and recruitment in a changing workforce.

The ministry said it also maintains operating capacity during fuel shortages, natural disasters, and transport disruptions.

Potential savings include transport, toll, fuel, maintenance, and in-office support resources, alongside reduced absenteeism.

World.title: Twinkle Brothers honoured on home turf
World.content:
Councillor for the Falmouth Division Garth Wilkinson (left) shares a light moment with Twinkle Brothers band member Ralston Grant and his wife Della following the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony in Falmouth on Monday.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — There was a flood of emotions as reggae musicians Ralston and Norman Grant, of the Twinkle Brothers, Falmouth natives, were recognised for their contribution to Jamaican music at a National Heroes’ Day awards ceremony in historic Water Square in the parish.

Norman is currently on tour, but for Ralston, the occasion held special significance, as decades ago the siblings operated a record shop almost on the exact spot where the awards ceremony was held, long before their music took them to audiences around the globe.

The recognition came through the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), during its 2026 National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony.

Reflecting on the moment, Ralston said the honour was particularly meaningful because it was his first award in their native Trelawny, despite receiving international recognition for the band’s musical achievements since they started out in 1962.

“It means everything, you know, because I’ve never got one from Trelawny before,” he said.

The musician recalled the brothers’ early accomplishments in the Jamaica Festival Song Competition in 1970, where they placed third behind winner Hopeton Lewis and the Jamaicans.

Their musical journey also includes performances before former Governor General Sir Clifford Campbell during an era when their talent was gaining recognition at home.

The citation accompanying the award praised Norman and Ralston for their outstanding contribution to Jamaican music, cultural heritage, and the country’s representation on the international stage.

It also traced their beginnings on how they fashioned their own musical instruments, demonstrating the ingenuity and determination that would underpin their careers that have spanned more than six decades, with an extensive catalogue of albums and singles.

Through their commitment to independent music production, conscious reggae and roots culture, the brothers helped preserve the tradition of live-band reggae while introducing Jamaican sounds to audiences beyond the island.

Their collaboration with Polish group Trebunie-Tutki was also highlighted as an example of their ability to bridge cultural divides through music.

Despite spending more than four decades living largely overseas, Ralston maintains ties to Jamaica, travelling between the island and California, with his wife Della.

The Twinkle Brothers boast an extensive catalogue of songs which include

Faith Can Move Mountains, Never Get Burn, Jahoviah, Since I Threw the Comb Away, Give Rasta Praise, Rasta Pon Top, Enter Zion, among many others.

World.title: Jamaica braces for cyber stress test
World.content:
JAMAICA’s ability to withstand and recover from major cyberattacks will be put to the test later this month when the Jamaica Cyber Incident Response Team (JaCIRT) stages a national exercise — CyberXJM26 — aimed at identifying weaknesses in the country’s cybersecurity defences and strengthening its response capabilities.

Scheduled for October 28 and 29, the exercise seeks to provide the first full test of the country’s ability to coordinate its response to a major cyber incident.

“CyberXjm26 puts national readiness to a public test, showing how well agencies, security forces, and the private sector can coordinate during an incident, identifying gaps that can be fixed before a real one,” JaCIRT director Lieutenant Colonel Godphey Sterling told the Jamaica Observer during a recent interview.

“The aim is to cut the number of attacks that succeed and to recover quickly when one does,” he added.

Dubbed Operation Sargasso Surge, the exercise seeks to simulate a single, escalating cyber incident, starting with minor activity before progressing through serious disruptions to a multi-sector national crisis.

During the exercise participants will investigate incidents, solve challenges, and make decisions under pressure. The initiative is designed to test existing procedures, strengthen communication and collaboration, and identify weaknesses that need to be addressed before an actual emergency.

It will bring together representatives from government ministries, departments and agencies, private-sector organisations, critical infrastructure operators, financial institutions, telecommunications providers, academic institutions, and other stakeholders. Activities will also extend to schools, universities, cybersecurity enthusiasts and professional incident-response teams.

The initiative forms part of activities planned for National Cybersecurity Awareness Month, observed this October under the theme ‘One Nation, Cyber Strong’. The month-long programme of events includes lectures, webinars, in-person sessions, a social media awareness campaign, and a cyber careers symposium. A national cyber exposé, scheduled for October 29, will also feature demonstrations and exhibits as it recognises contributors and volunteers who have helped to build Jamaica’s national incident-response capabilities for more than a decade.

“The 2026 campaign seeks to change behaviour as it brings more awareness so that the public and organisations can begin to adopt habits that close off the easiest routes for attackers,” he said.

“The cyber careers symposium, the competition tracks, and the Cyber Reserve also strengthen the talent pipeline, giving students and professionals a route into the field while giving the division a pool of skilled people it can call on before seeking outside help,” the lieutenant colonel added.

Providing an update on Jamaica’s cybersecurity posture, Sterling said progress had been made, although significant gaps remain.

“Key foundations are now in place — the Cybercrimes Act was amended in February and the national cybersecurity standards framework and incident response plan are finalised. A national coordinating council is proceeding to Cabinet and a Cyber Reserve is being established to draw on students, professionals, and members of the security forces during national incidents. However, some gaps are remaining,” Sterling said, as he pointed to the more than 35,000 instances of cyberattacks that originated from Jamaica since the start of this year, in addition to approximately 12 million vulnerability instances that have affected local systems and services.

“These continue to be monitored and prioritised for mitigation by the CIRT Division. The principal active threats are ransomware, phishing, and AI-assisted attacks,” he added, while noting that opportunistic fraud, including fraudulent donation websites that emerged following Hurricane Melissa, remains a concern.

Going forward, Sterling said that improving the country’s defences will require greater investment in modern detection and automation tools, stronger vulnerability management, and closer information-sharing arrangements with banks, telecommunications providers, and other critical sectors.

He also underscored the need for stronger legislative authority to empower JaCIRT to require organisations to meet cybersecurity standards and report incidents in a timely manner.

To build long-term capacity, Sterling said the entity is relying on the Strengthening Cybersecurity in Jamaica (SCIJ) Project, supported by the Inter-American Development Bank and implemented through the Office of the Prime Minister. The project, which runs from September 2025 to March 2031, aims to bolster cybersecurity protection across public institutions as it expands the pool of specialised professionals available locally.

“JaCIRT’s work is about shifting from reacting to incidents towards preventing them, building a deeper pool of skilled people and ensuring that the country can withstand and recover from an attack. The SCIJ Project is the long-term engine behind much of this as it aims to turn the completed standards framework and incident response plan into practical protection and a stronger workforce across the public sector,” he said.

Beyond testing national readiness, JaCIRT is stepping up its monitoring of cyberspace as it urges individuals and businesses to remain vigilant ahead of the busy Black Friday and Christmas shopping periods, when financially motivated cybercrimes are expected to intensify.

“The outlook for the rest of 2026 is for high, seasonal threat activity, with the main risk shifting to fraud and financially motivated attacks,” Sterling said.

“Phishing and WhatsApp account takeovers remain the most common routes to harm individuals, while ransomware and credential theft remain the main risks for organisations, especially over the holidays when staffing is reduced and detection is slower,” he further said.

World.title: A CLASS ABOVE
World.content:
Calabar’s Christopher Taylor, seen here competing in the Class 2 boys’ 400m at the ISSA Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships in 2016, is one of several athletes, who started their Champs careers in Class 3 despite being young enough to compete in Class 4 at regional championships. ISSA is reportedly contemplating adding a Class 4 age category for next year’s staging of the championships.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) Boys’ Championships-winning Coach Neil Harrison has thrown his support behind reported plans for the high school sports administrative body to introduce Class 4 boys’ competition at the annual track and field championships, although questions remain about the potential long-term developmental implications for younger athletes.

There have been persistent whispers that ISSA plans to introduce Class 4 boys at next year’s staging of the five-day championships, along with other changes.

Presently, there are three age classes for boys — Classes 1, 2 and 3 — unlike the girls, who compete across four age groups: Classes 1, 2, 3, and 4. For years, ISSA has resisted requests to add an age group for younger boys. The lowest class currently for boys, Class 3, includes athletes under the age of 13.

Earlier this week, ISSA President Keith Wellington said the organisation had discussed a number of changes but was awaiting feedback from principals and coaches.

Two proposals he mentioned were allowing first-year Class 3 boys to compete in more than one individual event and adding the 400m to the Class 4 girls’ events.

While David Riley, head coach at Excelsior High and a member of the coaching staff when Wolmer’s Boys’ won Champs in 2010, declined to comment, saying, “I cannot comment at this time until the details are released for us as coaches to digest.” Harrison is among those who are leaning towards the change.

Harrison, who is currently the head boys’ coach at St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS), having previously held the position at Jamaica College, Kingston College and Munro College, said that, given Class 4 boys have been competing at regional championships, the proposed inclusion at the national high school championships would not be that big of a jump.

“Yes, I think so,” Harrison told the Jamaica Observer. “Class 4 boys compete in our regional championship, so why not the ultimate? It’s a good motivation for them because when they are not allowed to compete, not only the interest in the sport is lost, but sometimes they get lost in the school system as well.”

Meanwhile, Machel Woolery, head coach at Petersfield High, pointed out that Class 4-aged boys have in fact been competing at Champs, but against generally older boys.

“It is just that they will now be separating them and having them run independently and in their own class,” said Woolery before weighing up the pros and cons of their potential inclusion at Champs.

“It can be a plus as well as can be a negative.”

Woolery noted that Class 4 girls have been competing at Champs for a long time, but raised concerns that younger boys, who are good enough to qualify for the championships and compete in an age group above their own, may already be facing excessive demands on their developing bodies.

From a physiological perspective, the doubts linger.

Supporters of the potential move have argued that the introduction of a separate Class 4 boys’ category could provide younger athletes with a more appropriate competitive environment, reducing the need for some to compete against older and potentially more physically developed opponents.

However, such a move would not come without some opposition.

Detractors have raised questions about training loads, recovery, injury risk and the demands placed on boys who are still undergoing significant physical growth and maturation.

There is also a broader question about whether introducing another competitive category would improve long-term athlete development or place additional pressure on schools and young competitors to achieve results at an earlier age.

The challenge for ISSA, the coaches note, would be to ensure that any new category serves as a developmental pathway rather than simply creating another level at which young athletes are expected to produce results.

Woolery suggested that ISSA introduce restrictions for Class 4 boys, similar to those already in place for the girls.

“Maybe they can be limited to one event and a relay,” he added.

World.title: Still sold on 90
World.content:
Petrojam says motorists whose vehicles are designed for 87 octane generally gain no improvement in power, mileage or engine protection by choosing 90. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

MONTHS after Petrojam urged motorists to stop paying for higher-octane petrol their vehicles may not need, some taxi operators remain convinced that 90 is cleaner, gives more power, or lasts longer in the tank.

Drivers who depend on their cars to earn a living may see the extra cost as money well spent if they believe it protects the engine or takes them further. But Petrojam says those using 90 in vehicles designed for 87 are generally spending more without getting those benefits.

“The general view is that 90 is cleaner. The 87 kinda dirtier and heavier than the 90. That’s why most people use the 90, because they feel it cleaner. But the 87 burns better to me,” said one operator who gave his name as David during a Jamaica Observer vox pop.

With world oil prices climbing again, that extra spending deserves another look. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 4.9 per cent last week to close at US$109.86 a barrel on October 16,

Reuters reported. While that does not mean an immediate increase at Jamaican pumps, it puts the possible savings from choosing the correct grade back in focus.

Another operator, identified as “Bigga”, associated 90 with greater power and newer vehicles.

“The 90 burns better to me. The newer type vehicles work with 90 better. The older type vehicles you have to work with the 87. The 90 puts a stronger power on the system and a stronger revv.”

The interviews offer a glimpse of beliefs surrounding fuel purchases rather than a measure of how all taxi operators choose. They also do not establish whether participants had heard Petrojam’s earlier advice.

In May, the refinery encouraged motorists to check their manufacturers’ requirements, explaining that using 90 in a vehicle designed for 87 usually offered no benefit.

Yet Petrojam told the Business Observer that its sales still reflect a stronger preference for 90, even though most vehicles on Jamaica’s roads are designed to operate on 87.

“It is a misconception that 90-octane gasoline is inherently ‘stronger’ than 87. Both 87 and 90 contain 10 per cent ethanol (E-10) and have broadly similar energy content per litre. A higher octane rating means greater resistance to engine knocking, not more energy or power,” the company said in written responses.

“For years we’ve been advising the motoring public that 90-octane fuel is only required for high-compression, turbocharged, or spotrs car engine. However, because the premium grade is really for those types of vehicles, people are often mistaken in their belief that adding 90-octane gas to a non-high-performance vehicle will make it run faster,” Petrojam said.

The refinery, which is the only internationally rated fuel testing facility in Jamaica, also dismissed claims that 90-octane gas “burns” slower or stronger than 87-octane.

“Both grades operate at the same rate…For vehicles designed to operate on 87-octane gasoline, the additional octane generally provides no meaningful benefit.”

Petrojam attributes some of the preference to the instinctive belief that a higher number means a better product, alongside established buying habits and perceived performance benefits.

“The 90 lasts longer in the car. They say 90 is for certain cars and 87 is for the older cars. 90 is for the higher end vehicles,” motorist Renea told the Business Observer.

Meanhile, Kema Neil follows her mechanic’s advice.

“My mechanic always tells me to use 87, so I just work with the 87. He said that depending on the vehicle, it can take 90, but the older vehicles take 87 and they run much better.”

However, a vehicle’s age alone does not determine the correct grade, according to Petrojam. The octane number measures resistance to knocking — abnormal combustion inside the engine — rather than cleanliness or how much energy the petrol contains.

Petrojam says servicing, tyre pressure, and driving habits have a far greater influence on fuel efficiency than switching to 90 in an engine designed for 87.

For a taxi operator buying fuel regularly, the price difference can add up. At an illustrative pump-price gap of $30 per litre, purchasing 40 litres of 87 instead of 90 would save $1,200. Repeated weekly, that would amount to $62,400 over a year, assuming purchases and the price gap remained unchanged.

Actual savings depend on prices at the station, and apply only where 87 meets the vehicle’s requirements.

Understanding the octane numbers

Even motorists who check their manuals can become confused if the number printed there differs from those displayed at Jamaican pumps.

Petrojam explained that Jamaica uses the Anti-Knock Index, or AKI, while many vehicle manuals use the Research Octane Number, or RON. AKI is calculated by averaging RON and another measure, the Motor Octane Number.

The different scales mean a manual specifying 91 RON does not automatically rule out Jamaica’s 87-octane petrol.

“As a general guide, 87 AKI is approximately equivalent to 91 RON, while 90 AKI is approximately equivalent to 95 RON. Motorists should therefore compare their vehicle manufacturer’s minimum octane requirement with the corresponding local grade,” Petrojam said.

Under that guide, local 87 is generally suitable where the manual specifies a minimum of 91 RON or lower. Local 90 is generally appropriate for a 95 RON requirement. The refinery added that motorists whose manuals specify above 95 RON should check the manufacturer’s requirements against the available fuel specifications.

The wording in the manual also matters. A higher grade being “required” establishes a minimum the fuel must meet. A recommendation can allow more flexibility.

“Where a higher grade is recommended but regular gasoline is permitted, the lower grade may be used, although some reduction in performance or fuel economy may occur,” Petrojam explained.

Meanwhile, the refinery acknowledged that it sees an opportunity for vehicle dealers to clear up these questions before customers establish their buying habits.

“We think that it is important for motor vehicle dealers to advise owners that, where applicable, 87-octane should be the recommended fuel type,” it said.

In response to queries from the Business Observer on what more can the industry do to explain fuel requirements clearly, Petrojam reasoned that dealers could explain at the point of sale that Jamaica’s 87 is approximately equivalent to 91 RON, helping buyers match the instructions in their manuals to the grades available locally.

The refinery said it also supports making that information easier to find when motorists pull up to refuel.

“In this regard, Petrojam would also support clearer fuel grade labelling at service stations, including a simple RON-to-AKI conversion guide at the pump, to help motorists make informed purchasing decisions.” That would give drivers a reference when deciding what to buy, alongside advice from mechanics and fellow motorists.

—Additional reporting by Jason Cross

World.title: Former CMU worker details university’s accounting, banking systems
World.content:
Campus of Caribbean Maritime University in Kingston (Photo: CMU)

A former senior member of staff of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) is expected to continue testimony regarding the school’s finances on Wednesday, with information on the now-defunct CAP-YES programme, in the fraud trial of former CMU boss Fritz Pinnock along with former education minister Ruel Reid and their co-accused.

The witness, appearing before Senior Parish Judge Sanchia Burrell at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court on Tuesday, testified how money came into and left certain bank accounts controlled by the university between 2016 and 2019, including accounts for payroll, CAP (Career Advancement Programme) and CAPYES (Career Advancement Programme – Youth Empowerment Services) programme, among others.

The department in which they worked was guided by the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit Act) and PBMA ( The Public Bodies Management and Accountability Act), the witness said, adding that it oversaw payroll, including salary deductions for CMU employees; accounts receivable, which dealt with collecting money owed to the school; and accounts payable, which dealt with any money the school owed to vendors or debt obligations.

While testifying, the witness indicated that the weekly accounts payable process included the submission of documentation verifying the debt obligation, which would be entered on CMUs system and included in an aged payables report. Any vendors to be paid by the school would then be selected from that report.

When pressed on what type of vendors this included, the witness listed utility entities, suppliers of goods to the school’s tuck shop and others undertaking special projects.

The witness also told the court that the school received a monthly subvention from the Ministry of Finance through the Ministry of Education that was deposited to a specific bank account.

When asked where that subvention was funded from, to their understanding, the witness said “from taxes”.

That account, the witness said, was used as a flow-through to other bank accounts, including payroll accounts.

The witness also touched on the operations of the school’s canteen or tuck shop, which had multiple accounts associated with it. The witness testified that cash proceeds would be deposited into the accounts and canteen vendors paid from it, adding that when enough cash was not in the account to pay vendors, the canteen would be provided with an advance by CMU, which would also go to the account.

The school also received money from the government for the operation of the CAP and CAP-YES programmes, deposited directly into accounts set up by CMU, the witness told the court. The witness said accounts were used for expenses associated with CAP and CAP-YES, including paying some salaries as well as stipends for students in need and other initiatives.

CAP, which is carried out at institutions across the island, was intended to provide technical, vocational, and academic training to youth, and CAP-YES was a programme offshoot attached specifically to the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

CAP and CAPYES were shuttered at the Caribbean Maritime University in 2020 with instructions to complete the course for those already in training and take in no further applicants.

During testimony, the witness identified Pinnock as the former head of the university, pointing out his striped shirt and orange tie. Pinnock, who has sought leave to take notes during the trial, did not react visibly at being identified. He was represented by a junior of his attorney in the matter, Hugh Wildman.

Pinnock, Reid and their co-accused, Reid’s daughter Sharelle Reid and wife Sharen Reid and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence’s are before the court on a 35-count indictment, accused of participating in a scheme with others unknown that siphoned off more than $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU.

They have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Issues with disclosure were also put before Burrell in the courtroom on Tuesday with defence attorney Linda Wright, who represents Reid, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Sharelle and Kevon Johnson, who holds for Brown Lawrence’s attorney Oswest Senior Smith, all rising to express concern.

Wright maintained that more documents relating to certain witnesses, including the witness scheduled to be called that day, had been shared by the prosecution at a late hour, thus creating challenges for the defence to go through the documents and take instructions from their clients.

Wright maintained that this was not a “trial by ambush”, describing the disclosure as untidy.

The prosecution maintained that the documents in relation to Tuesday’s witness were not new and that any late disclosure of new documents was not a deliberate effort on its part.

Burrell, who reminded counsel to exercise care around disclosure, is expected to grant a brief adjournment in relation to the issue.

World.title: AfD’s Alice Weidel urges quick Ukraine talks and a return to cheap Russian energy
World.content:
Weidel made the comments during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where she unveiled her opposition AfD party’s EU program at an event organized by the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations group.

The party aims to shrink the Commission, turn the European Parliament into an assembly of delegates appointed by national parliaments, and seek an opt-out for Germany from EU policies it can’t reform to its liking — potentially including an exit from the Schengen border-free travel area, she told reporters.

During an event following the press conference, Polish MEP Tobiasz Bocheński, from the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group, asked what she thought of Poland’s fears regarding Russia. Weidel said her party “puts German interests first,” insisting that “now we are in a critical phase that our industry is dying without Russian gas and oil.”

Germany needs “a sustainable, reliable and cheap energy resource that has been guaranteed by Russia for the last four decades,” she added, claiming that sanctions on Russia have “destroyed” Germany’s “business model.”

German industry is shedding jobs amid high energy costs, Chinese competition and U.S. tariffs, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz continues to push for reforms to revive a stagnant economy.

Weidel said that Russia, the U.S. and China are the only ones steering talks on Ukraine while European leaders aren’t even invited to sit at the table. The EU should have pushed for peace since the start, she added, as “four years down the road, it’s in a much worse position going into negotiations with Russia.”

World.title: Talking to Putin: Europe seeks a negotiator-in-chief for Ukraine
World.content:
“President Putin disregards the European Union as an authority,” Czech President Petr Pavel said Tuesday in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters’ Network, of which POLITICO is a part. “He doesn’t want to talk to Ursula von der Leyen, he doesn’t talk to Kaja Kallas. He stopped talking to other European leaders, including Emmanuel Macron.”

He added that the EU should “identify a person or a group of people who would speak for Europe. Not necessarily representatives of the EU or NATO, but simply leaders who would be given a mandate by the others to negotiate.”

Czech President Petr Pavel speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, on September 23, 2026. | Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images

In recent days, Trump has dismayed Ukraine and its European allies by talking over their heads with Putin and appearing increasingly willing to take Russia’s side in the almost five-year war.

That has reignited debate in Brussels and beyond about the need for Europe to have its own direct line to the Kremlin to safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Ukraine’s ability to resist a lopsided deal.

“Much as it sticks in the craw, I do think a channel of some kind to Putin would be a good thing to have,” said David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London. “I am not optimistic that it would achieve anything much in the short term, but to have a channel which can then be used as and when an opportunity arises is not a bad thing.”

Diplomats and officials disagree on who would be the best person to represent Europe.

World.title: Russia ready for 3-way talks on Ukraine war, Kremlin says
World.content:
Witkoff confirmed on X that discussions “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.”

His visit was the latest in a new round of U.S. attempts to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end its war against Ukraine. The special envoy also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, subsequently announcing a proposal for a three-way leaders’ negotiation.

There have been several rounds of talks between the U.S. and Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The most recent discussions stalled in February when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran.

Previous negotiations were largely political theater and failed to yield any broader breakthrough on halting hostilities, prisoner-of-war exchanges or a truce regarding strikes on energy infrastructure.

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine.

On Wednesday, footage emerged of Witkoff praising Putin during their face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, after the Russians released a U.S. prisoner from captivity.

World.title: Ex-DUP chief faces new allegation of raping woman inside Westminster
World.content:
A woman visiting the House of Commons in 2016 alleges that Jeffrey Donaldson tried to sexually assault her inside the Democratic Unionist Party’s Westminster offices.

The jailed former leader of Northern Ireland’s Democratic Unionist Party, Jeffrey Donaldson, is facing a new allegation that he raped a woman inside the DUP’s Westminster offices in 2016.

Donaldson, who last week received a 15-year prison sentence for sexually assaulting two girls, is serving his punishment in an isolated wing for sex offenders in Northern Ireland’s Maghaberry Prison. Donaldson — who is tentatively scheduled for release by 2033 after serving half of his sentence — is appealing his conviction on 18 counts, including one of rape.

The Metropolitan Police in London said Wednesday it has opened its own investigation after receiving an evidence file from Police Service of Northern Ireland detectives, who interviewed the woman on October 13.
