World.title: Le coût des ex-Premiers ministres a baissé de 500 000 euros
World.content:
L'ancien Premier Ministre Michel Barnier, alors nouvellement nommé au poste, serre la main de l'ancien Premier Ministre sortant Gabriel Attal lors d'une cérémonie à Matignon, Paris, le 5 September 2024. | Photo pool par Sarah Meyssonnier via AFP/Getty Images

Les avantages accordés aux anciens chefs du gouvernement ont augmenté en 2025, avant une première baisse attendue cette année, selon un document budgétaire obtenu par POLITICO.

PARIS — Voici une ligne budgétaire symbolique qui va dégonfler en 2026. Selon un document parlementaire consulté en avant-première par POLITICO, le coût des avantages réservés aux anciens Premiers ministres est estimé à environ 1,2 million d’euros, en baisse d’un demi-million d’euros par rapport à 2025 (1,72 million). Une baisse d’une ampleur inédite depuis 2019, selon les données rassemblées par la députée Marie-Christine Dalloz (LR) dans son rapport spécial au projet de loi de finances.

La diminution a deux explications. D’abord, la disparition de Lionel Jospin en mars et d’Edouard Balladur en août, qui mobilisaient les moyens mis à leur disposition à hauteur de 260 000 euros en 2025. Ensuite, le décret pris par Sébastien Lecornu à son arrivée à Matignon qui met fin, depuis le 1er janvier et de manière rétroactive, à la possibilité pour ses prédécesseurs de bénéficier d’un chauffeur avec véhicule de fonction, dix ans après avoir quitté leurs fonctions.

En théorie, Dominique de Villepin, François Fillon, Alain Juppé, Laurent Fabius, Jean-Marc Ayrault et Edith Cresson ont donc perdu cet avantage. Sauf que cette dernière a obtenu le maintien de cette largesse d’après Mediapart.

World.title: Perquisitions au Parlement européen dans une enquête visant l’ancien groupe du RN
World.content:
Les perquisitions ont eu lieu dans les bureaux du secrétariat général du groupe, selon deux responsables qui ont souhaité garder l’anonymat pour s’exprimer au sujet de l’enquête en cours.

Lorsqu’ID a été dissous en 2024, bon nombre de ses membres ont rejoint les Patriotes, notamment des élus du Rassemblement national, du Parti de la liberté d’Autriche (FPÖ), du Fidesz hongrois, du Vlaams Belang (Intérêt flamand) belge, de l’ANO 2011 tchèque et du parti espagnol Vox.

Dans un communiqué, les Patriotes insistent sur le fait qu’il n’existe “aucune continuité juridique” avec le groupe ID, et qu’ils “ne sont pas visés” par les perquisitions.

Les soupçons portent sur l’utilisation du budget alloué chaque année par le Parlement européen aux groupes politiques pour couvrir leurs frais administratifs et opérationnels. Le Parquet européen enquête pour déterminer si le groupe ID a versé des dons irréguliers à des organisations régionales dans plusieurs pays de l’Union européenne, et s’il a enfreint les règles relatives aux appels d’offres dans le cadre de contrats attribués à des entreprises proches du groupe.

En 2025, le service financier a ordonné aux Patriotes de restituer 276 967 euros de fonds européens qui, selon lui, auraient été indûment dépensés au cours du second semestre 2024, dans le cadre de procédures d’appel d’offres irrégulières similaires.

“Comme toujours lorsqu’on le lui demande, le Parlement coopère avec les autorités compétentes. Nous n’avons pas d’autres commentaires à faire”, a déclaré un porte-parole du Parlement européen dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

World.title: Water sector to wait until 2027 for full details of Burnham’s overhaul
World.content:
Water UK Chief Executive David Henderson urged the government to move ahead with reforms suggested last year by former Bank of England Deputy Governor Jon Cunliffe, before ministers decide the overall path of how the sector is owned.

The Cunliffe report “was given to the government 15 months ago and the credit rating agencies are watching,” Henderson told POLITICO. “If the government doesn’t pretty soon decide what it wants to do with that report, then we risk a downgrade, as Moody’s has indicated. And if there’s a downgrade, that would sadly see £40 being added to every single water bill across England and Wales. That’s the last thing anybody wants.”

He added: “We still have no idea how [a proposed] new regulator will look, what status it will have, what its duties will be, which parts of the Environment Agency will stay in the Environment Agency, and which parts will go into the new regulator. That is causing uncertainty … an important consideration for any investor.”

One government official insisted the 10-year plan would contain some finer details of plans to overhaul the water industry, though they accepted that fiscal implications were always dealt with in fiscal events such as the spending review.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is also due to bring a water bill to parliament before Christmas with separate policy, such as closing what Burnham has called “loopholes used to pay excessive bonuses” to water company executives. It will also contain scrutiny powers for regional mayors.

Burnham announced last month that the bill would lift a ban on the government owning more than 3% of shares in any English water firm. But he has also long made clear that he would not fully nationalize the industry, a move the government previously estimated would cost £100 billion for England and Wales together.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, one of Burnham’s most powerful allies in government, is leading three task forces including one on public control of water alongside housing, energy and transport.

Officials have been working through a “spectrum of options” for how public control in the water sector will look, a second government official said. They added that ministers are due to begin deciding which option — or combination of options — will be taken forward before the 10-year plan.

World.title: Prosecutor searches far-right group offices in EU Parliament
World.content:
The EPPO confirmed it carried out searches in the Parliament’s buildings in France and Belgium “as part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European funds by a former political group in the European Parliament.”

The searches took place at the group’s secretariat offices, according to two officials, granted anonymity to speak about the ongoing investigation.

When ID dissolved in 2024, many of its staff moved to the Patriots, including lawmakers from France’s National Rally, Austria’s Freedom Party, Hungary’s Fidesz, Spain’s Vox, Belgium’s Flemish Interest and Czechia’s ANO 2011.

In their statement, the group insisted “there is no legal continuity with the ID Group” and that “it is not involved in the ongoing investigations.”

The allegations of mismanagement of funds relate to the budget allocated annually by the Parliament for political groups to spend on administrative and operative costs. EPPO is probing whether ID made irregular donations to regional organizations in several EU countries, and whether the group breached tender rules in contracts awarded to companies friendly to the group.

In 2025, the finance department ordered the Patriots to give back €276,967 in EU funds it says the group misused during the second half of 2024, related to similar irregular tender procedures.

World.title: Yemen: Tanks fire as fighting erupts on the outskirts of Taiz
World.content:
Yemeni government forces and allied Popular Resistance fighters clashed with Houthi fighters on the western outskirts of Taiz on Wednesday, 21 October, near the city’s old airport and Jabal Han mountain. The internationally recognised government said its forces repelled the attack, while reporting air strikes on Houthi positions, vehicles and a missile launchpad west, south and east of the city.

 

Footage showed a government tank firing towards Houthi positions as gunfire echoed across the area. The fighting comes as Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, faces mounting pressure from Houthi forces, which have largely encircled it and cut key supply routes, including the main road to Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised government.

The restrictions have also disrupted access to the city’s main landfill, leaving rubbish to pile up along major streets. Sanitation workers say they can no longer reach the dumping site because of the clashes and have resorted to burning waste in the streets.

Footage showed waste burning beside busy roads, thick smoke rising over neighbourhoods and goats feeding among the rubbish. Aid agencies said fuel shortages were also disrupting water pumps, hospitals and waste collection, deepening fears of disease outbreaks.

“If we don’t die from Houthi shelling, we’ll die from this rubbish,” one resident said.

World.title: Disappointed after meeting, French unions call for 5 November action
World.content:
Union leaders who met Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the Matignon on Wednesday left the nearly two-and-a-half-hour meeting disappointed.

 

According to Sophie Binet, head of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), Sébastien Lecornu did not announce "any measures" to respond to the multiple protests. There was "no consideration of our demands", she lamented.

The CGT, which took part in the 17 October demonstrations that degenerated into riots and looting in several cities over the weekend, will once again take to the streets on Saturday for the "act II" of the cost-of-living mobilisation announced by a "yellow vest" coordination.

For the unions, the central objective remains the mobilisation launched by almost all of them among private- and public-sector employees for 5 November. "The time has come to move the mobilisation up a gear; from that date strike action must take over", said Sophie Binet.

By then, the secretary-general of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT, the country’s largest union), Marylise Léon, expects "social responses" to workers’ expectations.

According to the president of the French Confederation of Christian Workers (CFTC), Cyril Chabanier, the government has nonetheless "opened the door" to "a discussion" on raising the minimum wage. On this issue, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has called for things to "move quickly".

At Matignon, the unions also regretted that secondary school and student organisations had not been invited to the meeting.

They are expected to be received again on Monday by the education minister. Édouard Geffray has promised initial measures to respond to the demands expressed on the platform set up by the government. Secondary school pupils have been mobilised for several weeks, with the support of university students, calling for more resources for education, improvements to the state of school buildings, replacement for absent teachers and the scrapping of the Parcoursup platform which handles tertiary education access and is seen as deeply flawed.

On a Middle East tour, Emmanuel Macron calls for "firmness"

Speaking from Qatar, Emmanuel Macron called for "firmness" towards those responsible for the violence and on Thursday convened a meeting with the intelligence services to examine the failings of 17 October. The president, however, made no announcements on the many demands voiced by the protesters, including on purchasing power or funding for schools and universities.

Emmanuel Macron, who then travelled on to Saudi Arabia where he was received by crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman, said the French would get a "fair return" from this tour, notably on diesel prices.

On Wednesday, several political figures from across the spectrum again condemned what they see as a failure of those in power. Édouard Philippe, the Horizons presidential candidate, criticised Emmanuel Macron’s decision to maintain his trip to the Gulf. Former head of state François Hollande, for his part, attacked a government he considers weak. Marine Le Pen, the National Rally candidate for the presidential election, targeted what she called the "waning power".

Several curfews renewed

In Paris, the police prefecture has imposed a new curfew in certain areas for the night from Wednesday to Thursday.

The decrees "ban the presence of adults and minors alike in the areas around Place de la République and the Les Halles district from 11 pm today until 6 am tomorrow", the police prefecture said on X.

In Lyon, the Rhône prefecture has decided to renew the curfew and the ban on gatherings, extending the measures that were in force on the previous two nights in Lyon. The curfew runs from 11 pm to 6 am, two hours later than the previous ones, which started at 9 pm.

Around 2,500 people in police custody and 174 jailed

During a visit to Marseille, which saw violent clashes at the weekend and where the town hall was vandalised, justice minister Gérald Darmanin reported 2,500 people taken into police custody following the violence and the looting of numerous shops during the 17 October mobilisation.

Of these, 917 people have been brought before prosecutors with charges to be tried in immediate appearances. The minister, who pledged that justice would be firm, said this figure had doubled, or even tripled.

In Paris, of the 557 people taken into custody after the violence and looting in the capital, 300 appeared before a magistrate by midday on Wednesday. On Tuesday evening, Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said that none had claimed a motive "of whatever political nature", even as the government accuses "the ultra-left" of being largely behind the violence.

The strategy for maintaining public order has also been called into question for several weeks. The Defender of Rights announced on Tuesday that it had received 46 complaints since the start of the secondary school students’ movement, more than ten of which concern incidents from the weekend. At the same time, the IGPN, the police internal affairs body, has been tasked with at least six investigations relating to those two days.

World.title: Greece: Thousands flood Athens streets in education protest
World.content:
Students, teachers and public-sector workers marched through central Athens on Wednesday, demanding more funding for education, smaller classes, better facilities and affordable student housing.

 

Aerial footage showed crowds filling major streets as protesters made their way from the University of Athens towards the Greek Parliament. Some banners written in French reflected the Greek protesters' solidarity with, and inspiration from, recent student demonstrations in France. Organisers presented the march as part of a broader European movement calling for better-funded education, affordable housing and relief from rising living costs.

Police officers, including riot police carrying shields, accompanied the march and blocked nearby roads. Some shops and cafés closed their shutters as a precaution.

The demonstration was part of a nationwide protest movement, with rallies also held in Thessaloniki, Patras, Larissa and Crete. Police estimated that around 10,000 people took part in Athens and its suburbs, although organisers claimed a higher turnout.

Some demonstrators had camped overnight outside Parliament, calling for rent controls, greater housing support and more investment in public education.

The rally ended peacefully shortly before 2pm, reflecting mounting pressure on the Greek government to address education funding and the financial difficulties facing students.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV post-op results show no further treatment required as tumour was localised
World.content:
Final histological tests and molecular biology analyses carried out on tissue removed during Pope Leo XIV’s surgery have confirmed the presence of a localised pulmonary adenocarcinoma.

 

A subsequent oncological assessment has determined that no further therapy is necessary.

The update was given by the Pope’s doctors, Dr Luigi Carbone and Prof Stefano Margaritora, as they reported on the pontiff’s postoperative progress.

The examinations confirmed that the disease had not spread beyond the lung. In light of these results and the specialist evaluation, no additional oncological treatment has been deemed necessary.

It was the Pope himself who, during the Angelus prayer on 11 October, revealed that he had a nodule in his right lung. He was then admitted to hospital and underwent surgery on 13 October, in an operation lasting around an hour and a half.

World.title: Aberfan: King Charles marks Welsh mining disaster that killed a generation of children
World.content:
King Charles III has led tributes to the people of Aberfan on the 60th anniversary of the disaster, in which 116 children and 28 adults died when a colliery spoil tip collapsed onto Pantglas Junior School in Wales in 21 October 1966.

 

The King, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales met survivors in the Welsh village. The King and Prince William laid wreaths at the memorial garden, and the Queen placed a posy.

"We have heard stories of heartbreak, but also of heroism," the King said. "We have heard of the most agonising grief, but also of the most inspiring grace."

King Charles III and members of his family laid a wreath at the Aberfan memorial to mark the disaster. 21 October, 2026. AP Photo

Coal bosses had been warned of the danger beforehand, yet no one was prosecuted or lost their job.

What happened at Aberfan?

Aberfan is a small coal-mining village in the valleys of south Wales, in the United Kingdom. For decades, waste from the local colliery had been dumped in huge heaps, known as tips, on the hillside above the houses.

These tips had moved before - the heap of coal waste had slid in 1944 and again in 1963, but the warning signs were not acted on.

Rescue workers dug through the mining waste that buried the Junior School in Aberfan in 1966. FILE. AP Photo

On the morning of Friday 21 October 1966, one of the tips gave way. Shortly after 9.15am, over 100,000 cubic metres of sodden waste poured down the mountain and onto the village school, just as lessons were starting.

The last child to be found alive was pulled out at 11:00 that morning.

The scale of the loss is still hard to grasp. The disaster claimed the lives of 144 people, 116 of them children, and an entire generation of the village was all but wiped out. Within days, the UK Parliament ordered an official inquiry.

What did the inquiry find?

On 26 October 1966, the UK government minister for Wales appointed a tribunal led by senior judge Lord Justice Edmund Davies. It heard evidence first in nearby Merthyr Tydfil and then in the Welsh capital, Cardiff.

Its verdict, published in August 1967, was unequivocal - "Blame for the disaster rests upon the National Coal Board," the state-owned body that ran Britain’s coal industry. As a result of the inquiry, information about every one of the board’s tips was gathered for the first time.

People across Britain and around the world sent money to help the grieving village, and the disaster fund grew to £1.75m (€2.08m).

What happened to the money donated?

In 1968, UK Prime Minister Harold Wilson’s government forced the disaster fund to give up £150,000 (€178,000) to pay for removing the remaining coal waste heaps above Aberfan, even though those tips belonged to the National Coal Board.

The village had to wait almost three decades for the money to be returned. Ron Davies, the UK government’s minister for Wales, repaid it in 1997, and the Welsh Government later gave Aberfan charities a further £2m.

Queen Elizabeth II visited the site shortly after the disaster. FILE AP Photo

The fund made equal payments to every bereaved family. The UK's Charity Commission tried to block these payments as it wanted the trustees to be satisfied that each parent had been "close" to the child who died. The trustees defied the Commission and paid the families anyway.

The fund was attempting to support families because the National Coal Board was paying them very little. The board raised its compensation offer from £50 to £500 (€596) per bereaved family.

Sixty years later, organisations across Wales were invited to observe a minute’s silence at 9.15am on Wednesday, the moment the tip collapsed.

World.title: Lithuania seizes major synthetic drugs lab run by Dutch national
World.content:
Lithuanian authorities have uncovered one of the largest synthetic drugs laboratories in the Baltics, seizing hundreds of kilograms of drugs and thousands of litres of chemical precursors at a site near Vilnius allegedly run by a Dutch national of Turkish origin.

 

“[Drugs] were being produced on an almost industrial scale,” Saulius Briginas, Deputy Chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told journalists during a press briefing on Wednesday.

Investigators believe the Dutch citizen organised the laboratory's work and coordinated its illegal activities alongside three other members who were all Lithuanian nationals.

Preliminary figures indicate that police recovered more than 3,000 litres of BMK, a chemical precursor used in the production of amphetamines; more than 500kg of methamphetamine; more than 300kg of amphetamine; and around 4.5kg of the synthetic cathinone 3-CMC. This amounts to over 4 million single doses, Briginas said.

“On the wholesale illicit market, the drugs would be worth more than €2 million,” he said. “At street level, the value could be ten times higher.”

Such figures, Lithuanian authorities believe, indicate that the drugs could not have been intended solely for the Lithuanian market.

Instead, the operation was geared towards markets across Europe, with the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and the Czech Republic among the countries to which the drugs may have been destined.

The investigation also uncovered the industrial-scale procurement of chemicals needed to manufacture synthetic drugs. The group sourced laboratory equipment and chemical substances from China, India and several European countries, while also purchasing some uncontrolled substances from specialist suppliers in Lithuania.

Police found 380 cylinders of hydrogen originating from China at the laboratory. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of synthetic drugs, while sulphuric acid was reportedly purchased in quantities of one tonne per transaction.

The operation extended beyond the laboratory itself. Police intercepted a shipment intended for the Czech Republic after finding 17kg of amphetamine crystals in two plastic containers inside cargo handled by a Lithuanian logistics company.

Under Lithuanian law, offences involving the illegal production, possession and smuggling of particularly large quantities of narcotic or psychotropic substances can carry prison sentences of up to 18 years.

World.title: Colombia seizes 7.6 tonnes of Netherlands-bound cocaine at Cartagena port
World.content:
Colombian police have seized 7.6 tonnes of cocaine bound for the Netherlands at the port of Cartagena, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Tuesday.

 

"The National Police has just achieved the largest cocaine seizure in the port of Cartagena in the last 10 years," he wrote on X.

According to Colombia's National Police, the drugs were hidden in powdered panela, an unrefined cane sugar, and were found by its anti-narcotics directorate in an operation coordinated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

De la Espriella said security forces had seized 132 tonnes of cocaine, worth around $6.1 billion, in his government's first 75 days.

"There is no truce against narco-terrorism! Every dose we prevent from reaching the streets saves lives, and every dollar we take from them weakens their criminal structures," he added.

Separately, the Dutch Public Prosecution Service (OM) confirmed to the Dutch newspaper AD that two Dutch nationals had been arrested in Colombia at its request.

Colombian prosecutors named them as Ronny and Ulrich. Neither authority has linked the arrests to the seizure. According to the EU Drugs Agency, 330 tonnes of cocaine were seized in the EU in 2024, down from 419 tonnes in 2023.

World.title: Thélyson Orélien row: publisher says AI used to write 'C'était ça ou mourir'
World.content:
The case has been shaking the French-language publishing world for weeks. On Wednesday 21 October, the Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal announced via a press release (source in French) that Thélyson Orélien had indeed used artificial intelligence (AI) to write his novel "C'était ça ou mourir", contrary to what he had previously claimed.

 

"New information, confirmed in recent days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process (of the novel), even though the author had assured us, on several occasions, that he had never resorted to it in creating his book", the publisher said in a statement on Wednesday.

"As a result, Boréal will not reprint the novel and will not publish any further books by Thélyson Orélien."

This announcement comes just a week after the publisher had said it was backing the author, insisting it had no evidence that would make it possible to establish with certainty that AI had been used.

In the face of mounting doubts, and after Thélyson Orélien "announced that he would not provide any further material", the publisher says it has "commissioned an in-depth external analysis" of "all the working versions of the novel".

"We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of "C'était ça ou mourir", and we will probably never have a definitive answer on that point" but "for us, the fundamental issue is the relationship of trust between authors and publishers", the publishing house added.

The controversy was sparked by accusations from the X account "Balance ton Claude", which claimed to have identified extensive use of AI in the novel. The affair has since shaken the sector and, for weeks, fuelled questions about the future of the writing profession.

World.title: Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment — Vatican
World.content:
Pope Leo's lung cancer surgery last week was a success, the Vatican said. The pope broke with traditions of secrecy around papal health issues after announcing he needed surgery to remove a nodule on his lung.

Pope Leo XIV will not require further cancer treatment, his doctors announced on Wednesday, after the pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer last week.

The Vatican cited the pope's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora, as saying the pope's disease was localized and that "no further treatment" was necessary.

This confirms earlier prognoses suggesting the pope's cancer was caught early.

Pope Leo last week underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on October 13 at Rome's Gemelli hospital.

What did Pope Leo's doctors say about his health condition?

The 71-year-old pontiff's doctors said the final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during his surgery were issued on Wednesday.

"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the Holy See said.

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The pope's surgeon added that there was "no clinical reason to cancel" the pope's visit to South America.

The ambitious trip, initially scheduled for November 6-17, would take the pontiff to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, involving a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and stops at high altitude.

Pope Leo's transparency around illness breaks with tradition

Leo was discharged from the hospital on Saturday, saying he would resume his activities gradually.

His illness shocked the Catholic Church, stoking concern that any potential prolonged treatment, such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy, could have affected the pope's ability to head the church.

Pope Leo first announced his condition during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, telling followers that he would be having a nodule surgically removed.

The announcement broke away from long-held traditions of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.

Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: German youth plan France-style mass protests
World.content:
A youth-led movement in Germany has called for demonstrations in major cities of the country on October 31.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

World.title: France bans protests in parts of Paris as Macron slams Trump
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron railed against "stupid" comments made by foreign leaders for their political purposes. Plus, Paris police are set to extend restrictions on gatherings in parts of the city on Thursday.

As France braces for more protests on Thursday, Paris police said participants will be banned from gathering at the Elysee presidential palace, the Bastille Square, both houses of parliament, and several tourist areas, including the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees.

The curfew is set to apply between 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) and 8 p.m. local time.

French authorities have sought to reassure the public after the country was swept by violent unrest last weekend. The ongoing crisis started with students protesting high prices and demanding education reform, but it soon escalated, with masked rioters looting shops and clashing with police. On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted the authorities "lost control" and failed to anticipate the scale of the violence.

Violent unrest rocks France after nationwide protests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Large-scale protests are also expected in Paris this weekend. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has already pledged a "massive" security deployment for the event.

Trump blames 'migrants, jihadists, and communists' for unrest

While the European nation has seen two relatively quiet nights in a row, images of burning cars, broken store windows and ransacked buildings have been used by politicians inside and outside of France to increase pressure on the current government, led by President Emmanuel Macron.

Notably, US President Donald Trump attributed the unrest to "migrants, jihadists, and communists," saying they had "conquered, looted, and burned (France) to the ground." While campaigning for the US midterm elections, Trump also said he had warned Macron about immigration, but the French president refused to close the borders.

Macron claims images of protest manipulated, triggering 'stupid' comments

While visiting Qatar on Wednesday, Macron fired back at Trump, implying that the US leader and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were trying to gain political capital from the unrest in France. Netanyahu also spoke of an "invasion of extremist Islam" earlier this week.

"There are people who campaign at France's expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," Macron told reporters on Wednesday.

When asked if his comments were about Trump, Macron replied: "Among others."

President Macron urges distinction between protesters and vandals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said information about the crisis has been manipulated, including "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened." This, according to Macron, prompted comments that are "as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders."

"We've had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said.

Le Pen says Macron to blame for 'sad reality' of protests

Later on Wednesday, Macron's far-right rival Marine Le Pen sought to dismiss his account as "conspiratorial."

"The images we saw last Saturday are not generated by artificial intelligence: they show the sad reality of what France has become after 10 years of Macronist rule," said Le Pen.

The far-right leader is currently the favorite to win the 2027 presidential election in France, followed by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon.

World.title: Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
World.content:
Alice Weidel (center) said the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more Image: Ann-Krisitn Wenzel/dpa/picture alliance

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi at one table, without Ukraine. What Moscow wants from the proposal and why Beijing might agree.
World.content:
Moscow is pushing for a summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Kyiv or the EU. What does Russia hope to gain, and why might China be willing to take part?

The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions.

Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on October 21.

Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war."

US special envoy Steve Witkoff at and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting in St. Petersburg on October 21 Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS

According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting.

Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine

Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia.

Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account.

According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference, referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe.

The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table.

What does China stand to gain from the talks?

Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power.

The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible.

Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play?

Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said.

China's leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to hold a trilateral summit with Russia in Shenzhen Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship."

Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation.

However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia.

Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW.

He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington.

Is Putin's political survival crucial for China?

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war.

Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said.

President Zelenskyy said deciding on Ukraine's future without Ukraine was unacceptable Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way.

He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness?

Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China.

Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence.

In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak.

Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations.

He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe.

Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries.

He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said.

He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence.

"The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine.

Umarov offers another perspective.

He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground.

"China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said.

"Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone."

This article was originally published in Russian.

World.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
World.content:
A New Mexico judge ordered Facebook's parent company, Meta, to pay $25 billion for misleading users over the Cambridge Analytica breach, which took place during Donald Trump's first presidential campaign.

US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.

"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge ⁠Francis ⁠Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.

The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.

New Mexico rejects deal with Meta

Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.

Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.

In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.

In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."

Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system

Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.

US jury fines Meta in landmark child‑safety case To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is ​money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.

On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.

While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.

"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.

The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.

World.title: PHP developers say key patches available after global scare
World.content:
Newly discovered vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language have put millions of websites at risk, with government agencies sounding alarms and taking down sites. Developers say updating systems is "imperative."

The updates patching the recently leaked PHP security issues are now online , developers of the open-source programming language said on Wednesday afternoon.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the team said in an online statement.

Millions of websites worldwide, including critical infrastructure and government portals, as well as news sites and online shops, rely on PHP. The software is free.

The new patches aim to fix two "critical vulnerabilities" hackers could exploit to remotely take control of websites and servers, bypassing usual obstacles such as password-protected accounts. The gaps were labeled CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

How did hackers trick Berlin's city government? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

By exploiting them, malicious actors could gain access to government databases and customer data, deface websites, or compromise entire businesses or other online services.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a blog post.

Cloudflare reports 'early attacks'

The weaknesses were flagged by two separate security companies, Calif and Wiz, this August. Both of the firms used AI tools to detect the PHP issues.

PHP developers kept the flaws confidential while working on the fix. News of the security issues, however, leaked on Tuesday, a day before the scheduled update.

Hours before the PHP update, Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of security firm Cloudflare, said hackers were already trying to exploit these weaknesses.

"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," he said in an online post.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

Is AI the new weapon of mass data theft? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

NSA urges taking websites offline if update not feasible

Authorities in multiple countries, including Australia, Japan, and several European nations, issued warnings and took down government websites in an effort to preempt potential attacks.

In France, the website of the Paris Police Prefecture was taken offline due to "detection of a critical security vulnerability," along with local government pages. Germany's government IT service took down some sites that used PHP. Belgium's Foreign Ministry temporarily blocked its own online presence, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency took itself online as a precaution.

The US National Security Agency (NSA) warned that vulnerabilities "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database."

"If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," they said on X.

Meanwhile, the White House said it was informed of the issue last week and that US federal agencies were assessing the potential impact to government systems and infrastructure.

World.title: Raids at far-right group's offices at European Parliament
World.content:
Authorities searched the Patriots for Europe's European Parliament offices in a long-running funding inquiry. The group says the charges pertain to its predecessor and there is "no legal continuity" between the two.

The third-largest alliance of parties in the European Parliament, the right-wing nationalist Patriots for Europe (PfE) group, on Wednesday said searches had been carried out at "administrative offices" at the European Parliament buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.

PfE said the searches appeared to be tied to the long-running probe into alleged misuse of funds by members of the now-disbanded Identity and Democracy (ID) Group.

PfE formed out of the ashes of ID, losing and gaining some members along the way, after the last European Parliament elections in 2024.

What did the investigative body say about the searches?

The European Public Prosecutor's Office — the independent body that investigates and prosecutes crimes against the EU budget, such as corruption or misuse of EU funds — said it searched premises in France and Belgium.

It said this was part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European Union funds by a former European Parliament group.

EPPO did not say which group was involved and said it would not publish further details for now for fear of compromising the investigation.

What did the PfE say about the searches?

PfE, meanwhile, confirmed the activity around its offices but also tried to stress its distance from the case since its rebrand and reformation — even though its constituent political parties are largely the same with the notable exception of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) now being excluded.

"Since this morning, the European Public Prosecutor's Office has been carrying out searches in administrative offices at the European Parliament in Brussels and Strasbourg. It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy Group (ID) dissolved in 2024," it wrote in a statement.

"The Patriots for Europe Group emphasizes that there is no legal continuity with the ID Group and that it is not involved in the ongoing investigations," it said.

A French member of the European Parliament for the Rassemblement National or National Rally (RN) party, Jean-Paul Garraud, said that "the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy group" were targeted.

What were the details of the ID misuse of funds probe?

European Parliament auditors concluded last year that ID members had misused at least €4.3 million (roughly $4.8 million) in EU funds during the previous legislative term from 2019 to 2024.

According to their report, the money flowed to companies close to the group and to associations supporting anti-abortion campaigners.

The case was reminiscent of, but separate from, the conviction against RN leader Marine Le Pen, herself a former MEP, that for a time looked set to stifle her bid for the French presidency.

Appeals court clears way for Le Pen's presidential bid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ID group existed for one term in the European Parliament, from 2019 to 2024. It included France's RN, Germany's AfD, Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) and Italy's Lega, among other members.

It fell apart after major internal friction during the 2024 European election campaign, not least because of dissatisfaction within the group with their lead candidate Maximilian Krah of the AfD over a number of issues — from controversial remarks about Nazi Germany through to allegations of his close allies being Russian and Chinese influence, with one of Krah's aides since convicted of spying for China.

RN, FPÖ and Lega are part of the new PfE group, which claims "no legal continuity" to the dissolved ID alliance, but the AfD was not invited to join the PfE.

PfE has 85 seats in the 719-seat European Parliament, making it the third-largest group in the chamber, but a rather distant third behind the center-right European People's Party (184) and the center-left Socialists and Democrats (135).

The European Parliament relies heavily on such groupings, which try to unite political parties from various member states with broadly comparable policy positions and political alignment.

The AfD set up a much smaller splinter far-right grouping called Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), with just 27 seats, 15 of them held by the AfD.

World.title: Un negocio con muy buen olfato
World.content:
Más de la mitad de los hogares españoles cuenta con una mascota, un indicativo de la pujanza de un sector que mueve a 15.121 empresas, da trabajo a 91.700 personas y que trata de atender el creciente interés de los dueños por la calidad de vida de sus perros y gatos

Los nuevos hábitos de vida de los animales de compañía ya no caben en una tienda de mascotas tradicional... Se extienden por las clínicas veterinarias, los laboratorios farmacéuticos, las carnicerías, incluso por las guarderías y los salones de belleza. Cada vez más propietarios, o tutores, como prefieren llamarlos en el sector, tratan a sus perros y gatos como miembros de la familia y ya no buscan únicamente cubrir las necesidades básicas, sino mejorar su bienestar. Y esto se traduce en un auge del sector, explica Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance y uno de los protagonistas de este capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen. Su compañía, que comenzó en 2020 con un pequeño local cerca de la estación de Joaquín Sorolla, en Valencia, se ha especializado en hamburguesas para perros que siguen la dieta BARF (por sus siglas en inglés, biologically appropriate raw food, que significa alimento crudo biológicamente apropiado), un modelo de nutrición a partir de ingredientes frescos y crudos.

La revolución en el cuidado animal ha comenzado por la alimentación. El pienso común ha dado paso a otros que no tienen saborizantes ni colorantes artificiales, con conceptos como el NøPienso®, de la propia Wild Balance, producto en el que se observan a simple vista los ingredientes, como la carne y las verduras, y a dietas alternativas sin cereales, hipoalergénicas o que replican la de los humanos. Y recientemente se ha extendido al campo de la cosmética, para incluir productos ecológicos y con formulaciones más respetuosas con las mascotas, señala Alba Ciordia, fundadora de The Doog Life, marca ecológica que comercializa champús, dentífricos, espumas de limpieza en seco y suplementos alimenticios para perros y gatos, quien comparte protagonismo con Domingo en el pódcast de Banco Sabadell.

Cuenta Ciordia que se inició en el sector gracias a una de sus dos perritas, Claire, a la que los productos convencionales le producían reacciones cutáneas debido a la presencia de determinados ingredientes sintéticos. Encontrar alternativas no era sencillo. Por eso, Ciordia se formó en campos como la nutrición para perros y gatos y la fitoaromaterapia, un tipo de tratamientos complementarios a partir de aceites esenciales y extractos vegetales. Con ese conocimiento se embarcó en el desarrollo de soluciones junto a laboratorios especializados. Lo que comenzó como una búsqueda personal terminó por convertirse en una marca que hoy comercializa más de 30 referencias.

La conversación entre los empresarios sirve como hilo conductor para explicar un sector que hoy representa el 0,38% del producto interior bruto (PIB) español, cuenta con 15.121 empresas y da trabajo a 91.700 personas, de acuerdo a las estimaciones de la Asociación Española de la Industria y el Comercio del Sector del Animal de Compañía (AEDPAC). Su secretario general, Ignasi Solana, celebra, en conversación telefónica, el éxito de esta industria que, según él “aún se encuentra dando sus primeros pasos”.

“El subsector de la alimentación natural y de los cuidados naturales ha crecido mucho más rápido que el resto” Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance, acerca del auge de las alternativas a las dietas habituales para perros y gatos

Las fortalezas Una industria que se expande y encuentra nuevos modelos de negocio

Un sector en expansión. El negocio del cuidado de los animales de compañía crece cada año, de acuerdo con el Informe sectorial 2026 de la Asociación Madrileña de Veterinarios de Animales de Compañía, que analiza su evolución a nivel nacional. La facturación de las clínicas veterinarias, los laboratorios farmacéuticos y los fabricantes de alimentación aumentó un 7,4% en 2025 respecto al año anterior. Una cifra similar a la que ofrece el informe Pet-money: la economía de las mascotas y su impacto en el hogar español, de EAE Business School, que cuantifica la expansión en el 8,3%. Además, el sector exporta cada año más, en 2025, el 30% del valor del mercado de la producción de alimentos fue a Europa, Magreb, América y Sudeste Asiático, destaca Santiago de Andrés, secretario general de la Asociación de Fabricante de Alimentos para Animales de Compañía (ANFAAC).

Basado en productos de primera necesidad. Se caracteriza por una demanda constante en artículos de alimentación y atención sanitaria, lo que genera actividades con ingresos recurrentes, como las suscripciones de alimentación para recibir la comida de la mascota en casa, los planes veterinarios y los seguros.

Diversificado y con enorme potencial para la innovación y la especialización. El sector se expande continuamente hacia nuevos modelos de negocio como la cosmética canina y felina, el ocio y los viajes. También está abierto al desarrollo de productos nuevos en campos como la nutrición especializada, la telemedicina y los dispositivos inteligentes.

Con consumidores que buscan lo mejor para los animales a su cargo. La cesta de la compra para perros y gatos cada vez se parece más a la de los humanos. A veces, incluso, la supera en calidad en determinados artículos, especialmente en los alimentos, explica Ignasi Solana, de AEDPAC. “El ejemplo más claro es que los responsables de perros y gatos apuestan por comida de marca antes que por las genéricas, conocidas como marcas blancas, porque la asocian a mayor calidad. Es un fenómeno que se extiende a otros campos como la cosmética y que nosotros denominamos como premiumización”, indica para describir la estrategia comercial que consiste en ofrecer productos o servicios que son percibidos por su presentación o su precio como de mayor calidad.

“Hay un potencial muy grande de dispositivos inteligentes para la prevención que buscan detectar cambios en la salud del animal y que ayudan al veterinario” Alba Ciordia, fundadora de The Doog Life, sobre las posibilidades de innovación dentro de la industria

Los desafios El reto de luchar contra la pseudociencia y multiplicar los espacios para mascotas

Luchar contra la desinformación. Internet y, en especial, las redes sociales han multiplicado la información que reciben los propietarios o tutores, lo que puede generar confusión y dificulta la capacidad para distinguir los contenidos basados en evidencia científica, en publicidad, en opinión o en pseudociencia. Santiago de Andrés, de ANFAAC, señala que aún hay margen de mejora en la comunicación entre veterinarios y tutores, con datos precisos y basados en ciencia.

Atender a la sostenibilidad. La fabricación de alimentos implica un gran consumo de recursos a través de la producción ganadera. Además, genera gran cantidad de emisiones contaminantes. Los piensos, aperitivos y productos de higiene requieren de envases plásticos muchas veces difíciles de reciclar. La industria ya trabaja en proteínas alternativas y en el aprovechamiento de productos de la industria alimentaria para desarrollar formulaciones de menor impacto. Igualmente, investiga nuevos métodos de almacenamiento y distribución de los productos que permitan reciclar y reutilizar envases.

Potenciar la digitalización. La modernización del sector requiere un avance en dos de sus patas, señala Solana, de Aedpac. Por un lado, las tiendas de artículos para mascotas, como las pajarerías, habitualmente negocios familiares, están hoy en manos de la segunda o la tercera generación de comerciantes que afrontan paulatinamente la digitalización de sus sistemas y el desarrollo de sus comercios electrónicos. Por otro, la irrupción de la telemedicina y los dispositivos inteligentes abren nuevas oportunidades en el sector sanitario, pero requieren de grandes inversiones.

Contribuir a la creación de espacios adaptados a las mascotas. En España, señala Solana, aún hay mucho recorrido para convertir los lugares públicos en sitios propicios para el acceso con animales de compañía. La Ley de Bienestar Animal establece que hoteles, bares y restaurantes, entre otros establecimientos, pueden permitir su entrada y, en caso de no admitirlos, han de indicarlo en el exterior de manera visible. Solana es uno de los promotores del certificado ITVET, un protocolo de inspección técnica organizado por una empresa privada que acredita las buenas prácticas para facilitar la presencia y el tránsito de animales de compañía en instalaciones que se definen como pet-friendly (aptas para mascotas).

“Europa es mucho más ‘pet friendly’ en general que España” Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance, sobre la presencia de animales de compañía en comercios y en el transporte público

World.title: Feyenoord second best to Betis as Isco is on the spot for CL win
World.content:
Feyenoord endured a frustrating evening in Spain as a penalty by Real Betis’s outstanding player, Isco, secured a 1-0 win for the La Liga side.

The Rotterdammers were second best for most of the game, but held out until the 59th minute, when Abde Ezzalzouli’s cross hit the arm of Jeremiah St. Juste in front of goal.

Isco, who was at the heart of Betis’s attacks all evening, grabbed the ball and gave Tjark Ernst no chance from the penalty spot.

Ernst had made good saves from former AZ Alkmaar striker Troy Parrott and Marc Batra to keep Feyenoord in the game in the first half, but Feyenoord had the best chance of the opening period when Gjivai Zechiël shot over the bar from close range.

The visitors had a claim for a penalty of their own turned down in the 68th minute when Givairo Read claimed he had been pushed by Ezzalzouli, but referee Simone Sozza waved the appeals away.

The result leaves Giovanni van Bronckhorst’s side in 26th place in the Champions League table, with Internazionale up next in De Kuip on November 3.

World.content:
