World.title: DFA to China embassy: Escalatory, undiplomatic posts not helping bilateral ties
World.content:
SUMMON. DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro summons Chinese ambassador Jing Quan on October 19, days after he made a barely-veiled threat against the Philippines in a media interview.

‘The recent public statements of the Embassy do not reflect the longstanding spirit of constructive engagement between the two countries and the two foreign ministries,’ the DFA says

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines on Thursday, October 22, called out the Chinese embassy in Manila for the “escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language” in their social media posts that “erode mutual trust and confidence” as the online word war between the embassy and various Philippine agencies and officials continues to intensity.

“[The DFA] firmly reminds all diplomats accredited to the Philippines to exercise restraint and responsibility in their public statements. The escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language used in the latest social media statements of the Chinese Embassy erode mutual trust and confidence, and severely undermines the efforts to stabilize and improve bilateral relations,” said the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) in a statement, their second since Chinese ambassador to Manila Jing Quan said on October 15 that Filipino should be grateful that Beijing doesn’t use force in its disputes with Manila.

“All diplomats are expected to conduct and express themselves in a manner befitting diplomatic envoys, especially on social media,” added the DFA.

Jing’s statement and the social media posts of the embassy he heads were the subject of an October 19 summon by Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro.

The Chinese ambassador’s October 15 statement has triggered a maelstrom in the Philippines, with several legislators filing resolutions urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr or the DFA to either kick Jing out or ask China to recall him as envoy. In response, the embassy has taunted legislators in posts on social media.

Since Jing arrived in Manila in December 2025, the Chinese embassy had taken on a decidedly more provocative tone in its social media posts, sparring with Philippine government spokspersons and elected officials who criticized China’s actions in the West Philippine Sea.

One China Policy

The DFA, in its statement, said the Philippines adheres to the One China Policy, in response to a post by the embassy asking the department to clarify the Philippine position after a verified Facebook account linked to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. reposted a list of areas where China has disputes with, to include self-governed Taiwan.

In that post, the embassy said Teodoro was “openly challenging” the “One China principle” — which Manila does not adhere to, in the first place. Adherence to the One China Principle means that a country, in starting diplomatic ties with Beijing, recognizes the legitimacy of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as the sole governing body of the country and agrees with its position that Taiwan is a part of China.

In contrast, under One China Policy which Manila follows, there is just acknowledgment of the PRC’s position that Taiwan is a part of China. Manila, of course, recognizes the PRC as the sole government of China.

In response to recent postings on social media, the DFA reaffirmed the Philippines’ continued adherence to its One China Policy, anchored on the 1975 Philippines-China Joint Communique.

The 1975 Philippines-China Joint Communique, which established diplomatic ties between the two Asian nations, “underscores [the Philippines’] consistent position that the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government of China, and that we fully understand and respect the position of the Chinese Government that there is but one China and that Taiwan is an integral part of Chinese territory,” said the DFA.

It added: “Throughout the years, the Philippines’ relevant regulations reflect the country’s unwavering implementation of its One China Policy.”

The One China policy means that while Manila has no diplomatic relations with Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, it maintains cultural and trade ties with Taipei. – Rappler.com

World.title: The tree Quezon planted, and Bacolod nearly forgot
World.content:
QUEZON'S TREE. Bacolod's only surviving tindalo tree, planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon at the city plaza 88 years ago, is still standing tall and healthy.

The endangered tree was planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon on October 19, 1938, to mark Bacolod's proclamation as a chartered city

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – It had survived World War II, the city’s worst fire in the 1950s and generations of powerful typhoons. Yet for decades, a tree planted by one of the key figures in Philippine history stood in the heart of Bacolod, its history fading from public memory.

The endangered tindalo (Afzelia rhomboidea) was planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon on October 19, 1938, to mark Bacolod’s proclamation as a chartered city. Quezon, the country’s first president of the Commonwealth, was a central figure in the campaign for Philippine independence from the United States and in the creation of institutions that would shape the country before independence.

The tree was a living link to that chapter of Philippine history. But its story had become almost as obscure as its species.

NEW MARKER. Bacolod City and Negros Occidental Historical Council officials lead the unveiling of the replacement marker for the tindalo tree at the Bacolod Public Plaza. Bacolod PIO

Enclosed by a rustic steel gate in the city’s now-controversial public plaza, the tree had lost much of its public identity. Its brass marker, once meant to preserve the story of its planting, had long since become illegible. During the plaza’s controversial redevelopment which started in January of last year, the marker was reportedly stolen, further severing the connection between the tree and the event it was planted to commemorate.

Planted 88 years ago by a president who helped steer the Philippines toward self-government, the tindalo had nearly become a stranger in its own home, a silent witness to Bacolod’s history, standing in a 99-year-old plaza while the story of its own place in that history slipped from view.

Then came the controversy over the P80-million redevelopment of the plaza by the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA), a project that included the cutting of trees. Officials of the Negros Occidental Historical Council (NOHC) were alarmed when they learned that the brass marker identifying the historic tree had been stolen.

The redevelopment was part of a P300-million tourism project intended to improve public spaces in the city. Instead, the project became a source of frustration, with work unfinished and questions mounting over construction quality, public safety and the treatment of a historic landmark.

City hall said it would not sign the project’s acceptance documents, citing defects and safety hazards that it asserted had to be addressed before the local government could accept the work.

But the dispute was about more than unfinished construction given that the public plaza is a designated national historical landmark, putting the redevelopment under scrutiny over whether it complied with heritage-preservation laws and followed the original project proposals.

“We felt very sad knowing the reports of a stolen marker, and so we checked and we found it was for the historic tindalo tree planted by ex-president Quezon,” NOHC president Solomon Locsin told Rappler on Tuesday, October 20.

The council decided to replace the marker with black granite engraved with historical details to prevent it from being stolen again.

On Monday, October 19, the 88th anniversary of the proclamation of Bacolod as a chartered city, the marker was reinstalled in a simple ceremony commemorating Quezon’s planting of the tree and its place in the city’s history.

The ceremony did not have much fanfare although it featured a reenactment of Quezon planting the tree and brief messages from Locsin, Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya and Councilor Wilson “Jun” Gamboa Jr., chairman of the City Council’s committee on history.

Locsin said Bacolod was fortunate to have a historic tree planted by a former Philippine president.

Under Department of Environment and Natural Resources Administrative Order No. 2017-11, tindalo is classified as an endangered species in the Philippines.

Called balayong in Bacolod and Negros Occidental, only a few trees of the species can be found in the Campuestohan area of Talisay City, part of the protected Northern Negros Natural Park, according to Randy James Rojo, founder of the nonprofit Group of Environmental Socialists (GOES).

Gamboa said he was glad that the NOHC provided a new marker for what he described as Bacolod’s only known surviving tindalo tree, saying it would help younger generations recognize its historical and environmental significance.

Gasataya, meanwhile, said city hall will protect the tree, including its new marker.

“I hope that [the] collective memory of the community will be recast for the younger generations to appreciate the history of Bacolod plaza, which is celebrating its centennial next year,” Locsin said. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Play Video

LATEST UPDATES

World.title: [Puso at Diwa] Sara Duterte trial: Is the space for political impunity finally closing?
World.content:
Can the Philippines begin to turn the corner from a culture of impunity toward one of responsibility and the rule of law?

The decision of the House prosecution panel to drop three of the four articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte and concentrate on alleged unexplained wealth marks a consequential turn in a case that could shape the country’s political future well beyond 2028.

The prosecution believes that the remaining charge, covering alleged unexplained wealth, violations of the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) requirements, and prohibited business interests, is sufficiently supported by evidence to warrant her removal from office. By streamlining the trial, prosecutors hope to prevent procedural delays from dragging the proceedings into the presidential election season, when political calculations could overwhelm the merits of the case.

The strategy has its risks.

Dropping the allegations concerning confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats from the impeachment trial may shorten proceedings, but it also raises a legitimate question: will the public see this as a sharper, more focused prosecution or as an abandonment of issues that demand accountability? The answer will depend partly on what happens next.

True, the withdrawal of impeachment charges does not, by itself, establish innocence or extinguish any criminal liability that may arise from the underlying acts. The prosecution has committed to making its evidence available to the Office of the Ombudsman, which has expressed interest in examining the confidential-fund allegations. This is particularly important because the House committee on good government and public accountability had already investigated the questioned expenditures and submitted its findings to the Ombudsman in 2024. The Commission on Audit’s (COA) final denial of the motion for reconsideration concerning ₱73.287 million in disallowed confidential expenses of the Office of the Vice President adds another significant development to the public record. These matters deserve an independent, evidence-based determination rather than being allowed to disappear with the withdrawal of an impeachment article.

The implications extend beyond the fate of one public official.

In September, the Supreme Court declared that Congress’ failure over 39 years to enact an anti-political dynasty law constituted grave abuse of discretion. The ruling was a forceful reminder that constitutional obligations cannot be indefinitely postponed to protect political convenience or entrenched interests. Although Congress retains discretion over the law’s specific provisions, it cannot simply disregard the constitutional mandate to prohibit political dynasties. Together, these developments expose a central weakness of Philippine governance: formal institutions and constitutional safeguards may exist, yet their effectiveness depends on whether those entrusted with public power are willing to enforce them.

The stakes for Vice President Duterte are substantial. A conviction in the impeachment trial could result in her removal from office and disqualification from holding public office, jeopardizing her potential presidential bid in 2028. Separately, an Ombudsman investigation could lead to criminal charges and, if a competent court ultimately finds her guilty, imprisonment. These are distinct proceedings, with different purposes, evidentiary requirements, and consequences. Neither outcome should be presumed.

Duterte is entitled to due process and the opportunity to answer the allegations, just as the public is entitled to a credible accounting of public funds and the impartial enforcement of the law. The principle is simple: neither political prominence nor political vulnerability should determine the outcome.

There is, moreover, a broader question of institutional respect. Vice President Duterte is within her rights to be represented by counsel and to decide whether to appear personally before the Senate impeachment court. Her absence should not, in itself, be interpreted as an admission of wrongdoing or a violation of the law.

Yet legal rights and respect for constitutional institutions are not mutually exclusive. When public appearances and press conferences appear to be directed more toward discrediting the Senate, attacking individual personalities, or challenging the legitimacy of the proceedings than toward addressing the substance of the allegations, the distinction between defending oneself and undermining an institution becomes blurred.

Public officials need not agree with every action of an investigating body, and they are entitled to challenge its decisions through lawful remedies. But the credibility of constitutional government suffers when its highest officials appear to demand accountability from others while showing little regard for the institutions through which accountability must be pursued.

Meaningful accountability

The issue is not whether the Vice President must submit to public opinion, but whether political influence is being used to strengthen the rule of law or to weaken public confidence in it.

What signals are these developments sending to the country?

For years, the perception that powerful political families and influential officials could evade meaningful accountability has weakened public confidence in government. When investigations stall, constitutional mandates remain unfulfilled, and allegations involving public money fail to reach a credible conclusion, impunity becomes more than a failure of enforcement. It becomes a governing culture. It tells ordinary citizens that the rules may be strict for some and negotiable for others.

We may now be approaching a turning point, but it would be premature to declare victory. The impeachment court must assess the evidence fairly and independently. The Ombudsman must determine whether the available records justify criminal proceedings and pursue them without fear or favor. Congress must comply with the Supreme Court’s directive on political dynasties rather than find new reasons for delay. And all institutions must demonstrate that accountability is not merely a weapon deployed against political opponents, but a consistent obligation of public service.

Ultimately, the measure of progress is not whether Sara Duterte wins or loses her political contest. It is whether the country establishes a more durable standard of public accountability, one in which unexplained wealth is properly examined, confidential funds are subject to meaningful safeguards, constitutional duties are fulfilled, and allegations against powerful officials are resolved on their merits.

If these processes are pursued with integrity, the Philippines could begin to turn the corner from a culture of impunity toward one of responsibility and the rule of law. If they falter once again, the message will be that even the most serious questions of public trust can be subordinated to political survival. – Rappler.com

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.

He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

He also serves as principal advisor for New York-based GlobalSourcePartners. He remains in the advisory board of ASEAN Macroeconomic Research Office and Singapore Management University’s Sim Kee Boon Institute for Financial Economics.

He is the senior pastor of the Fullness of Christ International Ministries in Mandaluyong.

World.title: Intense rain possible in Batanes even as Super Typhoon Rosal weakens further
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 22, 2026, 4 am.

Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon, October 22, and Friday morning, October 23

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) weakened further while moving east of Batanes before dawn on Thursday, October 22, but it remains a powerful tropical cyclone.

In a bulletin issued at 5 am on Thursday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Rosal’s maximum sustained winds slightly decreased from 205 kilometers per hour to 195 km/h. Its gustiness eased from 250 km/h to 240 km/h.

At its peak, Rosal had maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h. PAGASA’s latest forecast shows it is likely to be downgraded to a typhoon on Thursday.

As of 4 am, Rosal was already 495 kilometers east of Basco, Batanes, moving northwest at 20 km/h.

It remains unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, October 23.

On Thursday, moderate to intense rain may hit at least three provinces in Northern Luzon. Here is the weather bureau’s updated rainfall outlook for the next 48 hours, also released at 5 am:

Thursday, October 22

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan, Apayao

Friday, October 23

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan

Aside from the provinces mentioned above, Ilocos Norte and Isabela are also likely to have rain with gusty winds from Rosal on Thursday.

The rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Bicol, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Aurora, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar may have scattered rain and thunderstorms as well, still due to the super typhoon.

PAGASA added that Rosal’s trough or extension might cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Zamboanga Peninsula, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan.

Winds from the super typhoon are already reaching portions of Northern Luzon, too. Tropical cyclone wind signals are in effect in the following areas as of 5 am on Thursday:

Signal No. 2

Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property

Batanes

northeastern part of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan Island)

Signal No. 1

Strong winds (39 to 61 km/h), minimal to minor threat to life and property

rest of Babuyan Islands

mainland Cagayan

eastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)

Ilocos Norte

Apayao

Signal No. 3 could be raised in Batanes, unless Rosal’s track shifts further north northwest.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Thursday, October 22

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Northern Mindanao, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Saturday, October 24

Batanes, Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Capiz, Iloilo, Negros Occidental

Conditions in affected seaboards are worsening further on Thursday. Waves in Batanes could reach 12 meters or around 39 feet high.

Up to very rough, high, or very high seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes – waves up to 12 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Batanes; seaboards of Babuyan Islands; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 9 meters high

Remaining seaboards of mainland Cagayan; seaboard of northern Isabela – waves up to 7 meters high

Northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte; remaining seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 6 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 5.5 meters high

Seaboards of northern Ilocos Sur and northern Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands and Catanduanes; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Remaining seaboard of Aurora; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon; northern seaboard of Northern Samar – waves up to 4 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Ilocos Sur and Northern Samar; western seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboards of La Union and Eastern Samar – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands, Siargao-Bucas Grande Islands, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Oriental; remaining eastern seaboard of Quezon; remaining seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboard of Zambales; western seaboards of Bataan and Batangas; northern and western seaboards of Lubang Islands; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Rosal might exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.

After leaving PAR, Rosal is likely to be downgraded to a severe tropical storm on Saturday.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations
World.content:
Unprogrammed funds are here to stay, but they will ideally be harder to abuse

The Supreme Court decision that voided congressional increases in past national budgets, including in the highly controversial unprogrammed appropriations, vindicates watchdogs and critics who have repeatedly warned against government officials’ manipulation of the national spending plan.

But what does the High Court ruling mean moving forward?

Rappler breaks down the impact of the decision on our historically corruption-ridden budget process.

1. Unprogrammed appropriations are here to stay, but they will ideally be harder to abuse.

The Supreme Court is clear in its press release: unprogrammed appropriations, in general, are not unconstitutional.

UA provide flexibility for the president to “adequately respond” to unforeseen circumstances, such as foreign-assisted programs that are not yet approved when the budget plan is drafted, but likely to be approved in the coming fiscal year.

The High Court, however, is insisting on providing safeguards to keep spending of the executive branch in check.

This means that if UA will be used for more than one purpose, Congress must clearly lay out the prioritization order.

The Supreme Court also called out the legislative branch for failing to be transparent during its bicameral committee deliberations. It said past budget bicams had no record of discussions and reports explaining adjustments in budget items.

Its call for transparency in Congress will echo through the halls of the House and the Senate. In the wake of the ruling’s release, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto already promised livestreamed bicam deliberations for the proposed 2027 budget.

2. Unprogrammed appropriations should no longer be treated like a blank check by the executive.

In past years, unprogrammed appropriations essentially became a blank check for the executive.

The Supreme Court singled out the line item Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP) that was lodged under UA; it had no breakdown in the signed General Appropriations Act. This gave the executive the power to identify beneficiaries even though the budget is already being enacted, and even though that is supposed to be Congress’ responsibility.

The Supreme Court called the UA a “covert repository of lump sum allocations for DPWH [Department of Public Works and Highways] infrastructure,” paving the way for the flood control corruption scandal.

Marcos himself signed off on the Department of Budget and Management’s UA releases for DPWH projects through Special Allotment Release Orders. These releases did not undergo public oversight, and insiders said executive officials and legislators negotiated privately to insert and move project items.

In short, unprogrammed appropriations have become pork.

Now, the Supreme Court is clear: there should be no lump sums in the UA.

Play Video

3. Congress can no longer use UA to circumvent the constitutional rule that it cannot increase the president’s proposed national budget.

Section 25(1) of the 1987 Constitution reads: “Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the government as specified in the budget.”

This means that if the executive asked for P4 trillion only, Congress can only give them P4 trillion or lower — not P5 trillion, not P4.5 trillion, not P4.1 trillion.

Congress found a workaround, believing that the constitutional ceiling only applied to programmed, but not unprogrammed, appropriations.

Take the 2024 budget for example. The executive sought P4.019 trillion in programmed funds, so Congress seemingly complied with that limit and approved that exact amount. The UA that year, however, ballooned from the original request of P281.9 billion to the approved P731.45 billion.

The P449.5-billion jump, the Supreme Court ruled, is unconstitutional.

Why did Congress spike the funding for UA? In the Supreme Court’s words, Congress created an “artificial fiscal space” in the programmed appropriations for financial aid programs — ayuda projects that budget watchdogs have criticized as lawmakers’ pork barrel — by shifting funds for projects that should have been programmed, such as the Metro Manila Subway and MRT-4, to unprogrammed appropriations.

Additionally, the Supreme Court struck down Congress’ decision to increase the proposed programmed appropriations of the President by P17.99 billion, through the Special Road Fund, in the 2025 budget.

Congress can no longer do that in future budgets, because the Supreme Court said the constitutional ceiling “applies to the total appropriations, both programmed and unprogrammed.”

4. The use of unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 budget has just become tougher.

The current budget in effect is the 2026 General Appropriations Act. It’s also not spared from the Supreme Court ruling.

The High Court struck down two conditions that Congress had set in activating unprogrammed appropriations.

For example, just because the Bureau of the Treasury collected more than its target from a particular non-tax revenue source does not automatically mean the government can release unprogrammed funds. The government’s total revenue collections must exceed the overall target set in the budget. It is unclear whether that threshold has been met.

Aside from that, unprogrammed funds in the 2026 budget can be used only when loans for foreign-assisted projects are approved.

Now that congressional increases for the 2024 and 2025 GAA have been declared unconstitutional, what happens to the money that had already been spent?

The Supreme Court said the doctrine of operative fact applies. This means completed programs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith won’t be undone.

“The Court acknowledges that the unprogrammed appropriations under the 2024 GAA…have already funded numerous government programs and projects with far-reaching effects. The Court is mindful that Filipinos have already benefited from these laws and that the difficulties that would be borne by the public far outweigh a rigid insistence on their legal nullity,” the ruling read.

However, the doctrine does not provide immunity from criminal, civil, or administrative liability to budget authors, proponents, or implementors.

The SC, in the landmark decision, either partially or fully ruled in favor of four group of petitioners.

The petition of the late congressman Edcel Lagman listed as respondents then-Senate president Juan Miguel Zubiri, then-speaker Martin Romualdez, then-budget chairpersons Sonny Angara and Zaldy Co, then-executive secretary Lucas Bersamin, then-DBM chief Amenah Pangandaman, and then-treasurer Rosalia de Leon.

The petition of former senator Koko Pimentel and former congressman Pantaleon Alvarez listed Bersamin and Pangandaman as respondents.

The petition of Filipinos for Peace, Justice, and Progress Movement, Inc. listed Romualdez, then-Senate president Tito Sotto, Bersamin, and the DBM as respondents.

The petition of House lawmakers Edgar Erice and Leila de Lima listed then-Senate president Tito Sotto, House Speaker Bojie Dy, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, and then-DBM secretary Rolando Toledo as respondents.

Holding the people behind the unconstitutional budget provisions is an uphill battle though, constitutional lawyer Dan Gatmaytan said in the podcast of former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno.

“I cannot imagine what criminal case you would file in this situation. This is not technical malversation,” Gatmaytan explained. “Technical malversation occurs when you use money appropriated for one purpose for something else. That is not what happened here. They are still in the process of appropriating the funds.”

“Does it extend to the President? Still no, because of immunity,” Gatmaytan added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Part 1: New candidates in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice
World.content:
This batch of new applicants is composed of big names, like COA chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba and Sandiganbayan chief Geraldine Faith Econg, among others

First of 2 parts

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will pick his second Supreme Court (SC) associate justice appointee in November.

This is for the position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier who is set to retire on November 16. This will be Marcos’ second appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025.

So far, there are 19 applicants in total, majority of whom are incumbent government officials.

The Judicial and Bar Council — tasked to screen the candidates and submit a short list of nominees to Marcos — divided the bets into two categories.

New applicants attended the public interviews on October 13 and 15, while the old bets no longer took part in the event because their past interviews are still valid.

Get to know the new candidates vying to replace Associate Justice Lazaro Javier below.

1. Aldwin Alegre

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Deputy Commissioner, Bureau of Immigration (BI)

Appointed by former president Rodrigo Duterte to the BI in January 2019, replacing former Commission on Elections (Comelec) commissioner Aimee Torrefranca Neri.

Admitted to the Bar on April 30, 2007, with Roll No. 53915.

He is a Certified Public Accountant (CPA).

Inside the BI, he sat as Bids and Awards Committee chairperson, and then as head of the bureau’s COVID-19 Task Force.

Alegre is also a movie producer, and as he calls himself, a cameo actor.

In 2022, a Manila Bulletin article identified him as president and chief executive officer of AQ Prime, a streaming and entertainment platform.

Alegre is the producer of the film “Nelia,” a suspense and thriller movie starring Wynwyn Marquez. It was an entry to the 2021 Metro Manila Film Festival.

Alegre’s AQ Prime is also behind the P-pop group, “Bilib.”

2. Jason Barlis

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Chairperson, Legal Education Board (LEB).

LEB is a government agency mandated to oversee the country’s legal education and system, as well as to supervise and accredit law schools in the Philippines.

Barlis is a senior partner at Oracion Barlis and Associates law firm.

According to his profile, he is also a certified public accountant and had served at Saint Louis University (SLU) in Baguio City in different capacities.

He was SLU’s vice president for administration from 2016 to 2020, then as dean of SLU School of Law from 2014 to 2016. Barlis was also the former head of SLU’s Department of Remedial Law and Legal Ehics, as well as the Department of Commercial and Taxation Laws.

Barlis has taught Taxation, Commercial, and Remedial Laws.

The LEB chairperson is an alumnus of SLU through and through.

He obtained his accountancy degree from the university, graduating cum laude. He became a CPA in 1997. He obtained his law degree from SLU and graduated cum laude and class valedictorian.

Barlis was admitted to the Bar in May 2002, with Roll No. 46627.

While taking up law, Barlis worked as a court legal researcher at La Trinidad, Benguet Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 62.

As a lawyer, Barlis has handled cases that range from civil, criminal, administrative, labor, and even corporate and tax.

3. Lily Biton

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Current Court of Appeals (CA) 21st Division chairperson. Appointed to the appellate court by Duterte on July 10, 2019.

Biton, according to her profile from the Central Philippine University (CPU) based in Iloilo City, started her career as a senior lawyer, court attorney, and executive clerk of court at the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan.

In 2009, she was picked as presiding judge of San Mateo-Rodriguez, Rizal RTC Branch 77.

Biton earned her biology degree in 1982 and then her law degree in 1986 from CPU. She also earned 33 units of Master of Laws from the University of Santo Tomas.

According to her profile, she received awards such as the Chief Justice Award for Outstanding Service in the Judiciary, the Distinguished Centralian Award in Government Service/Judiciary, and the Most Outstanding Alumna Award of the CPU College of Arts and Science, among others.

She also does volunteer work for the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City. The CA associate justice is also a musician and song writer who is behind the lyrics of the Sandiganbayan hymn.

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Presiding Justice of the Sandiganbayan. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed her on January 7, 2025, replacing retired presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje Tang.

Econg has been sitting as Sandiganbayan associate justice and is currently the chairperson of the anti-graft court’s 2nd Division. The late former president Benigno Aquino III appointed her to the said court in January 2016.

She applied for the position of Ombudsman in 2025, but ultimately lost to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla. In 2014, she was shortlisted by the JBC for the Deputy Ombudsman for the Visayas position.

Econg, before her Sandiganbayan stint, was the presiding judge of Cebu City RTC Branch 9. She also headed some Municipal Trial Courts in Cities.

The SC applicant is among the Sandiganbayan justices who are part of some controversial rulings.

In 2018, she was one of the justices who voted to acquit former senator Bong Revilla of plunder in relation to the scam. “It is an unpopular decision. I would have loved to be a heroine, that I convicted him, but at the end of the day we are bound by evidence,” Econg said after the promulgation of the ruling that freed Revilla.

She was also among the justices who dismissed the pork barrel-related plunder case of the late former senator Juan Ponce Enrile in 2024.

Econg also authored the ruling that dismissed the last six coconut levy cases against late tyrant Ferdinand E. Marcos, former first lady Imelda Marcos, Enrile, businessmen Cesar Zalamea and Jesus Pineda, and the heirs of former Zamboanga mayor Maria Clara Lobregat.

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Current chairperson of the Commission on Audit. He was appointed by Marcos in October 2022.

He is a member of Fraternal Order of Utopia. Served as an undersecretary at the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Political Affairs, under the Office of the President. He also used to work as a board member of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

Cordoba is a long-time commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), having served since the administration of former president Gloria Arroyo in 2009. In 2016, under Duterte, he was able to retain his post in the commission.

It was under him when the Duterte government pushed for the shutdown of media giant ABS-CBN.

Under Cordoba, the Duterte government also pushed for the blocking of the website of alternative news site Bulatlat. Before the end of Duterte’s term, then national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. requested “Philippine Internet Service Providers to block access” to several sites, including Bulatlat. The alternative media’s website was later unblocked after the news site won against the NTC and Esperon in court.

A Rappler investigation revealed that Cordoba is married to Monica Elena Cordoba, whose family partly owns the commercial fishing company Mercidar Fishing Corporation. In 2024, the SC affirmed the decision of a Malabon court allowing Mercidar to fish within municipal waters, an area usually designated for small fisherfolk.

Under Cordoba, the NTC did not issue service identity numbers essential for the system that tracks commercial vessels at sea.

6. Solomon Hermosura

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Government Corporate Counsel since March 4, 2024.

Before his stint at the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel (OGCC), Hermosura worked for 28 years under the Ayala Group. The OGCC is the principal law office of government-owned and controlled corporations, government instrumentalities with corporate powers, and government corporate entities.

He held the following positions under Ayala Corporation: senior managing director, chief legal officer, group head of corporate governance, corporate secretary, compliance officer, and data protection officer.

Hermosura also worked as group general counsel and corporate secretary of Ayala Land, corporate secretary and management committee member of Manila Water Company, and corporate secretary of Globe Telecom, ACEN Corporation, AREIT, Integrated Micro-Electronics, and Ayala Foundation.

He worked for nine years as a private lawyer under Roco, Buñag, Kapunan, Migallos & Jardeleza law firm, before joining the Ayala Group.

Hermosura finished his law studies at the San Beda College of Law and as valedictorian of class 1986. He placed third during the 1986 Bar Examinations. He also taught at San Beda from 1987 to 2000, and then from 2018 to 2023.

During the 2024 Bar Examinations chaired by retired Associate Justice Mario Lopez, Hermosura sat as one of the examiners for Commercial and Taxation Laws.

Hermosura also represented the OGCC during the oral arguments at the SC on the PhilHealth fund transfer issue.

7. German Lichauco II

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Senior Partner at Siguion Reyna, Montecillo, and Ongsiako Law Offices.

According to his profile at his law firm, Lichauco’s areas of expertise are the following: heinous crimes, medical malpractice, construction and commercial arbitration, personal injuries, and business tort.

Currently, he’s a member of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines Makati Chapter and the Aquila Legis Fraternity.

Lichauco also sits as a director and corporate secretary of the following companies: Hereaus Electronic Materials Philippines, Inc., Casa Cebuana, Inc., Cebu Figueroa Estate Corporation, and Coco Properties, Inc.

He is serving as compliance officer of Medical Doctors, Inc., the company that manages Makati Medical Center Hospital. He is also the corporate secretary of Orca Energy, Inc., a power corporation owned by RollsRoyce Power Ventures Limited, and Island Power Corporation.

Lichauco earned his law degree from Ateneo with honors in 1991. He was admitted to the Bar in 1993, with Roll No. 38552.

The aspiring SC justice was part of the defense team of the late former chief justice Renato Corona during his 2012 impeachment trial.

In 2023, Marcos named Lichauco as director of the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC), which governs the country’s first sovereign wealth fund. Lichauco’s name is no longer included in the list of MIC directors as of writing.

Supreme Court of the Philippines

Current commissioner of the Commission on Elections, with a fixed term of seven years (2022 to 2027). Appointed by Marcos to his position in October 2022.

He is the son of the late former Senate president Ernesto Maceda, who served as executive secretary of Marcos Jr.’s father, late dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.

At age 23, he was elected Manila City councilor in 1987. Five years later, at 28, he became the city’s vice mayor.

He also worked as chief of staff to former House speaker Arnulfo Fuentebella.

Maceda also has experience working under the judiciary. He was appointed by the SC to the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Governing Board, and served as Board of Trustees of the Philippine Judicial Academy.

The aspiring SC justice also taught in law school. He was the longest-serving dean of the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (PLM), and later served as PLM’s executive vice president. He served as president of the Philippine Association of Law Schools, and as president of Universidad de Manila from 2015 to 2019.

He has been teaching constitutional law since 1990. He has taught in several schools, namely, Ateneo, PLM, Far Eastern University, and Arellano University.

Maceda obtained his political science degree from University of the Philippines Diliman, then his law degree from Ateneo. He also obtained his Master of Laws degree from Columbia University in 1996. – Rappler.com
